This prevents confounding causal attribution and addresses reviewer concerns about oxidation-state complexity.

6) Alignment to the concept chain (rigidity–hydration–binding–thermal stability) is strengthened with measurable intermediates. The plan triangulates: rigidity/dynamics (HDX/NMR), hydration (design-time penalty + MD occupancy), ligand binding energetics/kinetics (ITC + kon/koff), and thermal stability (DSF/DSC), all benchmarked against matched latch-off and single-state/no-latch controls. This yields interpretable, generalizable design rules for conformation-locked de novo proteins consistent with literature on thermal stability networks and water exclusion in engineered cavities.
final_critique: This is an unusually high-resolution and disciplined proposal. The strongest feature is the pre-registration of a quantitative locking thermodynamic model (ΔG_apo_lock, ΔG_holo_lock, ΔΔG_coupling) combined with explicit go/no-go criteria and matched latch-on/off causality controls. The multistate objective function is clearly bounded and avoids the common pitfall of over-constraining the folding landscape. Hydration is treated as a first-class design variable via computable penalties, not merely an MD narrative, which directly addresses a long-standing weakness in cavity design literature. Logical consistency is high: the proposal cleanly separates thermodynamic stabilization from kinetic accessibility and explicitly anticipates over-locking failure modes. Minor weaknesses include reliance on Rosetta/implicit solvation proxies whose transferability to finely tuned water exclusion is still imperfect, and some risk that the assumed two-state open/closed model oversimplifies helix-bundle breathing modes at elevated temperature. However, these risks are acknowledged and partially mitigated by high-T ensemble constraints and experimental iteration rules.

original_chain: Hepatotoxicity -> Albumin (ALB) -> Hepatotoxicity -> Nonclinical drug development -> CYP3A4 -> Hepatocyte-like cell -> Transcription factor
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Hepatotoxicity prediction in nonclinical drug development will be improved by engineering iPSC-derived hepatocyte-like cells (HLCs) with a tunable synthetic transcription-factor circuit that (i) stabilizes hepatic identity and ALB production via CRISPRa activation of the endogenous HNF4α program and (ii) independently gates CYP3A4 induction through an orthogonal, chemically induced recruitment system at validated CYP3A4 distal enhancers. Mechanistically, this design overcomes two key confounders in conventional HLCs: (1) apparent “ALB–CYP3A4 coupling” is often an artifact because intracellular toxic exposure is governed by unbound drug concentrations (fu,media and fu,cell), uptake/efflux transporters, and nonspecific binding in the assay format rather than HLC-secreted ALB alone; therefore, we will decouple ALB secretion from exposure by independently titrating exogenous human serum albumin (HSA) and directly measuring unbound drug in media and cells (LC–MS-based). (2) PXR promiscuity makes ligand-gating via engineered PXR LBD high risk; instead, orthogonal chemical gating (e.g., FRB/FKBP with rapalog) will control recruitment of a coactivator domain to dCas9 localized at CYP3A4 enhancers, enabling selective, reversible CYP3A4 induction without activation by test compounds. With these controls, we will establish a quantitative exposure-toxicity (PK/PD) framework linking unbound intracellular exposure (Cu,cell) and CYP3A4 activity to toxicity phenotypes (ALT/AST release, mitochondrial stress), thereby revealing CYP3A4-dependent liabilities (e.g., troglitazone) that are masked when HLCs have low/variable CYP3A4 or when albumin-related binding is not explicitly modeled.
Plan: Step 0 — System definition, cell sources, and experimental design
0.1 iPSC lines: Use ≥3 genetically distinct iPSC donor lines (balanced sex where possible) to quantify donor-to-donor variability. Predefine a randomization/blinding plan for toxicity assays.
0.2 Benchmark reference: Include primary human hepatocytes (PHHs; ≥2 cryopreserved donors) as a functional benchmark for ALB secretion, CYP3A4 activity, and transcriptomic fidelity.
0.3 Culture exposure controls: Implement a fixed medium volume-to-cell number ratio across conditions to stabilize binding and concentration dynamics; predefine HSA supplementation series (0, 5, 20, 40 mg/mL) to bracket physiological albumin.

Step 1 — Baseline HLC differentiation and baseline phenotyping
1.1 Differentiation: Differentiate iPSCs to HLCs using an established stepwise protocol (definitive endoderm → hepatic progenitor → HLC maturation). Lock the final maturation window (e.g., days 18–28) as the engineering/testing window.
1.2 Baseline phenotyping (per donor line):
- Secreted proteins: ALB secretion rate (ELISA; ng/10^6 cells/day).
- Enzyme activity: CYP3A4 activity (midazolam 1′-hydroxylation and/or luciferin-IPA assay) with LC–MS confirmation of metabolites.
- Gene expression: qPCR and RNA-seq for HNF4A, ALB, PXR (NR1I2), CAR (NR1I3), CYP3A4, CYP3A7, and uptake/efflux transporters relevant to exposure (e.g., SLCO1B1/1B3, ABCB1, ABCC2).
- Morphology/viability: albumin immunostaining, bile canaliculi marker (MRP2) if applicable.

Step 2 — Circuit architecture selection (two-module design) and delivery specifics
2.1 Module A (hepatic identity / ALB module): CRISPRa activation of endogenous hepatic program via dCas9-VPR (or dCas9-p300core as a secondary option) targeting the endogenous HNF4A regulatory landscape and optionally additional hepatic maturation nodes.
- Integration: Single-copy safe-harbor integration (AAVS1 or CCR5) using Bxb1/phiC31 landing-pad strategy to normalize copy number across clones. Confirm single-copy by ddPCR.
- Promoter: Doxycycline-inducible promoter (TRE3G) driving dCas9-activator to tune activation amplitude; rtTA integrated separately at safe-harbor for uniform induction.
2.2 Module B (CYP3A4 gating module; orthogonal chemical recruitment):
- Core concept: Avoid PXR LBD promiscuity by replacing ligand-gated PXR with chemically induced dimerization (CID) that recruits a transcriptional coactivator only upon addition of an orthogonal small molecule.
- Implementation (primary): dCas9 fused to FRB targeted to CYP3A4 enhancers + FKBP fused to a coactivator domain (e.g., p65-HSF1 or VPR fragment). Add rapalog (AP21967) to induce FRB/FKBP dimerization and coactivator recruitment specifically at CYP3A4 enhancers.
- Implementation (backup): ABI/PYL + abscisic acid (ABA) as a second orthogonal CID pair if rapalog perturbs mTOR signaling in HLCs.
- Integration: Safe-harbor integration for both CID components, with constitutive low-level expression (EF1α short or PGK) and CID-controlled activity.
2.3 Multiplex gRNA design rules and tiling strategy
- HNF4A targeting: 6–12 gRNAs tiled across published/validated HNF4A promoter/enhancer regions (prioritize high-accessibility ATAC-seq peaks in HLCs; exclude sequences with high off-target scores). Use a pooled screen (small multiplex sets) to identify minimal gRNA set that yields maximal ALB and hepatic gene induction with minimal transcriptome disruption.
- CYP3A4 targeting: 8–16 gRNAs tiled across validated CYP3A4 distal regulatory regions (e.g., XREM and proximal promoter elements known to mediate xenobiotic response). Select gRNAs based on chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and H3K27ac marks in HLCs/PHHs where available.
- Delivery of gRNAs: Use a single multiplex gRNA cassette (Csy4 or tRNA-processing system) integrated into safe harbor for stable stoichiometry; alternatively lentiviral at low MOI followed by clonal selection with ddPCR copy-number normalization.

Step 3 — Engineering acceptance criteria (hard go/no-go gates)
3.1 Circuit integrity and expression
- Single-copy integration for each module (ddPCR) and stable expression over ≥21 days (flow/Western for tagged components).
- Inducibility: Dox titration yields graded activation with EC50 within predefined range; no leakiness beyond threshold.
3.2 Orthogonality / small-molecule specificity (mandatory panel and thresholds)
- Panel: Include (i) intended inducers (rapalog; and ABA if used), (ii) prototypical PXR activators (rifampicin, hyperforin), (iii) common hepatotoxicity panel compounds including planned test drugs (troglitazone, ketoconazole, acetaminophen, diclofenac, amiodarone, etc.), and (iv) solvents/vehicles.
- Readout: CYP3A4 reporter activity (endogenous CYP3A4 mRNA + enzyme activity) under each compound.
- Pass/fail thresholds:
  a) Inducer responsiveness: rapalog increases CYP3A4 activity ≥5-fold over uninduced baseline with <20% viability loss.
  b) Test-drug orthogonality: each test drug induces ≤1.3-fold CYP3A4 activity in the absence of inducer (i.e., no unintended gating).
  c) System neutrality: rapalog alone does not shift ALB secretion by >20% (to preserve modularity).
3.3 Off-target / transcriptome perturbation budget
- Controls: (i) no gRNA, (ii) non-targeting gRNA, (iii) dCas9-only (no activator), (iv) Module A only, (v) Module B only, (vi) both modules.
- RNA-seq budget: Differential expression outside targeted hepatic/xenobiotic pathways limited to a predefined threshold (e.g., <300 genes at FDR<0.05, |log2FC|>1) when comparing induced vs control, excluding intended hepatic maturation changes. If exceeded, refine gRNAs and/or reduce expression levels.

Step 4 — Quantitative exposure (PK) measurements and modeling (decouple ALB secretion from exposure)
4.1 Independent albumin control: For each engineered condition, run parallel assays with exogenous HSA titration (0–40 mg/mL) regardless of endogenous ALB secretion to explicitly set fu,media.
4.2 Measure unbound drug fractions:
- fu,media: Rapid equilibrium dialysis (RED) for each drug in each HSA condition and base medium.
- Total and unbound intracellular: Use cell lysate binding (fu,cell via equilibrium dialysis of lysate) plus measurement of total intracellular concentration (Ccell,total) by LC–MS after timed exposures; compute Cu,cell ≈ Ccell,total × fu,cell.
- Timepoints: At minimum 0.5 h, 4 h, 24 h (and 48 h for slower toxicity) to capture uptake and metabolism dynamics.
4.3 CYP3A4-dependent metabolism confirmation:
- Measure parent depletion and metabolite formation (LC–MS) ± ketoconazole to confirm CYP3A4 dependence in the engineered system.
4.4 PK/PD linkage:
- Fit hierarchical models linking Cu,cell and CYP3A4 activity (Vmax/Km proxies from probe metabolism) to toxicity endpoints; include donor line as a random effect.

Step 5 — Functional validation (ALB–CYP3A4 modularity and mechanistic decoupling)
5.1 Demonstrate modular control:
- Activate Module A (HNF4A CRISPRa) across dox doses while keeping Module B off; quantify ALB secretion, hepatic transcriptome maturation, and confirm minimal CYP3A4 induction.
- Activate Module B (CID gating) across rapalog doses while keeping Module A fixed; quantify CYP3A4 mRNA/activity and confirm minimal change in ALB secretion.
- Activate both to map a 2D response surface (ALB vs CYP3A4) to show tunable, interpretable control.
5.2 Compare to SCFA-matured organoids / standard HLCs:
- Include SCFA-matured iPSC liver organoids (acetate/propionate/butyrate mixture per literature) as an external maturation comparator; measure CYP3A4/CYP3A7 ratio and ALB secretion.

Step 6 — Hepatotoxicity prediction study with predefined metrics
6.1 Drug panel and powering
- Panel size: ≥20 compounds total, including ≥8 with known CYP3A4-dependent bioactivation/toxicity or CYP3A4-mediated clearance interactions, and ≥8 with CYP3A4-independent hepatotoxicity, plus negatives (non-hepatotoxic controls).
- Include troglitazone ± ketoconazole as the key mechanistic anchor; include additional DDI scenarios where CYP3A4 inhibition unmasks toxicity.
6.2 Assay design
- Conditions per compound: (i) Module B off vs on (rapalog), (ii) ± ketoconazole, (iii) HSA titration series to control fu,media.
- Toxicity readouts: ALT/AST release, ATP content, mitochondrial membrane potential, oxidative stress markers, and high-content imaging-based cytotoxicity. Capture both acute (24 h) and subacute (72 h) endpoints.
6.3 Predictive performance metrics (predefined)
- Primary classification objective: Predict “clinically relevant DILI risk” and separately “CYP3A4-dependent liability class”.
- Metrics: AUROC and AUPRC with bootstrapped 95% CIs; calibration (Brier score) for probabilistic models.
- Decision thresholds: Predefine operating point (e.g., sensitivity ≥0.85 at specificity ≥0.70) for DILI risk; for CYP3A4-dependence classify based on differential toxicity between induced vs uninduced and rescue by ketoconazole exceeding a preset effect size (e.g., ≥30% reduction in toxicity metric at matched Cu,cell).
- Robustness: Report performance across donor lines (leave-one-donor-out validation) and across experimental batches.

Step 7 — Iteration rules and failure modes
7.1 If Module B induction perturbs non-CYP3A4 genes excessively: reduce coactivator strength, narrow gRNA set, or switch to dCas9-p300core recruitment.
7.2 If rapalog affects viability/maturation: switch to ABI/PYL+ABA gating, and/or reduce inducer dose; quantify mTOR pathway markers to document neutrality.
7.3 If ALB secretion does not increase with HNF4A targeting: expand Module A targets to include additional hepatic identity TF nodes (e.g., CEBPA, FOXA2) with strict off-target budget and PHH-guided transcriptomic benchmarks.

Feasibility: 1) Quantitative mechanistic grounding (addresses PK/PD critique): The revised plan no longer assumes that HLC-secreted ALB sets exposure. Instead, it explicitly controls extracellular albumin via HSA titration and directly measures fu,media and fu,cell plus intracellular concentrations by LC–MS. This yields Cu,cell-driven exposure metrics that can be quantitatively linked to toxicity and CYP3A4 activity, preventing mechanistic overreach and enabling interpretable exposure–response modeling.

2) Reduced feasibility risk vs engineered PXR LBD (addresses orthogonality critique): Because PXR is inherently promiscuous, engineering an inducer-selective PXR LBD that excludes all test drugs is high risk. The proposal therefore replaces PXR-LBD gating with an orthogonal chemically induced dimerization system (FRB/FKBP with rapalog; ABI/PYL+ABA backup) to gate coactivator recruitment to dCas9 positioned at CYP3A4 enhancers. Orthogonality is validated using a predefined small-molecule panel including the test drugs, with explicit pass/fail thresholds.

3) Engineering specificity and safeguards (addresses architecture/off-target critique): The circuit is specified with (i) safe-harbor, single-copy integration and ddPCR copy-number normalization; (ii) inducible promoters for amplitude control; (iii) multiplex gRNA tiling across validated CYP3A4 distal enhancers and HNF4A regulatory regions guided by chromatin accessibility; and (iv) a transcriptome perturbation budget with required CRISPRa/dCas9 controls and RNA-seq-based acceptance criteria. This de-risks clonal variability, uncontrolled expression, and unintended transcriptional rewiring.

4) Decoupling contributions of Module A vs Module B (addresses mechanistic attribution): A 2D induction matrix (dox × rapalog) plus Module A-only and Module B-only controls will quantify separable and combined effects on ALB, CYP3A4, and global hepatic fidelity, allowing causal attribution of phenotypes to each module.

5) Defined predictive performance claims (addresses metrics/power critique): The revised proposal predefines a sufficiently sized compound panel, includes CYP3A4-dependent and -independent hepatotoxins and negatives, and uses AUROC/AUPRC with preset operating thresholds and donor-wise validation to assess robustness. Comparative advantage will be claimed only if the engineered system improves classification metrics and mechanistic CYP3A4-dependence calls relative to conventional HLCs and SCFA-matured organoids.

6) Alignment with literature assets: The approach leverages reported coupling between maturation markers (ALB) and CYP3A4 activity in PSC-derived HLCs (Asset 2) while addressing the documented need for improved CYP3A4-dependent hepatotoxicity prediction and benchmarking against SCFA-matured organoids that increase CYP3A4 and ALB (Asset 1). The proposal goes beyond correlation by imposing orthogonal control and quantitative exposure measurements.
final_critique: This is an unusually detailed and technically mature proposal that directly addresses known failure modes in iPSC-derived hepatocyte systems, particularly the conflation of ALB secretion with intracellular exposure and the promiscuity of PXR-based induction. Engineering resolution is high: circuit architecture, integration strategy, gRNA tiling, orthogonality testing, and go/no-go criteria are specified at a level consistent with execution. Logical consistency is also strong; the decoupling of ALB from exposure and CYP3A4 from xenobiotic sensing is mechanistically justified and aligned with PK/PD principles. Minor deductions stem from residual risk rather than conceptual weakness: (i) FRB/FKBP systems can still introduce subtle mTOR-linked transcriptional effects in hepatocyte-like cells despite rapalog variants, and (ii) transcriptome perturbation thresholds (<300 DEGs) may be optimistic given multiplex CRISPRa at distal enhancers. Evidence grounding is solid and remains within hepatotoxicity, hepatic maturation, and transcriptional control without drifting into irrelevant domains. The rationale is strong and creative, but it still builds atop an HLC platform whose absolute ceiling of adult hepatocyte fidelity may limit ultimate predictive gains relative to PHHs, a constraint acknowledged but not fully mitigated.

original_chain: Diploid -> Purine metabolism gene -> Loss-of-function screening -> Fluorescence-activated cell sorting -> Action potential
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Diploid human excitatory neurons require intact purine metabolism to preserve *repolarization reserve* during sustained high-frequency firing, and this requirement can be functionally decomposed into (i) an acute ATP-dependent arm that maintains Na+/K+-ATPase-driven K+ clearance and membrane polarization on the timescale of seconds, and (ii) a slower GTP-dependent arm that sustains surface density and availability of delayed-rectifier K+ channels (KV2/KV7) via vesicular trafficking and membrane recycling on the timescale of hours to days. Loss of specific purine metabolism nodes selectively collapses repolarization reserve before global excitability or viability fail, producing frequency-dependent spike broadening, afterhyperpolarization loss, and depolarization block. We further hypothesize that this collapse can be quantitatively encoded as a stable, extracellular surface barcode by coupling membrane depolarization to *chemically validated, extracellular proximity labeling chemistry* whose kinetics integrate spike frequency while remaining insensitive to subthreshold depolarization. By explicitly calibrating barcode accumulation against patch-clamp-derived repolarization metrics and correcting for expression and surface-area confounds via ratiometric normalization, this ‘Voltage-to-Genotype’ system overcomes prior feasibility concerns and enables pooled CRISPRi screening of purine metabolism genes in diploid human neurons with electrophysiological specificity.
Plan: ### Step 0: Reporter architecture selection and molecular de-risking (pre-screen gate)
0.1 **Labeling chemistry choice (proven extracellular system):** Use an engineered extracellular APEX2 peroxidase variant (APEX2-e) with demonstrated activity in oxidizing membrane-impermeant biotin-phenol analogs under controlled H2O2 pulses. APEX2 is selected over ligases due to millisecond-scale catalytic turnover and extensive prior kinetic characterization.
0.2 **Voltage coupling strategy (non-mechanical, rate-based):** Rather than relying on large conformational gating, fuse APEX2-e to the extracellular N-terminus of a fast, validated voltage sensor (e.g., ASAP-family VSD) via a *short, flexible linker* that preserves voltage-dependent membrane proximity. Depolarization increases residence time of the enzyme within ~10–20 nm of a fixed acceptor scaffold, increasing effective labeling rate without requiring steric on/off gating. This rate-integration model directly addresses reviewer concerns about mechanical feasibility.
0.3 **Acceptor scaffold:** Express a constitutive, inert single-pass transmembrane protein bearing (i) an extracellular tyrosine-rich acceptor peptide for phenoxyl radical capture and (ii) a spectrally distinct fluorophore (e.g., mTagBFP2) for abundance normalization.

### Step 1: Mandatory feasibility and calibration package (clonal reporter line)
1.1 **Clonal line generation:** Generate NGN2-inducible diploid human iPSC-derived neurons stably expressing (i) VSD–APEX2-e fusion and (ii) dual-color acceptor scaffold. Validate surface localization, voltage sensitivity, and absence of baseline excitability perturbation.
1.2 **Stimulation dependence:** Apply field stimulation at 0, 5, 10, 20, and 40 Hz during brief (1–3 min) exposure to membrane-impermeant biotin-phenol + low H2O2. Quantify covalent biotin accumulation by flow cytometry. Demonstrate monotonic frequency dependence.
1.3 **Specificity controls:** (i) Abolish labeling with TTX; (ii) show minimal labeling under sustained subthreshold depolarization (high-K+ ACSF without spikes); (iii) confirm no labeling in absence of H2O2.
1.4 **Ratiometric correction:** Normalize biotin signal to constitutive acceptor fluorophore and cell capacitance proxy (forward scatter). Define gating that regresses out reporter abundance and surface area, yielding a normalized ‘repolarization barcode index’.

### Step 2: Benchmarking against electrophysiological ground truth
2.1 **Patch-clamp correlation:** In the same clonal line, perform whole-cell recordings under identical stimulation paradigms. Quantify spike half-width, afterhyperpolarization amplitude, firing failure frequency, and depolarization block threshold.
2.2 **Pharmacologic calibration:** Apply acute perturbations with known mechanisms: low-dose ouabain (ATPase stress), 4-AP and KV7 blockers (repolarization machinery), oligomycin/rotenone (energetic stress). Correlate barcode index with repolarization metrics, not baseline firing rate.
2.3 **Decision criteria:** Establish that barcode index tracks repolarization reserve (e.g., spike broadening and failure) independently of spike initiation probability.

### Step 3: Pooled CRISPRi screening implementation
3.1 **Perturbation choice:** Use CRISPRi (dCas9-KRAB) to ensure uniform, rapid knockdown in post-mitotic neurons and avoid heterogeneous KO kinetics.
3.2 **Library design:** Focused purine metabolism library (de novo, salvage, IMPDH/GTP branch, mitochondrial one-carbon–purine coupling) plus controls (Na+/K+-ATPase subunits, Kv trafficking genes, non-targeting guides).
3.3 **Screen execution:** After knockdown stabilization, apply standardized high-frequency pacing and labeling. Dissociate neurons under TTX + cold conditions to prevent artifactual activity. FACS-sort top/bottom 15% by normalized barcode index.
3.4 **Analysis:** Guide enrichment analysis (MAGeCK), pathway stratification, and comparison with control gene behavior.

### Step 4: Mechanistic discrimination (ATP vs GTP arms)
4.1 **Temporal separation:** Acute (minutes–hours) metabolic inhibition versus chronic (days) knockdown to distinguish ATPase failure from trafficking defects.
4.2 **Biochemical assays:** LC–MS quantification of adenylate and guanylate pools; Na+/K+-ATPase activity assays; extracellular K+ accumulation during pacing.
4.3 **Trafficking assays:** Surface/total KV2.1 and KV7.2 quantification, Rab/Arf pathway readouts, and rescue with ATP precursors versus guanosine/IMPDH bypass.

### Step 5: Translational and robustness extensions
5.1 **Metabolic rescue:** Test nucleoside supplementation and transporter modulation.
5.2 **Reproducibility:** Replicate key findings across independent neuronal differentiations and stimulation geometries.
Feasibility: This revision directly addresses reviewer concerns by replacing speculative mechanical gating with a *rate-based proximity labeling model* grounded in well-characterized extracellular APEX2 chemistry, whose kinetics are sufficient to integrate thousands of action potentials over minutes without requiring per-spike toggling. Expression, surface-area, and health confounds are explicitly corrected through dual-color ratiometric normalization and FSC-based gating. A mandatory calibration phase benchmarks barcode accumulation against gold-standard patch-clamp repolarization metrics and pharmacologic perturbations, ensuring construct validity before pooled screening. The use of CRISPRi de-risks neuronal genetics, while cold/TTX dissociation preserves barcode integrity. Finally, explicit temporal and biochemical criteria disentangle ATPase-driven K+ clearance from GTP-dependent Kv trafficking, aligning the screening readout with a mechanistically precise definition of repolarization reserve rather than generic excitability or metabolic failure.
final_critique: This is an unusually well-structured attempt to make pooled electrophysiology-adjacent screening feasible in human neurons, and the staged gating (feasibility → calibration → screen) is methodologically disciplined. The central risk remains construct validity of the voltage-coupled APEX2 rate model: it is not yet demonstrated that physiological voltage excursions can produce a sufficiently large and specific modulation of extracellular APEX2 labeling rate to separate 5–40 Hz firing over minutes while remaining insensitive to subthreshold depolarization. The proposed coupling mechanism (“residence time within 10–20 nm”) is plausible but under-specified physically: APEX2 labeling depends strongly on local substrate availability, radical lifetime/diffusion, and microdomain geometry; small VSD motions may be dwarfed by membrane crowding, glycocalyx effects, and acceptor density heterogeneity. In addition, H2O2 pulses and peroxidase activity can induce oxidative membrane/protein changes that themselves alter excitability and channel trafficking, confounding the intended repolarization-reserve readout; the plan includes controls but not explicit quantitative thresholds for acceptable perturbation. Finally, the biological decomposition into ATP (seconds) vs GTP (hours–days) arms is compelling but may not be cleanly separable: purine node perturbations can co-vary ATP/GTP pools, redox state, and phosphoinositide-dependent Kv7 regulation, producing mixed phenotypes that complicate mechanistic attribution unless additional orthogonal readouts (direct Kv current density, membrane PIP2 status, etc.) are incorporated.

original_chain: Nanog -> Senescence -> Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition -> Bone morphogenic protein 4 -> Primary sclerosing cholangitis
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: In primary sclerosing cholangitis, chronic oxysterol exposure converts BMP-4 signaling from a developmental, differentiation-permissive program into a pathological driver of EMT and senescence by altering SMAD–chromatin coupling kinetics rather than ligand availability or spatial presentation. Specifically, we hypothesize that oxysterol-induced chromatin remodeling in human biliary tree stem/progenitor cells (hBTSCs) prolongs SMAD1/5/8 residence at EMT- and senescence-associated enhancers, enforcing a p53/p21-mediated senescence state that actively represses Nanog transcriptional circuitry. A structurally novel methodological adaptation—an optogenetically tunable BMP-4 receptor activation system combined with live-cell SMAD–chromatin residence-time recording—will allow causal dissection of signaling-duration–dependent fate decisions independent of extracellular ligand gradients or microfluidic architectures.
Plan: Step 1: System setup—engineering a signaling-duration–controlled BMP-4 pathway.
1.1 Generate hBTSC lines stably expressing an opto-BMPR1A construct, in which the intracellular kinase domain of BMPR1A is fused to a light-inducible dimerization module (e.g., CRY2/CIBN), enabling precise temporal control of receptor activation without exogenous BMP-4 ligand.
1.2 Introduce fluorescently tagged SMAD1 or SMAD5 (endogenous knock-in via CRISPR-HDR) to permit single-molecule tracking of nuclear translocation and chromatin binding dynamics.
1.3 Establish PSC-mimicking stress conditions using chronic low-dose cholest-4,6-dien-3-one exposure and inflammatory cytokine background (IL-6), while maintaining matched unstressed controls.

Step 2: Methodological adaptation—decoupling signaling amplitude from signaling duration.
2.1 Apply optogenetic stimulation paradigms that deliver identical total BMP pathway activation (matched integrated signal) but distinct temporal profiles (e.g., short pulsatile vs prolonged continuous activation).
2.2 Quantify SMAD–chromatin interaction kinetics using live-cell single-particle tracking and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), focusing on enhancer regions of EMT genes (SNAIL, ZEB2), senescence genes (CDKN1A/p21), and pluripotency regulators (NANOG).
2.3 Integrate CUT&RUN at defined timepoints to map SMAD1/5/8 and p53 co-occupancy at these loci under different activation-duration regimes.
2.4 Perturb chromatin accessibility mechanistically by targeted inhibition or activation of oxysterol-responsive epigenetic modifiers (e.g., histone acetyltransferases or HDACs implicated in bile-acid signaling) to test whether chromatin state gates SMAD residence time and downstream fate.

Step 3: Validation and analytical framework.
3.1 EMT assessment: transcriptional profiling (qPCR/RNA-seq), E-cadherin/vimentin protein ratios, and morphological metrics.
3.2 Senescence assessment: SA-β-gal staining, p16INK4a/p21 levels, γH2AX accumulation, and SASP cytokine secretion.
3.3 Nanog axis: Nanog mRNA/protein levels, enhancer accessibility (ATAC-seq), and reversibility upon shortening BMP signaling duration.
3.4 Causal modeling: construct a quantitative model linking SMAD chromatin residence time to probability of EMT induction, senescence entry, and Nanog repression, explicitly testing whether duration—not amplitude—of BMP signaling is the decisive variable.
3.5 Translational relevance: apply the same optogenetic stimulation paradigms to PSC patient–derived biliary organoids to determine whether pathological signaling-duration sensitivity is conserved ex vivo.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 2 establishes BMP-4 activation, EMT, and senescence as linked outcomes in PSC-relevant hBTSCs, while Asset 1 provides a mechanistic framework connecting senescence-associated p53 activation to Nanog repression. Developmental biology literature supports the concept that BMP/SMAD signaling outcomes are duration-dependent, yet this dimension has not been interrogated in PSC.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Bioengineering innovation here lies in adapting optogenetic receptor control—traditionally used in neurobiology and developmental systems—to hepatobiliary disease modeling, enabling unprecedented temporal precision in pathway activation without confounding extracellular variables.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike microenvironmental or ligand-presentation models, this approach isolates intracellular signaling kinetics as the causal driver of EMT–senescence coupling. It directly tests a mechanistic principle (SMAD residence-time encoding of cell fate) and identifies a new therapeutic lever: pharmacologically shortening BMP signaling duration or disrupting SMAD–chromatin dwell time, rather than globally inhibiting BMP-4.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and conceptually sophisticated proposal that correctly identifies signaling-duration encoding as an underexplored variable in PSC-relevant BMP biology. The opto-BMPR1A system and endogenous SMAD tagging are well chosen and, in principle, capable of isolating duration effects from amplitude. However, several deductions are warranted. First, the proposal under-specifies how equivalence of 'integrated BMP signal' will be validated across pulsatile versus sustained regimes (e.g., quantitative phospho-SMAD load calibration), which weakens causal claims about duration dominance. Second, the chromatin remodeling step attributed to oxysterols is treated largely as a black box; specific candidate modifiers are named, but no prioritization logic or preliminary linkage to SMAD dwell-time regulation is articulated. Third, while the p53/p21–Nanog repression axis is plausible, the proposal assumes rather than demonstrates that prolonged SMAD residence is upstream of p53 activation rather than a parallel consequence of stress-induced chromatin changes. These gaps do not invalidate the approach, but they limit mechanistic closure and slightly overextend the interpretive reach of the data as currently designed.

original_chain: Aging -> Cell fate transition -> Aging -> Glutathione -> Pancreatic fibrosis -> NF-kappaB -> Pancreatic fibrosis
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Restoring a high glutathione redox potential specifically within pancreatic stellate cell (PSC) mitochondria will prevent aging-associated pro-fibrotic cell fate transition into collagen-secreting myofibroblasts by suppressing redox-sensitive NF-kappaB activation that is amplified downstream of CTGF/integrin-alpha5beta1 signaling. Methodological adaptation: engineer a PSC-targeted, mitochondria-addressed, redox-activated prodrug-nanoparticle system (mGSH-PSC-NP) that releases an H2O2-cleavable cysteine/glutathione precursor payload only when PSC ROS is elevated, while co-displaying an alpha5beta1-binding ligand to concentrate delivery in activated PSCs; this overcomes systemic antioxidant dilution and off-target immunosuppression, and directly interrupts the ROS→CTGF→NF-kappaB→IL-6/IL-1beta inflammatory-fibrogenic loop that drives fibrosis progression with aging.
Plan: Step 1: Build mechanistic in vitro and ex vivo fibrosis models stratified by aging.
1.1 Establish primary human PSC cultures and iPSC-derived PSC-like cells; generate 'young' vs 'aged' states via replicative senescence and progeroid stress (low-dose chronic H2O2 and/or high-glucose oscillation), verifying aging hallmarks (p16INK4a, SA-beta-gal, mitochondrial dysfunction) and baseline glutathione (GSH/GSSG) redox potential.
1.2 Induce fibrogenic activation with TGF-beta and CTGF; quantify myofibroblast fate transition markers (alpha-SMA, COL1A1, FN1), CTGF secretion, and inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1beta).
1.3 Validate NF-kappaB pathway engagement using p65 nuclear translocation, IkappaB degradation, and NF-kappaB reporter assays; map whether CTGF/integrin-alpha5beta1 blockade reduces NF-kappaB and fibrotic markers.

Step 2: Implement the adapted methodology: PSC-targeted, mitochondria-addressed, redox-activated glutathione restoration.
2.1 Nanoparticle architecture adaptation: formulate a polymer-lipid hybrid nanoparticle with (i) surface-displayed alpha5beta1 integrin-binding peptide (adaptation: multivalent, low-affinity monomers arranged in defined spacing to maximize avidity on activated PSCs while minimizing binding to quiescent cells), (ii) a mitochondria-targeting moiety (e.g., TPP+ analog) conjugated through a pH-stable linker to promote mitochondrial accumulation post-endocytosis, and (iii) an H2O2-cleavable thioketal crosslinker in the core.
2.2 Payload adaptation: encapsulate a 'mito-restricted GSH precursor module' consisting of cysteine donor + glycine/glutamate equivalents plus a glutathione synthetase cofactor strategy (e.g., ATP-regeneration microdomain using phosphocreatine/creatine kinase mimic) to bias local GSH synthesis in mitochondria rather than diffuse cytosolic antioxidant effects.
2.3 Redox-gated release: tune thioketal density so that payload release kinetics sharply increase only above the ROS threshold measured in activated/aged PSCs; validate in cell-free ROS titrations and in PSCs using fluorescent release reporters.
2.4 Mechanistic perturbation tests: compare mGSH-PSC-NP vs (a) non-targeted NP, (b) non-cleavable linker NP, (c) cytosol-only GSH precursor, (d) free glutathione. Readouts: mitochondrial GSH/GSSG (targeted probes), mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX), NF-kappaB activation, CTGF expression, IL-6 promoter occupancy by p65 (ChIP-qPCR), and fate transition endpoints (alpha-SMA/COL1A1).

Step 3: Rigorous validation in vivo with causal inference and fibrosis outcome metrics.
3.1 Use two complementary rodent models: (i) long-term oscillating glucose (LOsG) to induce ROS/TGF-beta-driven pancreatic fibrosis, and (ii) aged animals (18–24 months) to capture aging-dependent susceptibility; optionally add caerulein pancreatitis as an inflammatory fibrosis amplifier.
3.2 Biodistribution and cell-type specificity: label nanoparticles and quantify uptake in PSCs (PDGFRbeta+/desmin+) vs acinar, ductal, macrophage populations by flow cytometry and spatial imaging.
3.3 Efficacy endpoints: pancreatic collagen deposition (hydroxyproline, Sirius Red), PSC activation (alpha-SMA), beta-cell function (glucose tolerance, insulin secretion), and inflammatory milieu (IL-6/IL-1beta).
3.4 Mechanism confirmation: assess NF-kappaB activation in isolated PSCs from treated animals; perform rescue/epistasis by administering an NF-kappaB inhibitor or CTGF knockdown to test whether mGSH-PSC-NP provides no additional benefit when NF-kappaB/CTGF is already disabled.
3.5 Safety/translation: evaluate systemic immune competence and liver/kidney oxidative markers to confirm that redox restoration is localized and does not broadly suppress NF-kappaB signaling in immune cells.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 2 supports that glutathione suppresses ROS-driven TGF-beta/SMAD activation and PSC activation in pancreatic fibrosis; Asset 3 shows CTGF activates NF-kappaB in PSCs to induce IL-6 and amplify inflammation/fibrosis. Redox control of NF-kappaB is mechanistically plausible because upstream IkappaB kinase activity and p65 nuclear signaling are sensitive to oxidative state, and mitochondrial ROS is a potent amplifier of inflammatory transcription.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Antioxidants fail clinically largely due to poor cell-type specificity and inability to correct subcellular redox microdomains. The adapted approach transfers established targeted nanodelivery and ROS-cleavable chemistry into a fibrosis-specific context, adding a structural modification (multivalent alpha5beta1 targeting + mitochondria addressing + ROS-gated release) to solve the domain limitation of non-specific glutathione supplementation.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with free glutathione or systemic NAC, mGSH-PSC-NP is designed to (i) concentrate in activated PSCs (the effector cell driving fibrosis), (ii) restore mitochondrial GSH where ROS amplification occurs, and (iii) release only under high ROS, reducing off-target NF-kappaB suppression and enabling higher effective local dosing. This should more effectively block the CTGF/integrin→NF-kappaB→IL-6 feed-forward loop and thereby prevent or reverse the aging-linked myofibroblast fate transition that sustains pancreatic fibrosis.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and mechanistically sophisticated proposal with strong internal coherence. The engineering plan is unusually detailed for a hypothesis-driven application, particularly in its multivalent integrin targeting logic, ROS-threshold tuning, and explicit epistasis testing in vivo. Logical consistency is high: mitochondrial ROS as an amplifier of CTGF–integrin–NF-kappaB signaling in aged PSCs is plausible and well-aligned with the intervention point. However, two deductions are warranted. First, the mitochondrial GSH synthesis bias (ATP-regeneration microdomain via phosphocreatine/CK mimic) is conceptually creative but under-specified and may be biologically unrealistic without preliminary validation, weakening engineering resolution. Second, while NF-kappaB redox sensitivity is real, the proposal underestimates pathway redundancy (e.g., SMAD, YAP/TAZ, p38) in PSC fate locking during aging, slightly overstating the sufficiency of NF-kappaB suppression alone. Evidence grounding remains strong, though some claims (e.g., strict mitochondrial confinement of GSH effects) verge on aspirational rather than empirically established.

original_chain: Epiblast -> 8-cell stage embryo -> Activin A -> Embryonic stem cell -> Cynomolgus monkey
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A geometry-calibrated, zona-tethered Activin cue can be engineered to *avoid* embryo-wide, TE-skewing Activin exposure while selectively reinforcing cynomolgus epiblast (EPI) competence by shaping (i) the spatial exposure gradient across the perivitelline space and (ii) the temporal SMAD2/3 pulse features during/after compaction. Specifically, we hypothesize that a bivalent ActivinA–Fc presented from a zona-adsorbed nanocoating at a controlled surface density (σ; molecules/µm²) and governed by an orthogonal, highly specific release mechanism (photocleavable or engineered protease–substrate) will produce a *short, moderate-amplitude* SMAD2/3 activation in outer cells (closest to the zona) but a *delayed, lower-amplitude, longer-residence* activation in inner cells after compaction due to: (1) compaction-driven changes in paracellular permeability and perivitelline transport that reduce direct ligand access to basolateral receptor pools on outer cells while permitting inward equilibration of a low free-ligand fraction; and (2) increased local rebinding near cell membranes when ligand is supplied from a surface reservoir (tethered/near-tether), which biases signaling toward sustained, membrane-proximal receptor engagement and reduced endocytic downregulation compared to a soluble bolus. This regime stabilizes NANOG/SOX2/OCT4 in inner cells (EPI reinforcement) without imposing sustained global Activin that has been associated with EPI suppression and TE promotion in early embryos. The key mechanistic claim is therefore not ‘inner cells see more ligand’, but that properly tuned zona presentation yields a prespecified *exposure inequality* and *pulse-shape inequality* (outer vs inner) that maps to distinct SMAD2/3 transcriptional programs. We will quantitatively measure and tune the ActivinA–Fc concentration field C(r,t) from zona → perivitelline space → embryo surface during compaction, and then test—via single-embryo correlation and mediation analysis—that ligand surface density and release kinetics determine SMAD2/3 pulse features which in turn mediate EPI allocation and ESC derivation efficiency.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registration, gating criteria, and quantitative targets
0.1 Pre-register primary endpoints: (i) EPI cell number per blastocyst (NANOG+/SOX2+), (ii) ESC derivation efficiency per plated blastocyst. Secondary: EPI:TE ratio, hypoblast fraction, developmental timing, hatching rate.
0.2 Define quantitative ‘exposure inequality’ metrics and target windows before optimization:
  - E_exposure = AUC_inner / AUC_outer for free ligand concentration at the embryo surface over a prespecified window (e.g., compaction onset to early blastocyst). Target: avoid outer-dominant sustained exposure (E_exposure not <<1 over long windows); tune to a regime that minimizes sustained outer exposure while allowing measurable inner exposure (e.g., E_exposure ~0.5–1.2 depending on empirical tuning).
  - P_pulse = (Amplitude_inner, Duration_inner, Time-to-peak_inner) relative to outer. Target: inner cells show longer effective duration with lower peak than outer (inner ‘sustained-low’ vs outer ‘transient-moderate’).
0.3 Establish go/no-go gating criteria for any release strategy: (i) ≥90% cleavage-stage progression vs untreated, (ii) no significant change in compaction timing, (iii) zona integrity (thickness/elasticity proxy) within ±10% by imaging-based metrics, (iv) hatching rate not reduced by >20% relative to controls.

Step 1 — Reagent engineering with explicit biophysical characterization
1.1 ActivinA–Fc design and quality control
  - Construct: mature Activin A fused to human IgG1 Fc with mutations that reduce FcγR/C1q binding (e.g., LALA-PG or equivalent) to minimize noncanonical Fc interactions while retaining dimerization/avidity.
  - Purity and oligomeric state: SEC-MALS to confirm dimeric species and exclude aggregates; endotoxin <0.1 EU/mL.
  - Potency: SMAD2/3 reporter assay to obtain EC50/EC90; compare to wild-type Activin A.

1.2 Receptor affinity/occupancy disentanglement (mandatory)
  - Measure binding kinetics by SPR or BLI using ectodomains of ActRIIA, ActRIIB, and ALK4 (and ALK7 if relevant): obtain kon, koff, KD for Activin A vs ActivinA–Fc.
  - Quantify whether Fc fusion changes receptor preference or residence time; explicitly incorporate these constants into the transport-signaling model (Step 2).
  - Control ligands: soluble Activin A; soluble ActivinA–Fc; inert Fc.

1.3 Zona-adsorbing nanocoating architecture (explicit parameters)
  - Base polymer: PEGylated poly(L-lysine) (PLL-g-PEG) or equivalent cationic PEG brush; tune charge density to adsorb to zona without impairing cleavage.
  - Functional groups: (i) high-affinity Fc capture (Protein A/G fragment or anti-Fc nanobody) at controlled grafting ratio; (ii) optional fluorescent tracer for coating quantification.
  - Parameter sweep: polymer MW (e.g., PLL 15–30 kDa), PEG chain length (2–5 kDa), grafting density (low/med/high) to tune ligand loading and release.
  - Quantify coating thickness/uniformity by confocal z-stacks with fluorescent polymer; report mean ± SD thickness and coefficient of variation per embryo.

Step 2 — Embryo-geometry–aware transport-and-retention framework (mandatory)
2.1 Build a minimal, geometry-aware reaction–diffusion model
  - Domains: zona surface reservoir (tethered ligand density σ), perivitelline space (diffusion coefficient D_pvs), embryo surface binding (effective kon_surf, koff_surf to receptors/ECM), and optional paracellular permeability change at compaction (P_compaction(t)).
  - Outputs: predicted C_outer(t) and C_inner(t) (free ligand at outer embryo surface and in internal intercellular spaces/ICM-proximal region), and receptor occupancy O(t) using measured binding constants.
  - Fit parameters to data from 2.3–2.5 (below): D_pvs, effective release rate k_rel, and adsorption retention k_ret.

2.2 Calibrated fluorescent ActivinA–Fc for quantitative imaging
  - Label ActivinA–Fc with a site-specific fluorophore (degree of labeling 0.5–1.5) and verify unchanged EC50 (≤2-fold shift) and unchanged receptor binding kinetics (SPR/BLI check on a subset).
  - Establish fluorescence-to-molecule calibration using fluorescent standards and imaging-matched conditions; express σ (molecules/µm²) and C (nM) with confidence intervals.

2.3 Spatiotemporal concentration profiling (mandatory)
  - Perform time-lapse confocal or light-sheet imaging from 8-cell through early blastocyst for embryos with zona-tethered fluorescent ActivinA–Fc.
  - Quantify: (i) zona surface fluorescence (σ proxy), (ii) perivitelline free fraction (C_pvs(t)), (iii) embryo surface proximal concentration at outer cells (C_outer(t)) and, after compaction, inner regions (C_inner(t)) using 3D segmentation.

2.4 FRAP/retention analysis on zona reservoir (mandatory)
  - FRAP on the zona-associated ligand to estimate lateral mobility and effective exchange with the perivitelline pool; extract effective diffusion/immobilization parameters.
  - Measure washout kinetics (media exchange) to estimate k_ret and the free fraction available to diffuse inward.

2.5 Compaction-linked permeability inference
  - Co-load inert fluorescent dextrans (e.g., 3 kDa and 10 kDa) to infer size-dependent transport changes at compaction; relate to P_compaction(t) and use as a covariate in modeling.

2.6 Tune to a prespecified exposure inequality (mandatory)
  - Using the fitted model, choose 2–3 operating points (σ_low, σ_mid, σ_high) and 1–2 release schedules predicted to meet the target E_exposure and P_pulse windows.
  - Lock these parameters before fate/ESC derivation experiments (to prevent post hoc tuning).

Step 3 — Replace broad proteases with orthogonal cleavage (mandatory)
3.1 Primary release mechanism: photocleavable linker (preferred for specificity)
  - Introduce a photocleavable moiety (e.g., o-nitrobenzyl-based) between Fc-capture module and ligand (or between polymer and Fc-capture) to enable timed partial release.
  - Calibrate light dose in embryo-compatible ranges (wavelength/intensity/time) using a mock fluorophore payload; establish a ‘partial release’ target (e.g., 10–30% release at compaction; remaining retained to maintain low-level reservoir).

3.2 Alternative release mechanism: engineered protease–substrate pair
  - Use an orthogonal protease (e.g., TEV protease or engineered split-protease system) with a unique cleavage site absent from embryo/zona proteins.
  - Validate specificity on a panel: zona proteins (ZP1-4 where feasible), albumin, embryo-culture supplements; confirm no cleavage by SDS-PAGE/LC-MS.
  - Establish kinetic constants for cleavage on the coating (kcat/KM apparent) under culture conditions; tune enzyme dose to reach the same partial release targets as 3.1.

3.3 Off-target and embryo safety panel (mandatory gating)
  - Zona integrity: measure thickness and birefringence/structural proxies pre/post exposure.
  - Hatching mechanics: assisted hatching requirement, spontaneous hatching rate.
  - Developmental timing: cleavage-to-compaction, compaction-to-blastocyst; discard conditions failing gating criteria (Step 0.3).

Step 4 — Experimental groups (updated to include quantitative tuning)
4.1 Randomize 8-cell cynomolgus embryos into:
  A) No Activin.
  B) Soluble Activin A (bolus; matched AUC to tethered conditions by measured C(t)).
  C) Soluble ActivinA–Fc (potency/stability control).
  D1–D3) Zona-tethered ActivinA–Fc at σ_low/σ_mid/σ_high (no release).
  E1–E3) Zona-tethered ActivinA–Fc at σ_low/σ_mid/σ_high + partial orthogonal release at compaction (photo or engineered protease), using prespecified release fraction.
  F) Zona-tethered inert Fc (nanocoating control).
  G) Zona removed prior to coating (tests necessity of zona reservoir; apply equivalent soluble AUC).
  H) Monovalent tethered Activin (e.g., site-specific monomeric format or alternative non-Fc tether) at matched σ to test avidity/rebinding contribution.
  I) SB431542 arm (subset of key groups) to confirm SMAD2/3 dependence.

Step 5 — Signaling dynamics matched to kinetic claims (quantitative readouts)
5.1 pSMAD2/3 pulse feature extraction
  - Immunostain at prespecified timepoints (pre-compaction, compaction, early blastocyst) plus an additional dense time-series in a subset to reconstruct pulse dynamics.
  - Quantify per-embryo pSMAD2/3 amplitude and nuclear occupancy time in outer vs inner cells (3D segmentation), yielding P_pulse metrics.

5.2 Receptor occupancy/proximity readouts aligned to model
  - Use proximity ligation assay (ActRII–ALK4 and receptor–ligand where possible) specifically as a *relative occupancy/clustering* metric, interpreted alongside SPR/BLI constants and modeled occupancy O(t).
  - Add an orthogonal readout: surface biotinylation/internalization assay in a reporter cell system exposed to (i) soluble Activin, (ii) surface-tethered ActivinA–Fc at matched effective concentration, to test whether tethering biases trafficking/endocytosis (mechanistic bridge to embryo).

Step 6 — Fate outcomes and ESC derivation
6.1 Lineage allocation
  - Multiplex immunostaining with cell counting: EPI (NANOG, SOX2, OCT4), hypoblast (SOX17, GATA6), TE (GATA3, CDX2).
  - Report absolute counts and ratios; include total cell number and blastocyst quality metrics.

6.2 Transcriptomic validation
  - scRNA-seq (or low-input multiome) on selected operating points meeting exposure inequality targets; score SMAD2/3 target modules, pluripotency networks, TE differentiation modules.

6.3 ESC derivation
  - Standardized cynomolgus ESC derivation protocol across groups; endpoints: outgrowth rate, derivation efficiency, karyotype stability, pluripotency markers, tri-lineage differentiation competence.

Step 7 — Causal linkage: prespecified mediation analysis (mandatory)
7.1 Single-embryo linkage dataset
  - For each embryo: σ (zona ligand density), modeled C_outer(t)/C_inner(t) or empirical proxies, pSMAD2/3 pulse features (outer/inner), and fate metrics (EPI count; EPI:TE).

7.2 Mediation model
  - Test the path: (σ and release parameters) → (pSMAD2/3 pulse features) → (EPI allocation) → (ESC derivation), using mixed-effects mediation with donor/batch as random effects.
  - Distinguish potency/stability effects: include SPR/BLI-derived affinity parameters and soluble dose-matched AUC controls; explicitly test whether outcomes are explained by exposure/pulse shaping rather than increased overall AUC.

Step 8 — Statistics and sample planning
8.1 Mixed-effects models with donor/collection batch random intercepts; adjust for multiple comparisons.
8.2 Power planning based on pilot variance of EPI cell counts and derivation rates; implement sequential design: transport/safety validation → limited fate study at prespecified operating points → scale only if mediation supports mechanism.

Feasibility: 1) Addresses the central geometry critique with measurable, tunable targets: The proposal now treats zona tethering as an experimentally quantifiable boundary condition rather than assuming inner-cell selectivity. By directly measuring C(r,t) with calibrated fluorescent ActivinA–Fc, fitting a minimal reaction–diffusion model, and tuning to a prespecified exposure inequality metric (E_exposure) and pulse-shape metric (P_pulse), we ensure that spatial logic is validated before scaling to fate/ESC endpoints.

2) Risk-managed, embryo-compatible release: Broad proteases are replaced with an orthogonal release system (photocleavable linker preferred; engineered protease–substrate as backup) with explicit partial-release targets and an off-target panel (zona integrity, hatching, developmental timing) as gating criteria. This directly mitigates uncontrolled zona/embryo-adjacent proteolysis and batch variability.

3) Quantitative linkage from ligand density/release to signaling to fate: The refined plan links controllable parameters (σ, k_rel) to predicted/observed concentration fields and receptor occupancy, then to pSMAD2/3 pulse features, and finally to EPI allocation/ESC derivation via a prespecified mediation analysis. This matches the reviewer request to connect ‘kinetics shaping’ to measurable kinetic parameters, rather than relying on qualitative PLA/proteomics claims.

4) Disentangles kinetic rebinding from altered potency/format artifacts: By adding SPR/BLI kinetic measurements for ActRII/ALK4 ectodomains and using Fc-silenced variants plus AUC-matched soluble controls, we can attribute effects to exposure/pulse shaping (rebinding/residence and spatial restriction) rather than simply increased stability or altered receptor affinity caused by Fc fusion.

5) Grounded in empirical precedent while adapting to primate constraints: The approach leverages established findings that Activin A can reshape early lineage allocation (Asset 1) and that primate ESC/chimera biology is sensitive to pluripotency state and survival constraints (Asset 2), but updates the intervention to a primate-embryo-appropriate, non-microfluidic surface engineering workflow with explicit quantitative validation steps prior to high-cost primate embryo scaling.
final_critique: This is a quantitatively structured and unusually well-instrumented embryo-surface engineering proposal, with strong alignment between controllable inputs (σ, k_rel, k_ret), measurable intermediate states (C(r,t), FRAP/washout, dextran permeability, pSMAD2/3 pulse features), and terminal outcomes (EPI counts, ESC derivation), plus a prespecified mediation framework. The main score deductions are for (i) residual biological plausibility gaps in the core mechanistic claim that zona-tethering can reliably invert/reshape inner-vs-outer SMAD2/3 pulse features during compaction—because basolateral receptor accessibility, ligand routing to ICM, and compaction-dependent permeability are not only time-varying but embryo-to-embryo heterogeneous and may dominate any engineered boundary condition; (ii) measurement limitations: calibrated fluorescence in the perivitelline/inner regions risks confounding by scattering, fluorophore quenching, ligand sticking to non-target matrices, and the inability to uniquely infer “free” vs “bound/near-membrane” ligand from intensity alone, which could weaken the claimed mapping from C(r,t) to receptor occupancy O(t); (iii) the Fc fusion format, even Fc-silenced, can still change avidity-driven receptor clustering and apparent potency in ways that are difficult to separate from “rebinding near a surface reservoir,” and the proposed embryo readouts (PLA, fixed pSMAD2/3) are only partially sufficient to disambiguate these effects in situ; and (iv) operational risk: photocleavage and/or exogenous protease exposure in primate embryos, even with gating, introduces additional perturbations (light dose, ROS, protease diffusion/adsorption) that may confound lineage allocation independently of Activin signaling, and the plan does not yet specify strong counterfactual controls that match these perturbations (e.g., light-only with identical coating but noncleavable linker, protease-only with non-substrate coating) as primary comparators in the causal chain.

original_chain: Hydroxypropylcarbamate -> Rational protein design -> Esterase -> Candida rugosa -> Biocatalysis -> Metal-organic frameworks -> Electrostatic interaction
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A glycoform-controlled Candida rugosa esterase (CreE) engineered with a quantitatively specified anisotropic electrostatic “docking field” (two spatially separated surface charge clusters creating a defined dipole/quadrupole moment, rather than a single diffuse patch) will preferentially adopt a narrow orientation distribution when immobilized on charge-tuned, water-stable UiO-66 derivatives whose zeta potential and surface charge density are pre-registered at the assay pH and ionic strength. This electrostatic co-design will (i) increase the fraction of enzyme molecules presenting an unobstructed active-site entrance toward the pore void/solution interface, raising the active-site accessibility factor (f_access) and thus apparent kcat, and (ii) modulate local substrate partitioning (Kpart) for ionizable hydroxypropylcarbamate analogs inside UiO-66 defect/pore microenvironments, which can reduce apparent KM only in regimes where transport is not rate-limiting. Mechanistically, the engineered docking field overcomes heterogeneous MOF binding sites by introducing a higher-order electrostatic constraint (dipole/quadrupole matching) that is less degenerate than net-charge matching alone; glycan heterogeneity is controlled or explicitly modeled to prevent shielding of the designed field; and pore-transport/partition measurements are coupled to diffusion–reaction modeling so that any KM shift is causally attributed to intrinsic binding/catalysis vs. MOF partitioning and diffusional effectiveness. The result will be a charge-matched enzyme–MOF system with higher retention, higher functional orientation fraction, and improved thermal/solvent operational stability for hydroxypropylcarbamate hydrolysis relative to (a) wild-type enzyme, (b) charge-mismatched MOFs, and (c) covalent/random immobilization controls.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registration of quantitative design targets and acceptance thresholds (addresses electrostatics ambiguity)
0.1 Define fixed assay conditions for all “charge-matching” claims: pH 7.50 (50 mM HEPES) and pH 6.50 (50 mM MES) as two operating points; ionic strength series 25, 100, 200 mM (NaCl). All zeta potential and binding/kinetic comparisons are reported at these conditions.
0.2 MOF electrostatic acceptance thresholds (must be met before enzyme immobilization studies proceed):
  • Charge-matched MOF: |ζ| ≥ 20 mV at 25 mM ionic strength and |ζ| ≥ 10 mV at 100 mM, with sign consistent with the intended docking field (positive MOF for negative cluster docking or vice versa).
  • Charge-mismatched MOF: ζ sign opposite to “matched” at the same condition, with |ζ| ≥ 10 mV at 25 mM.
  • Surface charge density estimate: convert ζ to σ using Gouy–Chapman (reported with assumptions, Debye length), target σ ≥ 0.005–0.02 C/m² at 25 mM as a practical window for multivalent electrostatic adsorption without irreversible denaturation.
0.3 Enzyme docking-field acceptance thresholds (computed on glycoform-resolved structures at assay pH):
  • Two-cluster design: Cluster A and Cluster B separated by 25–40 Å (Cα–Cα centroid distance) on the same face, each contributing net charge magnitude |Q_A| and |Q_B| of 4–8 (via Asp/Glu or Lys/Arg), yielding total engineered ΔQnet of 0 to ±4 (to avoid global overcharging/aggregation).
  • Multipole constraint: engineered dipole moment increase Δ|μ| ≥ 150 Debye relative to the baseline protein model at pH 7.5, and/or quadrupole tensor change (reported) that differentiates the designed face from the opposite face.
  • Stability: predicted ΔΔGfold (Rosetta/FoldX consensus) per variant ≤ +2.0 kcal/mol; no new exposed hydrophobic patches (SAP score threshold) in the docking face.

Step 1 — Enzyme selection, glycosylation control, and baseline kinetic/biophysical mapping (addresses isoforms/glycans)
1.1 Choose a single Candida rugosa esterase/lipase isoform with the best structural support (PDB if available; otherwise AlphaFold2 with pLDDT and PAEs reported). Select an isoform with a known secretion signal if secreted expression is used.
1.2 Glycoform strategy (two-pronged to de-risk):
  A) Recombinant expression in Komagataella phaffii (Pichia) using a glycoengineered strain (e.g., humanized/limited high-mannose) to minimize heterogeneity; include endoglycosidase-compatible glycans.
  B) Parallel “deglyco” construct set: mutate NXS/T motifs that are solvent-exposed and proximal (<15 Å) to the intended docking face (N→Q preferred) while preserving motifs near folding nuclei; additionally evaluate enzymatic deglycosylation (Endo H/PNGase F where compatible).
Decision gate: proceed with the glycoform (A or B) that yields ≤2 dominant glycoforms by intact mass (LC–MS) and shows ≤15% activity loss relative to WT under aqueous baseline.
1.3 Verify glycosylation state: intact-protein MS for glycoform distribution; site mapping by glycopeptide MS/MS. Quantify “glycan shielding index” for docking face: solvent-accessible surface area contribution from glycans on the docking hemisphere; target ≤20% masking of the designed clusters.
1.4 Baseline kinetics for free enzyme (WT and glyco-controlled baseline): hydroxypropylcarbamate panel with defined ionization states (at least one cationic, neutral, anionic analog if chemically feasible; otherwise adjust pH to vary substrate charge). Measure kcat, KM at pH 6.5 and 7.5 across 25–200 mM ionic strength; confirm no confounding aggregation by SEC-MALS/DLS during assays.

Step 2 — Quantitative electrostatic co-design (replaces speculative helix-lock with defensible geometric constraint)
2.1 Identify docking face away from catalytic triad and lid/active-site entrance: compute electrostatic potential maps (APBS) on glycoform-resolved structures at assay pH/ionic strengths; define active-site vector and “exclusion zone” (no mutations within 12 Å of catalytic residues and within 10 Å of lid hinge residues).
2.2 Design two separated charge clusters (A and B) to enforce a unique docking pose:
  • Cluster A: 4–6 substitutions within an 8–12 Å radius to create a localized high-density charge.
  • Cluster B: 4–6 substitutions placed 25–40 Å from cluster A on the same face.
  • Maintain near-neutral global ΔQnet (0 to ±4) to reduce nonspecific sticking and salt-sensitive aggregation.
  • Avoid creating protease sites or new N-glycosylation motifs; maintain disulfide patterns.
2.3 In silico screening pipeline:
  • Fold stability: Rosetta ddG + FoldX consensus; reject variants exceeding ΔΔGfold cutoff.
  • Aggregation risk: SAP/AGGRESCAN3D; reject if predicted aggregation propensity increases beyond pre-set threshold.
  • Electrostatic metrics: compute Δ|μ| and docking-face potential anisotropy (difference in mean surface potential between docking hemisphere and opposite hemisphere); accept variants meeting thresholds in Step 0.3.
  • Glycan shielding modeled explicitly: run APBS with and without glycans to ensure docking-face anisotropy is preserved; reject designs where glycan inclusion reduces anisotropy by >30%.
2.4 Construct a focused experimental library: instead of broad randomization, implement 2–3 “backbone” variants (best-scoring charge-field geometries) and a perimeter tuning set (site-saturation at 6–10 perimeter residues) to adjust cluster pKa and minimize local unfolding.
2.5 Expression, purification, and biophysical QC:
  • SEC-MALS for monodispersity (target <10% high-MW species).
  • DLS under immobilization buffers (target Rh stable; no salt-triggered aggregation up to 200 mM NaCl).
  • DSF/DSC to measure Tm and compare to WT; accept only variants with ΔTm ≥ −2 °C.

Step 3 — MOF synthesis with explicit surface-chemistry and defect controls (addresses UiO-66 charge ambiguity)
3.1 Synthesize UiO-66 derivatives with controlled functionalization:
  • UiO-66-X where X = NH2, SO3H, and mixed-linker UiO-66-(NH2/SO3H) at defined feed ratios (e.g., 0/100, 25/75, 50/50, 75/25, 100/0).
  • Include defect modulation via modulator concentration (e.g., acetic acid) to tune mesoporosity/defect density; pre-register acceptable ranges.
3.2 Characterize MOFs before enzyme contact:
  • PXRD (phase purity), BET surface area, pore size distribution.
  • Quantify functional group content: digestion + 1H NMR of linkers (NH2/SO3H ratio), FTIR for group presence.
  • Zeta potential measured in the exact buffers/ionic strengths in Step 0.1; only MOFs meeting thresholds are used for “matched/mismatched” claims.
  • Quantify external vs internal surface accessibility: dye uptake assays and/or N2 sorption hysteresis; record particle size (SEM/TEM).

Step 4 — Immobilization modality comparison with decision criteria and denaturation controls
4.1 Two immobilization routes run in parallel initially:
  A) Post-synthetic adsorption (PSA): incubate MOF with enzyme under controlled ionic strength (25, 100, 200 mM) to explicitly test multivalent electrostatic binding; include competitive salt elution to assess reversibility.
  B) Biomimetic encapsulation (BME): in situ growth in the presence of enzyme using mild conditions; include protective osmolytes (e.g., 5–10% glycerol/trehalose) and maintain pH 6.5–7.5; minimize exposure time to precursors.
4.2 Decision gate for choosing PSA vs BME for scale-out:
  • Functional retained activity per mg enzyme (≥60% of free enzyme initial rate under non-transport-limited conditions).
  • Leaching under shear/solvent (≤5% protein released over 24 h in assay buffer; ≤10% over 24 h in 20% v/v co-solvent).
  • Structural integrity: no major secondary-structure loss by CD/FTIR (relative metric) and no major activity loss after one regeneration cycle.
If BME fails due to denaturation (activity <30% or strong structural loss), focus shifts to PSA and defect-tuned MOFs to increase retention.
4.3 Quantify loading and location:
  • Total loading by BCA/Bradford with appropriate controls and by TGA (where feasible).
  • External vs internal fraction: protease shaving (external-accessible enzyme removed) combined with activity/protein quantification; and confocal mapping with labeled enzyme. Report “f_internal” explicitly.

Step 5 — Orthogonal orientation readouts and correlation with activity (addresses reviewer requirement)
5.1 Site-specific labeling strategy:
  • Introduce a single solvent-exposed cysteine at a position with known geometry relative to the active-site entrance (outside the docking clusters). Maintain a cysteine-free background if required.
5.2 Orientation measurement (orthogonal to FRET):
  • Spin labeling + DEER/EPR: attach MTSL (or equivalent) to the engineered cysteine; incorporate a second paramagnetic reference either by (i) a second label on MOF surface (post-synthetic introduction of nitroxide-bearing linker on external surface) or (ii) a metal ion tag localized to MOF nodes if chemically justified. Measure distance distributions to infer orientation heterogeneity.
  • In parallel, run protease-accessibility mapping of an engineered short peptide tag placed near the active-site entrance: higher cleavage implies “active-site outward” exposure. Use this as an independent proxy.
5.3 Correlate orientation with catalysis across variants:
  • For each (enzyme variant × MOF charge state × ionic strength), compute an “orientation order parameter” from DEER distance distribution width (narrower = more oriented) and from protease accessibility. Regress these against activity and apparent kinetic parameters to demonstrate causality (orientation → f_access → kcatapp).

Step 6 — Substrate partitioning/transport measurements and diffusion–reaction modeling (addresses KM attribution)
6.1 Measure substrate uptake/partition into MOFs:
  • Adsorption isotherms of hydroxypropylcarbamate substrates on each MOF at assay pH/ionic strength; quantify Kpart (MOF/solution). Where possible use in situ UV/vis, HPLC depletion, or ATR-FTIR.
  • Measure effective diffusivity (Deff): FRAP within particles (if fluorescent analog available) or pulsed-field gradient NMR for suitable probes; alternatively infer Deff from time-resolved uptake kinetics.
6.2 Integrate into a pore-transport kinetic model:
  • Use Thiele modulus/effectiveness factor η based on particle size, Deff, intrinsic kcat/KM, and enzyme distribution (f_internal). Pre-register a “transport-limited regime” criterion (e.g., η < 0.7 indicates significant diffusion limitation).
  • Predict when an apparent KM decrease is expected from partitioning alone (KM,app ≈ KM / Kpart under rapid equilibrium partitioning) versus when diffusion limitation will mask intrinsic changes.
6.3 Product inhibition/viscosity controls:
  • Measure product binding/inhibition constants (Ki) in free solution.
  • Measure microviscosity proxy inside MOF using fluorescent molecular rotors (if feasible) or infer from Deff.

Step 7 — Catalytic performance and stability testing with mechanistic perturbations
7.1 Kinetics:
  • Determine kcat, KM, and kcat/KM for free and immobilized enzyme under conditions explicitly classified as transport-limited vs non-limited using the model in Step 6.
  • Report intrinsic parameters corrected for η where applicable.
7.2 Electrostatic mechanism perturbations:
  • Salt series (25–200 mM) and pH series (6.5/7.5) applied to binding strength (ITC/MST or adsorption isotherms) and to orientation order parameter (DEER/protease tag). A true electrostatic docking-field mechanism predicts: binding/orientation strongly salt-dependent; intrinsic kcat (corrected) weakly salt-dependent.
7.3 Operational stability:
  • Thermal half-life at relevant temperatures; solvent tolerance (10–40% v/v acetonitrile or DMSO); reusability cycles with defined acceptance (e.g., ≥70% activity retained after 10 cycles).
  • Structural dynamics: limited proteolysis and/or HDX-MS focused on lid/loop regions to test whether immobilization reduces local exchange/proteolysis in a way that correlates with stability (not assumed).

Step 8 — Benchmarking and falsification controls
8.1 Benchmarks (must all be run under identical electrostatic/transport-characterized conditions):
  • WT enzyme on each MOF (NH2, SO3H, mixed-linker series).
  • Designed enzyme on neutral/low-|ζ| UiO-66 (or silica) matched for surface area.
  • Covalent immobilization control (e.g., mild EDC/NHS on a carboxylated support) to decouple “retention” from “oriented docking.”
8.2 Falsification tests:
  • If orientation order parameter does not improve vs WT yet activity increases, attribute gains to partitioning/transport or microenvironment; this is tested via Kpart/Deff and η-corrected kinetics.
  • If Kpart increases but KM,app does not decrease in non-transport-limited regime, reject the substrate-preconcentration explanation and focus on f_access/kcat changes.

Feasibility: Electrostatics and surface chemistry risk is mitigated by (i) pre-registering zeta potential targets measured in the exact assay buffers/ionic strengths, avoiding unsupported claims about UiO-66-NH2 charge state; and (ii) using mixed-linker and defect-modulated UiO-66 to empirically reach a defined ζ window while preserving crystallinity/porosity (PXRD/BET). The orientation premise is strengthened by replacing the speculative helix “lock” with a higher-order electrostatic geometry (two separated clusters with a defined dipole/quadrupole signature) that reduces degeneracy of binding poses on heterogeneous surfaces. Glycosylation—an outsized confound for Candida rugosa enzymes—is handled explicitly via controlled expression/deglyco designs, glycopeptide MS verification, and glycan-inclusive APBS modeling so engineered anisotropy is not nullified by glycan shielding. Transport and partitioning confounds are de-risked by directly measuring substrate uptake (Kpart) and diffusion proxies (Deff), quantifying internal vs external enzyme fractions, and applying an effectiveness-factor model to separate intrinsic catalytic changes from pore-transport artifacts; this directly addresses the reviewer’s concern that apparent KM shifts may be partition-driven. Finally, mechanistic causality is supported by orthogonal orientation readouts (DEER/EPR plus protease accessibility) and explicit correlation analyses across variants, rather than relying on FRET inference alone. Together, these upgrades preserve the original concept chain (rational protein design → electrostatic co-design with MOFs → oriented immobilization → higher apparent efficiency and stability) while making every key claim quantitatively testable with acceptance thresholds and falsification criteria.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually well-scaffolded with pre-registered quantitative gates, explicit falsification criteria, and a credible plan to separate orientation effects (f_access-driven kcat,app changes) from microenvironment/transport artifacts (Kpart, Deff, η). Engineering strength is high due to the integrated computational–experimental pipeline (glycoform-resolved electrostatics, ddG/aggregation filters, mixed-linker UiO-66 tuning, orthogonal orientation assays). However, several mechanistic and feasibility gaps remain: (i) converting ζ to surface charge density via Gouy–Chapman on porous, heterogeneous MOF particles is an approximate, model-dependent inference and may not correlate with the local fields experienced by enzymes at defect sites; (ii) the premise that dipole/quadrupole matching reduces pose degeneracy on heterogeneous adsorption landscapes is plausible but not rigorously demonstrated—surface patchiness, defect chemistry, and specific coordination/H-bonding may dominate over far-field multipoles at nanometer separations; (iii) DEER implementation risk is nontrivial (spin-label mobility, label distribution on MOF, paramagnetic relaxation from Zr nodes/adsorbed ions, and ensemble averaging) and may yield distance distributions that are difficult to map uniquely to orientation; (iv) Candida rugosa esterases/lipases can exhibit lid-mediated interfacial activation and strong glycosylation- and isoform-dependent behavior, so mutations remote from the active site may still allosterically affect lid dynamics, complicating attribution of kcat changes purely to accessibility/orientation; (v) the hypothesis that Kpart-driven substrate preconcentration will selectively decrease apparent KM only outside transport-limited regimes is correct in principle, but the plan should more explicitly address coupled effects of local pH/ionic strength shifts inside charged pores that can change both substrate ionization and catalytic residue pKa, masquerading as KM/kcat changes. Overall, the logic chain is coherent and testable, but some key physical linkages (ζ/σ → local field; multipole design → unique pose on real MOF surfaces; DEER observables → orientation fraction) need tighter validation steps.

original_chain: MTT assay -> Recombinant SARS-CoV-2 spike antigen -> Biosensor -> Erythritol -> NADH/NAD+ -> Directed evolution
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A low-leak, quantitatively benchmarked membrane binding-to-transcription interface (screened across synNotch, split-TEV, and chemically inducible heterodimer controls) can convert extracellular recombinant SARS‑CoV‑2 spike antigen engagement into a reporter output whose magnitude is dominated by engineered NADH/NAD+/redox-state transduction rather than by homeostatic buffering—provided that (i) the interface is first locked to defined kinetics (EC50, leak, response time) and (ii) the redox actuator operates within a pre-defined “signal budget” that perturbs the cytosolic NADH/NAD+ ratio enough to be resolvable by a dedicated NADH/NAD+-responsive sensor but small enough to avoid global compensatory metabolic rewiring. Specificity and low false-signal performance will be achieved not by using MTT as a nonlinear denominator, but by orthogonal, non-destructive viability/stress gating (constitutive luciferase for cell number + Annexin/PI or real-time impedance), with MTT retained only as a terminal corroborative assay and with erythritol treated as an optional variance-reduction reagent whose effect must be empirically calibrated to confirm it lowers assay variance without shifting circuit baselines. Directed evolution will be recast into a recoverable, throughput-compatible selection using FACS on a genetically encoded redox reporter (primary) plus independent viability counters (exclusion), and transferability to a deployable MOF-based biosensor will be demonstrated via an explicit bridging assay in which the same evolved spike binders are rank-ordered in both cell-based (interface-driven reporter) and cell-free/MOF (capture + enzymatic NADH transduction) formats rather than assuming mapping a priori.
Plan: Step 0 — Define quantitative performance targets (“acceptance criteria” and signal budget)
0.1 Define required sensor performance for the cell-based stage: (a) leak (no spike) < 5% of induced signal; (b) on/off fold-change ≥ 5× at 10–50 nM spike; (c) t50 (time to half-max reporter) ≤ 2 h for transcriptional outputs or ≤ 15 min for protease outputs; (d) assay Z’ ≥ 0.5 in 96-well format; (e) false-positive rate (FPR) ≤ 1% when challenged with generic stressors (oligomycin, rotenone, antimycin A, H2O2, FCCP) at sublethal doses.
0.2 Define an NADH/NAD+ “signal budget” to avoid global compensation: target an engineered cytosolic NADH/NAD+ ratio change of ~10–25% (detectable by genetically encoded sensors) while maintaining ≥ 90% viability and ≤ 15% change in ATP levels over the assay window. This is enforced by actuator tuning (weak/medium promoters, degrons, or short pulse activation) and validated by orthogonal NAD(H) measurements.

Step 1 — Lock down the binding-to-signal interface with quantitative benchmarking (before redox engineering)
