STEP 1 — ENGINEERED CELL LINES AND BENCHMARK CONDITIONS
1.1 Isogenic iPSC line engineering (single-cell cloned; at least n=3 clones per genotype):
  (i) Endogenous YAP1 fluorescent knock-in (C-terminus YAP-mNeonGreen) using HDR; validate YAP function by TEAD reporter response and naïve induction capacity.
  (ii) TEAD activity reporter: 8xTEAD-binding sites (MCAT elements) upstream of a minimal promoter driving destabilized NanoLuc (PEST-tag; half-life ~20–40 min) to match pulse kinetics.
  (iii) Cell-cycle staging: FUCCI (mCherry-Cdt1(30–120)/mVenus-Geminin(1–110)).
  (iv) Optional: dCas9-KRAB-MeCP2 inducible cassette for CRISPRi (Tet-On) to enable rapid repression at selected HERV-H LTRs.
  QC: karyotype at baseline (SNP-array), pluripotency markers, mycoplasma negative.

1.2 Benchmark naïve induction and YAP modulation conditions (to resolve state vs mechanism):
  A. Published constant LPA (e.g., 1–5 µM continuous; titrate) + naïve medium (match the Yin/Lin PSC induction context).
  B. YAP overexpression positive control (doxy-inducible; modest expression matched to avoid supra-physiologic).
  C. Mechanical activation only: defined hydrogel stiffness without LPA.
  D. Closed-loop pulsing (controller-defined below).
  E. Negative controls: YAP–TEAD disruption (e.g., verteporfin or inducible dominant-negative TEAD) and YAP S94A (TEAD-binding deficient) rescue line.

STEP 2 — MICROENGINEERED PLATFORM AND CONTROLLER SPECIFICATION
2.1 Culture substrate architecture (mechanical gating with defined parameters):
  - Micropatterned PEGDA or polyacrylamide hydrogels with collagen-I/laminin-521 functionalization.
  - Stiffness gradient spanning 0.5, 2, 5, 10, 20 kPa in discrete lanes to simplify assignment; micropattern islands of 400, 900, 1600 µm^2 to control spreading.
  - Confirm effective modulus by AFM indentation; confirm uniform ligand density by fluorescent ECM tagging.

2.2 Microfluidic delivery:
  - Two-input laminar flow device enabling rapid exchange between naïve medium ± LPA.
  - Exchange time constant target: <60 s in culture chamber (validated with dye).
  - LPA pulse library: 5, 15, 30, 60 min pulses at 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5 µM.

2.3 Quantitative feedback controller (pre-specified):
  - Sampling: image YAP-mNeonGreen and FUCCI every 5 min (low phototoxicity settings; red/green minimal exposure).
  - State estimation: compute nuclear/cytoplasmic YAP ratio (N/C) using automated segmentation; compute TEAD-NanoLuc luminescence every 10–15 min (integrated luminometer) or intermittent high-sensitivity imaging.
  - Control objective: maintain YAP N/C within a target band [r_low, r_high] during G1 and G2, and below r_S_max during S-phase (FUCCI-defined), where initial values are empirically set from Step 3 directionality mapping (e.g., r_low=1.2, r_high=1.8; r_S_max=1.1; placeholders until calibrated).
  - Controller logic: hybrid bang-bang + hysteresis with delay compensation:
      If FUCCI=S-phase → enforce LPA=OFF unless YAP N/C < r_min_safety for >15 min (prevents collapse).
      If FUCCI=G1 early (first 2–3 h post-mitosis) → allow LPA pulses to drive YAP N/C into [r_low, r_high] for T_on then OFF until N/C decays below r_low.
      If N/C > r_high → immediate OFF; lockout 30 min.
  - Performance metrics: (i) time-in-band (%), (ii) overshoot integral, (iii) mean S-phase fraction matched across conditions (see Step 5), (iv) robustness across clones (variance of N/C dynamics <20%).
  - Feasibility risk mitigation: run controller for 72 h first (short-term), then scale to weekly repeated cycles rather than continuous live control during months-long passaging.

STEP 3 — NODE 1: DIRECTIONALITY OF YAP EFFECT ON HERV-H (NAScent transcription, locus-resolved)
3.1 Define “active HERV-H loci panel” (pre-selected):
  - Use existing iPSC RNA-seq to nominate top 50 expressed HERV-H LTRs with unique flanking sequences (≥200 bp unique flank) enabling locus assignment.
  - Downselect to 20 loci with robust unique mappability (k-mer based) and validated expression by locus-specific RT-qPCR (primer in unique flank + LTR junction).

3.2 Acute YAP perturbation time course (to avoid confounding state transitions):
  - Conditions: (i) LPA step-on (1–5 µM), (ii) mechanical stiffening (move to 10–20 kPa), (iii) YAP–TEAD disruption, (iv) vehicle.
  - Sampling: 0, 15, 30, 60, 120, 240 min.
  - Assay: TT-seq or PRO-seq (preferred PRO-seq for immediate transcriptional engagement) with emphasis on uniquely mappable junction/flank reads to the 20 loci.
  - Output: per-locus transcription change sign and magnitude; classify loci as YAP-up, YAP-down, or YAP-insensitive.

STEP 4 — NODE 2: LOCUS-RESOLVED R-LOOPS AND DAMAGE WITH ORTHOGONAL ASSAYS (repeat-suitable)
4.1 R-loop mapping (two orthogonal methods + locus-resolved quant):
  (i) DRIP-qPCR on the 20 loci using S9.6 with rigorous RNase H controls (in vitro RNase H pretreatment; include RNase A/T1 to reduce RNA artifacts). Primers in unique flanks.
  (ii) R-ChIP: catalytically dead RNase H1 (D210N) expressed transiently (24 h) to pull down R-loops; qPCR to unique flanks and/or targeted sequencing.
  Decision criterion: concordance of direction across DRIP-qPCR and R-ChIP for ≥70% of loci.

4.2 Damage localization to HERV-H loci (repeat-compatible strategies):
  (i) CUT&RUN or CUT&Tag for γH2AX and 53BP1 with spike-in normalization; enrich and quantify signal using targeted capture to unique flanks adjacent to the 20 LTRs (hybridization capture panel) to overcome repeat multi-mapping.
  (ii) ImmunoFISH: design FISH probes to unique flanking regions (not LTR consensus) for a subset (e.g., 6 loci), co-stain γH2AX/53BP1; quantify co-localization frequency across cell-cycle stages.

4.3 TRC markers at loci:
  - pRPA(S33) CUT&Tag (or IF + locus FISH) and S9.6 IF with RNase H control; quantify enrichment specifically in S-phase (FUCCI gating).

STEP 5 — MECHANISTIC INTERMEDIATES CONNECTING YAP TO REPLICATION STRESS (required)
5.1 Replication timing / domain changes:
  - Repli-seq (Early vs Late fractions) under constant LPA vs pulsed vs control to test if YAP shifts replication timing of HERV-H-adjacent domains.
  - Alternatively/additionally EdU-seq for higher temporal resolution around pulse windows.

5.2 Fork dynamics:
  - DNA fiber assay with CldU/IdU labeling; quantify fork speed, asymmetry, and stall frequency under (i) constant LPA, (ii) closed-loop pulsing, (iii) YAP–TEAD inhibited.
  - Analyze separately for FUCCI-sorted S-phase cells to avoid distribution confounds.

5.3 Origin firing and pausing factors (chromatin/replication interface):
  - CUT&Tag for ORC2/MCM2 (licensing), BRD4 (elongation/TRC), TOP1, RAD21 (cohesin), and CTCF at unique flanks near HERV-H loci; integrate with ATAC-seq and H3K27ac/H3K9me3 to operationalize “mechanically gated chromatin state” as quantifiable accessibility/insulation/heterochromatin changes.

STEP 6 — NODE 3: DISCRIMINATING CAUSALITY (HERV-H as driver vs marker)
6.1 HERV-H transcription necessity/sufficiency tests:
  - Necessity: CRISPRi (dCas9-KRAB-MeCP2) targeting LTR promoters at the 20 loci (pool of 2–3 gRNAs per locus; validated repression by PRO-seq/RT-qPCR). Evaluate whether constant LPA-induced damage/SVs are reduced to pulsing-like levels.
  - Sufficiency: if YAP decreases HERV-H transcription and reduces damage, then targeted activation (dCas9-p300 or VP64) at selected loci during S-phase should reinstate R-loops/damage despite pulsing.

6.2 R-loop dependency:
  - RNase H1 overexpression (WT) vs catalytically dead control; test whether it rescues constant LPA condition and whether it eliminates additional benefit from pulsing (epistasis).
  - Short transcription inhibition windows (e.g., low-dose CDK9 inhibitor for 30–60 min) specifically during S-phase to mimic reduced transcription–replication overlap; compare to pulsing.

6.3 TEAD dependency:
  - Use YAP S94A (TEAD-binding deficient) and/or inducible dominant-negative TEAD during pulses; must abrogate any observed locus-resolved transcription change and genome-stability improvement.

STEP 7 — CONTROL FOR YAP-DRIVEN CELL-CYCLE REDISTRIBUTION (required)
7.1 Match on S-phase fraction:
  - For each condition, adjust seeding density and pulse schedule to achieve matched FUCCI-derived S-phase fraction (±5%) during sampling windows.
  - Perform analyses on FUCCI-sorted populations (G1 vs S/G2) when feasible.

7.2 Synchronization paradigm (orthogonal validation):
  - Thymidine double block or CDK4/6 inhibitor release into S-phase; apply YAP pulses strictly pre-S vs during-S to directly test timing causality while holding cell-cycle entry constant.

STEP 8 — LONGITUDINAL GENOME INTEGRITY AND SV READOUTS (karyotype endpoint)
8.1 Passaging study:
  - 20–40 passages with weekly sampling; controller applied in scheduled cycles (e.g., 72 h control per week) to reduce operational burden and phototoxicity.

8.2 SV detection optimized for repeats:
  - Low-pass WGS every 5 passages for CNVs/aneuploidy.
  - Targeted long-read sequencing (ONT/PacBio) with capture probes to HERV-H-rich regions and the 20 loci flanks to quantify SV breakpoints and rearrangements.
  - Statistical model: mixed-effects with clone as random effect; predictors include time-in-YAP-band, S-phase fraction, per-locus nascent transcription, per-locus R-loop and damage signals.

STEP 9 — NAÏVE PLURIPOTENCY MAINTENANCE (non-negotiable outcome)
9.1 State validation under each regimen:
  - Naïve markers (e.g., KLF17, TFCP2L1, DNMT3L), primed markers suppression, clonogenicity.
  - Transcriptomic resemblance to pre-implantation signatures (reference mapping).
  - Differentiation competence: in vitro trilineage and/or teratoma where appropriate.

DELIVERABLES / ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- A signed directionality map: per-locus YAP→HERV-H nascent transcription sign.
- A validated locus-resolved R-loop/damage toolkit (DRIP-qPCR + R-ChIP + γH2AX/53BP1 CUT&Tag with flank capture + immunoFISH).
- Replication-stress intermediates demonstrating whether pulsing reduces fork stalling/TRCs.
- A controller spec with quantitative performance metrics and robustness across clones.
- A mechanistic verdict: HERV-H transcription causal driver vs marker, based on epistasis (CRISPRi/RNase H1/TEAD dependence) and temporal precedence.
Feasibility: This revision directly addresses reviewer concerns by converting assumptions into a pre-registered, discriminating causal chain with explicit directionality tests, locus-resolved repeat-compatible assays, and replication-stress intermediates.

1) Directionality at HERV-H is not assumed: acute YAP perturbation with PRO-seq/TT-seq establishes whether YAP/TEAD increases or decreases nascent transcription at uniquely assigned active LTRs, and temporal sampling tests precedence over R-loops/damage.

2) HERV-H as driver vs marker is explicitly tested: CRISPRi repression of active LTRs, locus-specific activation (if needed), and RNase H1 epistasis experiments determine whether changing HERV-H output is necessary/sufficient for stability phenotypes.

3) Mechanistic intermediates connect YAP to replication stress: Repli-seq/EdU-seq, DNA fiber assays, and TRC markers (pRPA/S9.6 with RNase controls) operationalize the proposed ‘mechanically gated chromatin/replication’ link rather than leaving it as a conceptual bridge.

4) Repeat-appropriate localization reduces global-assay bias: DRIP is restricted to validated loci via qPCR, orthogonally validated by R-ChIP; damage is assigned using CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN with unique-flank capture plus immunoFISH on unique flanks, minimizing multi-mapping ambiguity.

5) Closed-loop control feasibility is de-risked: the controller is specified quantitatively (sampling rate, thresholds, hysteresis/lockout, performance metrics). To avoid long-term live-imaging fragility, control is deployed in scheduled short windows (e.g., 72 h/week) while still testing longitudinal genome outcomes. Robustness across clones is built into acceptance criteria.

6) Cell-cycle confounding is controlled: conditions are matched on S-phase fraction (FUCCI) and validated under synchronized release, ensuring any benefit is not merely due to YAP-driven redistribution of the cell cycle.

Finally, the plan remains coherent with the original concept—engineering YAP dynamics via mechanical and chemical inputs to stabilize naïve iPSCs—while making the mechanism testable at each link (YAP→HERV-H transcription→R-loops/TRCs→damage→SVs/karyotype).
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and over-specified proposal that directly addresses prior underdetermination. The strongest aspect is the pre-registered causal chain with explicit go/no-go criteria, which enforces falsifiability at each mechanistic link. Engineering resolution is exceptionally high: locus-resolved repeat handling, orthogonal R-loop assays, replication intermediates, and a quantitatively defined feedback controller are all state-of-the-art and coherently integrated. Logical consistency is also strong; the proposal convincingly argues that timing and amplitude of YAP-driven transcription—rather than steady-state levels—are the mechanistic levers connecting YAP to karyotypic instability via TRCs at HERV-H. Minor deductions arise from feasibility risk aggregation: the plan stacks multiple technically demanding platforms (live-cell control, microfluidics, PRO-seq, CUT&Tag with capture, long-read SV mapping) into a single project, increasing execution risk despite mitigation strategies. Evidence grounding is solid, though the causal prominence of HERV-H relative to other naïve-state repeats (e.g., LINE-1, SVA) is assumed rather than comparatively tested, which slightly weakens exclusivity of the concept chain. Rationale quality is high: the proposal does not merely apply YAP modulation but reframes it as a time-resolved control problem aligned with replication biology, which is a nontrivial conceptual advance.

original_chain: Urinary metabolites -> Cancer biomarkers -> Biodegradability -> Urea -> Hepatic stellate cell -> Homologous recombination -> Bioartificial liver device
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A bioartificial liver (BAL) containing gene-edited, urea-cycle–augmented hepatocyte-like cells and quiescence-biased hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), housed in a biodegradable, metabolite-permeable hydrogel barrier, will simultaneously (i) restore ammonia-to-urea detoxification and (ii) reduce pro-fibrotic HSC activation; this will generate a characteristic, quantifiable shift in urinary metabolite signatures that can serve as noninvasive cancer biomarker surveillance in patients with liver dysfunction. Mechanistically, precise homologous recombination will install a tunable CPS1–OTC–ASS1–ASL–ARG1 expression cassette at a hepatic safe-harbor locus to increase urea-cycle flux (lowering systemic ammonia and glutamine spillover), while a parallel knock-in in HSCs will enforce a quiescent transcriptional state (dampening TGF-β/LOX/SPP1-driven matrix remodeling). The methodological adaptation is a dual-function BAL cartridge that replaces standard inert hollow-fiber membranes with a two-layer architecture: an inner shear-protective microfluidic hepatocyte channel and an outer biodegradable hydrogel 'metabolite window' that is engineered to be selectively permeable to small nitrogen and cancer-related metabolites while excluding immune cells and high-MW proteins; the hydrogel is doped with cleavable crosslinkers to allow controlled biodegradation and real-time metabolite sampling without device disassembly.
Plan: Step 1: System setup and baseline mapping.
1.1 Build a benchtop BAL loop (recirculating plasma/albumin dialysate) with oxygenation control and integrated sampling ports for perfusate and urine-mimic collection.
1.2 Establish baseline metabolic panels linking nitrogen handling and oncologic metabolite proxies: ammonia, urea, glutamine/glutamate, lactate, bile acids, and a targeted urinary metabolite panel (LC-MS/MS) including tryptophan-kynurenine metabolites and polyamine-related metabolites relevant to cancer biomarker contexts.
1.3 Generate iHepSC/iEC-derived hepatic assembloids (per iHEA logic) and co-culture with primary-like HSCs in 3D to benchmark urea production and HSC activation markers (COL1A1, ACTA2, LOX, SPP1).

Step 2: Implement the adapted methodology (dual homologous recombination + biodegradable metabolite-window BAL).
2.1 Homologous recombination engineering in hepatocyte-like cells: use nuclease-assisted targeting (e.g., TALEN/ZFN-guided) to drive HDR into an AAVS1-like hepatic safe-harbor locus, inserting a doxycycline-tunable urea-cycle enhancement cassette (CPS1, OTC, ASS1, ASL, ARG1 under liver-enriched promoters with insulated elements). Include a fluorescent reporter and a kill-switch module for safety.
2.2 Homologous recombination engineering in HSCs: knock-in a quiescence-bias module (e.g., CRISPR/HDR insertion of an inducible dominant-negative TGF-β signaling node or a transcriptional repressor targeting LOX/SPP1 enhancers) while preserving viability and paracrine support; validate reduced activation under TGF-β challenge.
2.3 Methodological adaptation of the BAL cartridge: fabricate a microfluidic hollow-fiber–inspired device but replace conventional inert membranes with a two-layer barrier: (i) a thin, nondegradable endothelialized layer facing blood/plasma to minimize thrombosis; (ii) an outer biodegradable hydrogel layer (enzyme-cleavable peptide crosslinks; controlled mesh size) tuned for selective diffusion of small metabolites (ammonia, urea, selected cancer-related metabolites) while limiting immunoglobulin/complement penetration. Incorporate sampling microports embedded in the hydrogel to extract dialysate for continuous metabolomics.
2.4 Assemble a tri-culture module (engineered hepatocytes + iECs + engineered HSCs) within the protected channel; apply physiologic shear and oxygen gradients to promote maturation and stable urea-cycle activity.

Step 3: Validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Functional efficacy: quantify ammonia clearance kinetics, urea synthesis rate, and nitrogen balance under stepwise ammonia loading; compare (a) unedited cells in standard membrane BAL, (b) edited hepatocytes only, (c) edited hepatocytes + edited HSCs, with and without the metabolite-window hydrogel.
3.2 Mechanistic validation: use 13C/15N tracer flux analysis to confirm increased urea-cycle throughput and reduced glutamine siphoning; transcript/protein confirmation of cassette expression; assess HSC activation state by single-cell RNA-seq and ECM deposition assays.
3.3 Biodegradability and transport validation: measure hydrogel mass loss, pore/mesh evolution, and diffusion coefficients for representative analytes; test immune exclusion (IgG penetration) and hemocompatibility (complement activation, platelet adhesion).
3.4 Urinary metabolite-to-biomarker readout: in a rodent liver-injury model connected to an extracorporeal BAL circuit, collect urine longitudinally and perform targeted+untargeted metabolomics. Build a predictive model linking device performance (urea flux, ammonia clearance) to urinary metabolite patterns and to cancer-biomarker–adjacent signatures; verify that improved nitrogen detoxification reduces confounding elevations that otherwise mask biomarker interpretation.
3.5 Comparative advantage metrics: survival/encephalopathy scores (in acute failure models), reduction of fibrotic signaling, stability of hepatocyte function over time, and sensitivity/specificity improvement for urinary biomarker panels under impaired liver function.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 2 supports that assembloid architecture increases urea production and reduces HSC activation; Asset 3 supports leveraging enhanced homologous recombination/genome engineering and microfluidic/bioreactor contexts to sustain hepatocyte-like function relevant to BAL devices; Asset 1 supports nanosensor/metabolite detection logic and the practical importance of urinary metabolites and cancer biomarker detection, motivating the need to de-confound biomarker interpretation via controlled metabolic normalization.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Conventional BALs focus on detoxification but lack built-in, noninvasive biomarker interpretability and do not actively suppress HSC-driven fibrogenic signaling in the cell compartment. The adapted biodegradable metabolite-window barrier turns the cartridge into both a therapeutic reactor (enhanced urea-cycle flux) and an analytical interface (continuous, selective metabolite sampling) while protecting cells from immune attack; dual HDR engineering directly targets the mechanistic bottlenecks (insufficient urea-cycle capacity; HSC activation) rather than generic differentiation.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to standard BAL membranes and unedited hepatocyte-like cells, the proposed system should (i) increase maximal urea synthesis and ammonia clearance (cassette-driven flux control), (ii) prolong functional stability by reducing pro-fibrotic microenvironmental drift (engineered quiescent HSCs), and (iii) enable higher-fidelity urinary cancer biomarker monitoring by reducing liver-failure–induced metabolic noise and providing device-coupled metabolite ground truth through the engineered metabolite window.
final_critique: This is an unusually ambitious and technically dense proposal that largely succeeds in maintaining internal coherence across genetic engineering, biomaterials, and metabolomics. Engineering resolution is high: the HDR cassette design, flux validation via isotope tracing, and hydrogel transport characterization are well specified and non-generic. However, several risks reduce the score: (i) multiplex HDR in hepatocyte-like cells and HSCs is assumed to be efficient and stable without a realistic contingency for low knock-in rates or clonal drift; (ii) the hydrogel’s simultaneous requirements—immune exclusion, selective metabolite permeability, biodegradability, and embedded sampling—are individually feasible but collectively under-parameterized, particularly regarding long-term mechanical stability under flow; (iii) the leap from normalized nitrogen metabolism to improved cancer biomarker interpretability is conceptually sound but empirically thin, relying on correlation-heavy metabolomics rather than a priori causal biomarkers. Logical consistency is strong but strained at the final translational link (BAL performance → urinary cancer surveillance), where alternative confounders (renal handling, systemic inflammation) are not adequately controlled. Evidence grounding is solid and stays within bioengineering/biomedical domains, though some oncologic biomarker claims verge on overgeneralization. The rationale is creative and addresses a real BAL bottleneck, but breadth occasionally comes at the expense of depth in failure-mode analysis.

original_chain: Smart library -> Protein sequence -> Protein Data Bank -> Homology model -> I-Tasser -> Thermodynamic stability -> RNA-binding repressor of primer
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A thermodynamically stabilized RNA-binding repressor of primer (ROP) with preserved RNA-binding geometry can be engineered by a structure-informed “hydrophobic-core-and-interface smart library” that is constrained by multi-template homology models (PDB-derived) and I-TASSER, and filtered by ΔΔG-based stability calculations plus RNA-binding pose conservation. Mechanistically, enforcing (i) coiled-coil heptad-register hydrophobic packing at the ROP dimer core and (ii) electrostatic/hydrogen-bond complementarity at the RNA-contact surface reduces the unfolded-state entropy and lowers the free energy of the native dimeric fold without perturbing the RNA-binding conformation, yielding variants with higher thermodynamic stability (ΔGfold) while retaining primer-repression function.
Plan: Step 1: System setup and data preparation.
1.1 Select a canonical ROP/primer repressor sequence (or a close homolog) and collect homologous structures from the Protein Data Bank (including ROP-like folds and coiled-coil dimers) to maximize template diversity in the RNA-binding and dimerization regions.
1.2 Build an ensemble of homology models: (a) multi-template comparative models from PDB templates and (b) independent I-TASSER models; retain the top models by composite structural quality metrics (MolProbity + PROCHECK + WHAT_CHECK) and agreement across modeling methods.
1.3 Annotate functional constraints: map predicted RNA-binding residues (electrostatic patches, conserved basic residues) and dimer interface residues; define “no-mutate” positions using conservation + structural role (salt bridges, glycine/helix capping, interfacial hot spots).

Step 2: Adapted methodology—smart library design coupled to stability-and-geometry gates.
2.1 Methodological adaptation (core innovation): construct a smart library that is not residue-by-residue randomization, but a blockwise, heptad-register-aware design where mutations are proposed as coupled sets across the coiled-coil dimer (symmetry-enforced) to preserve packing periodicity. Specifically:
- Hydrophobic-core module: only mutate a/d heptad positions to a restricted alphabet (I, L, V, F, M) with pairwise coupling rules that maintain knob-into-hole packing across the dimer interface.
- Helix capping module: allow targeted N- and C-cap optimization (e.g., Asn/Asp/Ser/Thr at caps) to reduce helix fraying.
- Interfacial electrostatics module: propose compensatory charge-swap pairs (e.g., E↔K) across the interface to strengthen salt-bridge networks without changing net RNA-binding surface potential.
- RNA-binding preservation module: constrain mutations in the RNA-contact patch to conservative substitutions only, and require that the electrostatic potential map of the binding surface remains within a predefined similarity threshold to the parent.
2.2 Generate candidate sequences by integrating model ensemble uncertainty: accept mutations only if they are predicted stabilizing (median ΔΔG < 0) across multiple backbone models (homology + I-TASSER), thereby avoiding model-specific artifacts.
2.3 Stability filtering: compute ΔΔG for each candidate using two independent estimators (FoldX and Rosetta) and retain variants with concordant stabilization predictions; additionally enforce increased dimer interface energy (ΔGinterface improvement) while keeping monomer fold stable.
2.4 Geometry/functional filtering: dock/position a representative RNA/primer hairpin (or minimal RNA motif) onto the modeled protein using a restrained pose (based on conserved basic patch geometry); reject variants that shift key RNA-contact sidechains beyond a tight RMSD/angle tolerance or that alter predicted binding-pocket electrostatics.
2.5 Build a focused experimental library (10^2–10^3 variants, not 10^6) using multiplexed, degenerate codons encoding only the allowed amino-acid sets per module; include symmetry-linked mutations where required to preserve coiled-coil register.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Expression and biophysical stability: express/purify top variants; quantify thermodynamic stability via chemical denaturation (ΔGfold, m-value) and thermal melting (Tm) plus oligomeric state by SEC-MALS to verify dimerization.
3.2 RNA-binding and repression function: quantify RNA/primer binding affinity and kinetics (MST or SPR/biolayer) using the target RNA motif; validate repression activity in a cell-based reporter where primer-dependent expression is inhibited by functional ROP.
3.3 Mechanism tests: (i) HDX-MS or limited proteolysis to confirm reduced local unfolding in the core/caps, (ii) alanine-scanning of newly introduced salt bridges to verify causal contribution to stability, and (iii) correlate stability gains with preserved RNA-binding electrostatic potential and contact geometry.
3.4 Benchmarking: compare against (a) random mutagenesis library hits and (b) single-point “best-ΔΔG” designs lacking heptad-coupling rules to quantify the benefit of the adapted smart-library constraints on stability/function retention rate.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Hydrophobic core packing and coiled-coil heptad periodicity are established determinants of thermodynamic stability; ROP has prior evidence linking core arrangement to conformational specificity and function. Ensemble modeling (PDB-based homology + I-TASSER) plus structure validation metrics is an established route to usable structural surrogates when crystal structures are absent, and ΔΔG screening via Rosetta/FoldX is a validated approach to avoid destabilizing mutations.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal adapts semi-rational protein design concepts (smart libraries + stability scoring) to an RNA-binding repressor where function is geometry- and electrostatics-sensitive. The key adaptation is enforcing coiled-coil register/symmetry and multi-model consensus ΔΔG gating, which directly targets the dominant stability mechanism (core/interface packing) while constraining RNA-binding determinants.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with generic hotspot mutagenesis or random libraries, the heptad-coupled, symmetry-aware library increases the fraction of properly folded dimers and reduces functional attrition. Compared with single-model in silico design, multi-backbone consensus filters reduce false positives from modeling errors. The combined stability-and-geometry gates specifically address the common failure mode in stabilizing RNA-binding proteins: improved stability at the cost of altered binding surface conformation.
final_critique: This is a technically mature and unusually well-specified proposal that demonstrates strong command of coiled-coil protein physics, RNA-binding constraints, and modern semi-rational protein design workflows. The engineering plan is executable and goes beyond generic mutagenesis by enforcing symmetry, heptad periodicity, and ensemble-model consensus—all of which directly target known failure modes in stabilizing RNA-binding proteins. The logic connecting hydrophobic-core optimization, reduced unfolded-state entropy, and preserved RNA-binding geometry is largely sound and mechanistically grounded. Minor score deductions stem from two areas: (i) reliance on ΔΔG predictors (FoldX/Rosetta) for coiled-coil dimers, where absolute accuracy is limited and context-dependent, and (ii) the RNA-docking/pose-conservation filter is described conceptually but lacks specificity about how RNA flexibility and induced fit will be handled, which could inflate false negatives. These are limitations of rigor rather than imagination.

original_chain: Fibrogenesis -> Primary biliary cholangitis -> DHEA-S -> Dehydroepiandrosterone -> Androgen receptor -> Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) -> Dehydroepiandrosterone -> Estrogen receptor alpha
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: In primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), the disease-shifted steroid enzyme balance (↓SULT1E1, ↑STS) increases the local capacity of bile-duct epithelium to desulfate circulating/ductal DHEA-S into DHEA precisely at the inflamed ductular interface. Under bile-acid/ROS stress, a controlled pulse of intra-cholangiocyte DHEA can bias stress-response programs toward anti-apoptosis and redox buffering while dampening maladaptive cholangiocyte-to-portal paracrine outputs that drive portal inflammation and hepatic stellate cell (HSC) activation (TGF-β/PDGF/CTGF/CCL2/IL-6 axis), thereby reducing fibrogenesis (Asset 1 mechanistic link) and preserving duct integrity (Asset 2 cytoprotection link). To overcome the key translational risks identified by reviewers—(i) STS ubiquity and (ii) aryl-sulfamate triggers behaving as irreversible inhibitors rather than clean substrates—we will engineer and quantitatively validate a bile-duct-enriched, STS-activated “substrate-not-inhibitor” prodrug system whose activation is governed by: (a) demonstrable catalytic turnover by purified STS (high kcat with low time-dependent inactivation), (b) a PK/PD model integrating measured STS activity distributions across human PBC ducts/hepatocytes/immune cells and nanoparticle exposure to predict on-target DHEA release vs systemic burden, and (c) explicit control of downstream steroid metabolism (DHEA→androstenedione/testosterone/estradiol), enabling causal attribution to ERα and/or AR in cholangiocytes (with aromatase/17β-HSD blockade to isolate direct receptor signaling from downstream sex-steroid conversion). We predict that a duct-targeted, STS-activated DHEA prodrug will achieve higher cholangiocyte-local receptor engagement under cholestatic oxidative stress with lower systemic androgenic/estrogenic exposure than free DHEA/DHEA-S, yielding net suppression of immune-mediated portal injury and HSC-driven collagen deposition in both cholestatic injury (BDL) and bona fide autoimmune cholangitis models.
Plan: Step 1 — Quantitative human mapping (activity, not just expression) to parameterize selectivity and PK/PD.
1.1 Spatial “STS activity distribution” atlas in human PBC.
- Samples: human PBC explants/biopsies stratified early vs late stage; non-PBC cholestatic controls where available.
- Readouts:
  (i) Multiplex IF + RNAscope: STS, SULT1E1, ERα, AR co-registered with KRT19/SOX9 (ductular reaction), COL1A1/ACTA2 (fibrosis), CD68/CD163 (macrophages), EPCAM.
  (ii) Quantitative enzyme activity: apply sulfatase activity-based probes (ABPs) optimized for STS (fluorophosphonate/arylsulfate-mimetic ABPs where appropriate) plus orthogonal biochemical activity from laser-capture microdissected ducts vs periportal hepatocytes vs immune infiltrates; report activity as pmol substrate converted/min/mg protein.
  (iii) Single-cell/spatial transcriptomics (targeted panel acceptable): confirm STS/SULT1E1 and steroid-metabolism nodes (HSD3B, HSD17B isoforms, CYP19A1/aromatase, SRD5A1/2) in cholangiocytes vs macrophages vs HSC.
- Output: probability distributions of STS activity per cell-type compartment (duct epithelium, hepatocyte, macrophage) to feed Step 2 PK/PD.

1.2 Microphysiological PBC platform with compartment control.
- Chip architecture: dual-channel microfluidic device with (a) apical “bile” channel lined by cholangiocyte organoid-derived epithelium under flow, and (b) basolateral “portal” channel containing Kupffer-like macrophages and primary human HSC embedded in ECM hydrogel (collagen I/Matrigel blend, stiffness tuned 1–5 kPa).
- Stressors: deliver GCDC to apical channel; deliver controlled ROS flux (e.g., menadione or H2O2 microdosing) with real-time ROS sensors; maintain bile-acid gradients (apical>>basolateral) to mimic cholestasis.
- Patient relevance: prioritize PBC patient-derived cholangiocytes when feasible; otherwise iPSC-cholangiocytes conditioned with PBC-like cytokines (IL-17A, IFN-γ, TNF-α) to approximate inflammatory cholangitis.

Step 2 — Prodrug chemistry redesign and a mandatory substrate-vs-inhibitor validation package.
2.1 Trigger strategy: explicitly de-risk aryl-sulfamate irreversible inhibition.
- Parallel trigger families (screened head-to-head):
  A) Sulfate ester self-immolative prodrug (preferred “substrate-first”): DHEA-O-SO3− linked via a para-hydroxybenzyl (PHB) self-immolative spacer that releases native DHEA after STS-catalyzed sulfate hydrolysis and 1,6-elimination; electronics tuned (para substituents) to reduce non-enzymatic hydrolysis at pH 7.4 while maintaining STS turnover.
  B) “Soft-sulfamate” analogs only if A fails: N-alkyl/aryl sulfamates engineered to minimize time-dependent STS inactivation (avoid classic aryl-sulfamate motifs known for suicide inhibition); include leaving-group tuning and sterics to favor turnover.
- Decision gate: advance only triggers meeting strict enzymology thresholds in 2.2.

2.2 Mandatory substrate-vs-inhibitor validation (purified enzyme + cellular genetics).
- Purified STS assays:
  (i) Steady-state kinetics: measure kcat, KM, kcat/KM for each candidate trigger using recombinant human STS (membrane prep or nanodisc-reconstituted STS); quantify product DHEA by LC–MS/MS.
  (ii) Time-dependent inhibition (TDI): preincubate STS with candidate at multiple concentrations and times; measure residual activity on a standard fluorescent STS substrate; fit kinact/KI. Hard criterion: minimal TDI (kinact/KI below predefined threshold relative to a known irreversible inhibitor control).
  (iii) Partition ratio (turnover vs inactivation): determine molecules of DHEA released per STS molecule before activity loss.
- Cellular genetic rescue:
  (i) STS knockout (CRISPR) and STS overexpression in human cholangiocytes; confirm that prodrug→DHEA conversion and phenotypes scale with STS abundance.
  (ii) Rescue experiment: reintroduce STS in KO background to restore activation.
  (iii) Off-target sulfatase panel: evaluate activation in ARSA/ARSB/other sulfatases (purified or cell lines) to ensure specificity is not broadly sulfatase-driven.

2.3 Bile-duct enrichment: nanoparticle parameters specified and measurable.
- Carrier: PEG-PLGA nanoparticles (50–90 nm target hydrodynamic diameter; PDI <0.2) with (i) near-neutral zeta potential (−5 to +5 mV) to reduce nonspecific uptake, (ii) prodrug loading quantified (wt% and release stability in plasma/bile simulant).
- Targeting ligands (dual mode, tested empirically):
  (i) Basolateral cholangiocyte targeting: anti-EpCAM scFv or anti-KRT19-binding peptide (screen for internalization).
  (ii) Ductal retention: bile-acid-mimetic surface moiety (e.g., cholate-conjugated PEG) to enhance biliary/ductal association under cholestasis.
- Uptake benchmarking: quantify nanoparticle uptake (flow cytometry + confocal) in cholangiocytes vs hepatocytes vs macrophages under inflammatory conditions; report uptake rate constants for PK/PD.

Step 3 — PK/PD modeling that combines STS activity distributions with exposure to predict therapeutic index.
3.1 Model structure.
- Multi-compartment model: plasma, liver sinusoid, hepatocyte, portal immune compartment, bile-duct epithelium (apical/basolateral), bile.
- Processes:
  (i) Nanoparticle transport/uptake (measured from biodistribution/uptake assays).
  (ii) Intracellular prodrug activation: Michaelis–Menten using measured STS kcat/KM and cell-type STS activity distributions from Step 1.
  (iii) DHEA diffusion/efflux and metabolism.
- Outputs: predicted local ductal DHEA AUC, systemic DHEA AUC, and proportion activated in off-target tissues.
- Decision gate: proceed to in vivo only if model predicts ≥X-fold (predefined) ductal-vs-systemic exposure advantage relative to free DHEA.

Step 4 — Mechanistic causality with explicit steroid-metabolism mapping and receptor disentangling.
4.1 Steroid metabolite fate mapping (mandatory).
- LC–MS/MS steroid panel in chip and in vivo tissues: DHEA-S, DHEA, androstenedione, testosterone, DHT, estrone, estradiol; quantify in cholangiocytes, media (apical vs basolateral), and liver compartments.
- Enzyme-expression coupling: correlate metabolite patterns with HSD3B/HSD17B/CYP19A1/SRD5A1/2 expression.

4.2 Receptor and metabolism dissection controls.
- Receptor dependence:
  (i) ERα and AR CRISPRi/siRNA in cholangiocytes.
  (ii) Pharmacology: ERα antagonist (e.g., MPP) and AR antagonist (e.g., enzalutamide) in-chip, with dose–response.
- Metabolic blockade to separate direct DHEA actions from downstream sex steroids:
  (i) Aromatase inhibitor (letrozole) to block DHEA→estrogens.
  (ii) 17β-HSD inhibitors (isoform-appropriate; select based on expressed HSD17B in cholangiocytes).
  (iii) 5α-reductase inhibitor (finasteride/dutasteride) to block DHT formation.
- Interpretability: compare phenotypes under (a) receptor block, (b) metabolic block, (c) both, to assign causal weight to ERα vs AR vs downstream estradiol/testosterone.

4.3 Phenotypic endpoints aligned to fibrosis causality.
- Cholangiocyte stress survival: Annexin V/caspase 3/7, mitochondrial ΔΨm, Nrf2 targets, DNA damage markers.
- Ductular reaction vs “protective proliferation”: quantify Ki67/EdU along with differentiation/repair markers; explicitly test whether prodrug reduces maladaptive proliferative/inflammatory programs under stress despite preserving viability.
- Paracrine outputs to portal niche: TGF-β, PDGF, CTGF, IL-6, CCL2, osteopontin; multiplex ELISA + transcript.
- HSC response: α-SMA, COL1A1, hydroxyproline/procollagen I, MMP/TIMP ratio; include HSC RNA-seq module for activation states.
- Mediation analysis: pre-specified causal model where treatment → (cholangiocyte paracrine reduction) → (HSC activation reduction) → (fibrosis reduction).

Step 5 — In vivo translation with required autoimmune cholangitis + cholestasis model pairing.
5.1 Models (mandatory pairing).
- Autoimmune cholangitis: commit to at least one bona fide PBC-like model (choose based on facility):
  (i) dnTGFβRII mouse (autoimmune cholangitis with portal inflammation) and/or
  (ii) NOD.c3c4 (autoimmune biliary disease features).
- Cholestasis/fibrosis comparator: bile duct ligation (BDL) to test bile-acid/ROS injury context independent of autoimmunity.

5.2 Dosing, biodistribution, and on-target activation.
- Biodistribution: fluorescence/PET-labeled nanoparticles; quantify ductal enrichment by imaging + tissue LC–MS/MS.
- On-target activation: measure prodrug and released DHEA/metabolites in microdissected bile ducts vs parenchyma; align with STS activity.
- Comparator arms: targeted prodrug vs free DHEA vs DHEA-S vs inactive prodrug (non-cleavable analog).

5.3 Efficacy and immune-fibrosis linkage.
- Histology: ductopenia/ductular reaction (CK19), portal inflammation scoring, Sirius Red morphometry, second-harmonic generation collagen architecture, α-SMA.
- Molecular: portal cytokine/chemokine signatures; HSC activation signatures; oxidative stress markers.
- Functional: liver stiffness (where feasible), serum ALP/ALT/bilirubin.

5.4 Safety/therapeutic index.
- Endocrine burden: systemic steroid panel; reproductive tissue gene panels (uterus/prostate equivalents), lipid/coagulation profile.
- Off-target immune modulation: macrophage polarization markers; ensure no generalized immunosuppression driving false-positive fibrosis reduction.

Step 6 — Rigor, preregistration, and go/no-go criteria.
6.1 Pre-registered primary endpoints: (i) ductal DHEA exposure advantage (duct/parenchyma and duct/systemic AUC), (ii) cholangiocyte apoptosis under GCDC+ROS, (iii) HSC activation index, (iv) fibrosis area fraction.
6.2 Power calculations and blinded quantification for histology and image analysis.
6.3 Go/no-go gates:
- Chemistry gate: must meet substrate-not-inhibitor enzymology thresholds (2.2).
- Selectivity gate: PK/PD predicts and in vivo confirms ductal enrichment and reduced systemic exposure vs free DHEA.
- Mechanism gate: phenotype must be attenuated by ERα/AR perturbation and remain interpretable after metabolic-block controls.
Feasibility: 1) Enzymology/selectivity de-risking (addresses reviewer point 1): Rather than assuming aryl-sulfamates behave as clean substrates, the plan explicitly implements a substrate-vs-inhibitor validation package: purified STS kcat/KM, time-dependent inhibition (kinact/KI), partition ratio (turnover before inactivation), and cellular genetics (STS KO/overexpression/rescue). A parallel trigger strategy prioritizes sulfate-ester self-immolative designs to avoid the known failure mode of irreversible STS inhibition by classic aryl-sulfamates. Advancement is gated by quantitative thresholds, preventing mechanistic confounding from STS inhibition.

2) Quantitative therapeutic index via PK/PD modeling (addresses reviewer point 1): Because STS is broadly expressed, “kinetic gating” is insufficient without quantitative exposure modeling. The proposal therefore measures STS activity distributions in human PBC ducts vs hepatocytes vs immune cells and combines these with nanoparticle uptake/biodistribution data in a multi-compartment PK/PD model to predict on-target DHEA release and systemic steroid burden. This explicitly tests whether bile-duct enrichment + activation kinetics can yield a meaningful duct/systemic AUC advantage.

3) Causality under pleiotropic steroid biology (addresses reviewer point 2): Asset 2 supports DHEA/DHEA-S cytoprotection under bile-acid/ROS stress with ER involvement and AR contribution, but DHEA’s metabolism could redirect effects. The plan therefore includes mandatory LC–MS/MS steroid metabolomics (DHEA→androstenedione/testosterone/DHT/estrone/estradiol) and uses aromatase, 17β-HSD, and 5α-reductase inhibitors to separate direct ERα/AR signaling from downstream sex-steroid conversion. Receptor perturbations (ERα/AR CRISPRi/antagonists) are combined with metabolic blockade to tightly constrain mechanism attribution.

4) Biological coherence with PBC fibrogenesis (Assets 1 and 2) while avoiding overreach: Asset 1 indicates fibrogenesis in PBC-like disease is linked to inflammatory bile duct injury/ROS and portal crosstalk rather than “pure” cholestasis alone. The revised plan therefore commits to testing in at least one autoimmune cholangitis model (dnTGFβRII and/or NOD.c3c4) alongside BDL, ensuring immune-mediated portal inflammation claims are directly evaluated in a PBC-relevant context. The microfluidic platform explicitly models apical (bile) vs basolateral (portal) compartments, enabling compartmentalized exposure and paracrine-to-HSC causality testing.

5) Translational practicality: Each risk is tied to measurable go/no-go criteria (enzymology thresholds, predicted/observed ductal AUC advantage, receptor/metabolism-dependent phenotypes). This structure increases the likelihood of generating interpretable outcomes even if some components underperform (e.g., trigger family A vs B), while preserving the original concept chain: PBC enzyme asymmetry → cholangiocyte stress survival + reduced maladaptive paracrine signaling → reduced HSC activation → reduced fibrosis.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-structured proposal that directly addresses prior reviewer concerns through quantitative enzymology, genetic rescue, and PK/PD modeling rather than narrative argument. Engineering resolution is very high, with concrete specifications for enzyme kinetics, nanoparticle properties, microfluidic architecture, and decision gates. Logical consistency is strong: the disease-specific enzyme asymmetry (STS/SULT1E1), cholangiocyte stress biology, paracrine control of HSC activation, and fibrosis outcomes are coherently linked, and the plan explicitly tests each causal edge. Minor deductions arise from cumulative complexity and execution risk—particularly the assumption that ductal STS activity plus nanoparticle enrichment can overcome hepatocyte/macrophage activation in vivo, which remains empirically uncertain despite modeling safeguards. Evidence grounding is solid and remains within hepatobiliary immunobiology and steroid signaling, though some endpoints (e.g., Nrf2 biasing) rely on indirect inference rather than direct precedent in PBC cholangiocytes. Rationale quality is high: the proposal does not merely apply existing methods but redesigns steroid prodrug chemistry and validation frameworks to solve a recognized translational bottleneck (STS ubiquity and aryl-sulfamate failure modes).

original_chain: Liver organoid -> 3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine -> Prevotella copri -> 3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine -> Lox
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Prevotella copri mitigates DDC-associated cholestatic fibrogenesis by shifting a human-relevant bile-acid (BA) pool toward FXR-agonistic species (CDCA-conjugates and secondary BA derivatives within defined ranges) that activate hepatocyte/cholangiocyte FXR→SHP signaling, thereby dampening pro-fibrotic paracrine programs (TGF-β–permissive signaling, hypoxia stress) in the minimal fibrogenic unit and suppressing LOX-driven collagen crosslinking. This causal chain becomes testable in vitro only if (i) biliary solute export is physically routed into a collectable lumen via a biologically credible hepatocyte→cholangiocyte duct conduit (rather than assuming free hepatocyte canaliculi can be ‘plumbed’ to an outlet), enabling controlled BA flux under flow without polarity collapse, and (ii) BA speciation is perturbed with staged, genetically/chemically verified microbial biotransformation modules that produce predictable metabolite outputs in the human BA space. The refined platform overcomes prior confounders by decoupling BA toxicity/retention from BA receptor pharmacology and by restoring the missing cell circuitry that generates and responds to LOX/crosslinking (stellate/portal fibroblast ± macrophage cues), allowing FXR-dependent effects to be separated from canonical LOX drivers (TGF-β/HIF/inflammatory axes) using pre-registered decision criteria and orthogonal perturbations.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-register decision criteria and analyte panels (mechanistic guardrails)
0.1 Human-relevant BA panel (input and readout): CDCA, GCDCA, TCDCA, CA, GCA, TCA, DCA, GDCA, TDCA, LCA, GLCA, TLCA, UDCA, TUDCA (exclude muricholates from primary human organoid interpretation; if used, confine to mouse-only comparison datasets).
0.2 FXR pharmacology controls: (i) CDCA and obeticholic acid (OCA) as positive agonists; (ii) guggulsterone as antagonist; (iii) organoid FXR loss-of-function via CRISPRi/siRNA targeting NR1H4 (FXR) and/or SHP (NR0B2) for pathway necessity.
0.3 Pre-registered quantitative thresholds:
- FXR reporter dynamic range: ≥3-fold induction by OCA vs vehicle in the drained architecture sustained ≥48 h under flow.
- BA transport competence: biliary lumen enrichment ratio (bile-side : blood-side) ≥5 for CDFDA-derived fluorescent bile analog and detectable bile-side effluent BA by LC–MS without parallel leakage of 10 kDa tracer.
- Fibrosis endpoint: ≥30% reduction in LOX activity and ≥25% reduction in pyridinoline crosslinks vs DDC-only under identical total BA.

Step 1 — Build a physically credible biliary collection architecture (duct-first, not canaliculus-to-outlet by assumption)
1.1 Chip design (dual perfusion + collectable biliary lumen):
- Two parallel microchannels separated by a porous membrane (0.4–1.0 µm pores) or a thin ECM interface (50–150 µm) with defined compartments:
  A) ‘Blood-side’ endothelialized perfusion channel (iEC-lined) for nutrient/DDC/BA delivery.
  B) ‘Parenchymal’ chamber containing hepatocytes (organoid-derived hepatocyte-like cells or iHepSC-derived hepatocytes) in a collagen-I:Matrigel blend tuned for polarity (e.g., 2–4 mg/mL collagen I with 10–30% Matrigel).
  C) ‘Bile-side’ duct channel lined by cholangiocytes forming a contiguous duct epithelium that connects to a dedicated outlet reservoir for bile collection.
- Flow: blood-side 2–10 µL/min (shear ~0.5–2 dyn/cm^2 depending on channel dimensions); bile-side low flow 0.5–2 µL/min or intermittent suction to maintain a BA concentration gradient without collapsing the duct.
1.2 Positive-control “collectable biliary excretion” architecture (mandatory):
- Establish hepatocyte–cholangiocyte co-culture that forms duct-like conduits: embed hepatocyte spheroids adjacent to pre-formed cholangiocyte tubes (or cholangiocyte organoids) so hepatocyte canaliculi drain into cholangiocyte ductules (biologically plausible route). Operational criterion: visible continuity by 3D confocal reconstruction (MRP2/BSEP-positive canaliculi contiguous with KRT19/CFTR-positive duct lumen).
1.3 Polarity and junction integrity metrics:
- Immunostain and quantify: ZO-1/TJP1, E-cadherin, MRP2/ABCC2, BSEP/ABCB11 (hepatocytes); KRT19, CFTR, SLC10A2/ASBT (if relevant), and AE2/SLC4A2 (cholangiocytes).
- TEER across duct epithelium (if membrane-based) and permeability (Papp) using size-selective tracers: 0.5 kDa Lucifer yellow, 3 kDa dextran, 10 kDa dextran. Acceptance: stable TEER (or stable low Papp) over 7–14 days under flow; <5% appearance of 10 kDa tracer in bile effluent over 2 h while allowing BA analog enrichment.
1.4 Canalicular network mapping and time-stability:
- Live imaging of canalicular network using CDFDA and/or CLF (cholyl-lysyl-fluorescein) transport assays; compute network metrics (branch length density, connectivity, lumen continuity to duct) at baseline and after 24/72 h flow and injury.
- Structural stability criterion: no >20% reduction in canalicular connectivity index after 72 h under experimental flow.
1.5 Leakage and polarity collapse stress tests:
- Stepwise increase BA load (physiologic to cholestatic) with simultaneous tracer assays; define the ‘safe operating window’ where bile collection increases without epithelial leak.

Step 2 — Add the minimal fibrogenic unit and attribute LOX source (cell-of-origin rigor)
2.1 Cell components (minimum):
- iPSC-derived hepatic stellate cells (iHSCs) or portal fibroblasts (iPFs) incorporated in the parenchymal ECM at defined ratios (e.g., 5–15% of total cells) to provide the primary LOX/collagen-producing compartment.
- Optional but recommended: iPSC-derived macrophage-like cells (iMacs) introduced in the vascular channel or perivascular niche to supply inflammatory cues that modulate LOX (TNF/IL-1β/TGF-β induction). Use low-dose basal activation to avoid overwhelming the FXR axis.
2.2 Spatial patterning:
- Position iHSC/iPF in periductal/perisinusoidal mimic region (between hepatocyte compartment and endothelium) using layered hydrogel deposition (e.g., 50–100 µm stromal layer) to reproduce portal fibrogenic signaling gradients.
2.3 LOX origin attribution:
- Single-cell RNA-seq at key timepoints (baseline, DDC 72 h, DDC+BA inputs 72 h) to identify LOX/LOXL1-4 expression by cell type; validate with targeted proteomics (PRM) or multiplexed immunostaining.
- Functional attribution: cell-type-selective LOX knockdown (CRISPRi/siRNA) in iHSC/iPF vs epithelial compartments to confirm which compartment drives pyridinoline crosslinks.

Step 3 — Model cholestatic injury in a way that is interpretable in an epithelial-stromal chip (DDC plus mechanistically aligned adjuncts)
3.1 DDC use and limitations addressed:
- Apply DDC to blood-side perfusate at titrated concentrations that induce epithelial stress signatures without non-specific cytotoxicity; calibrate to achieve: (i) cholangiocyte injury markers (KRT19 up, inflammatory chemokines), (ii) impaired BA transport signature (reduced BSEP function), and (iii) stromal activation (COL1A1/ACTA2 up) in the presence of iHSC/iPF.
3.2 Complementary cholestatic stressor to improve construct validity:
- Add a clinically relevant BA overload component (e.g., GCDCA/TCDCA mix) to mimic bile-mediated toxicity and to engage FXR biology directly, while using the bile-drain to prevent non-physiologic accumulation.
- Optional: incorporate porphyrin/heme-pathway stress readouts (porphyrin accumulation assays) to document DDC-specific effects, acknowledging immune contributions are not fully replicated.
3.3 Readouts to confirm cholangiopathy/fibrogenic signaling:
- Epithelial stress/injury: KRT19, SPP1, IL-8/CXCL8, MCP-1/CCL2; bile transporter genes/proteins.
- Stromal activation: ACTA2, COL1A1/3A1, TGFB1, TIMP1; matrix remodeling.

Step 4 — De-risk microbial BA control with a staged metabolite-generator pipeline (deliverables before P. copri editing)
4.1 Stage A (highest feasibility): purified enzymes / cell-free biotransformation
- Identify candidate BA-transforming activities relevant to human FXR pharmacology (e.g., bile salt hydrolase, hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases, 7α-dehydroxylation is typically multi-gene and difficult; prioritize realistic conversions such as deconjugation and oxidation/epimerization steps that shift CDCA/GCDCA/TCDCA and downstream derivatives).
- Run anaerobic biotransformation with purified enzymes or lysates; confirm product formation and yields by targeted LC–MS. Deliverable: a reproducible ‘enzyme-conditioned BA’ input with controlled speciation at matched total BA.
4.2 Stage B (tractable anaerobe chassis): heterologous expression
- Express selected enzymes in a genetically tractable anaerobe (e.g., Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron or E. coli Nissle under anaerobic conditions if appropriate) with inducible control; quantify BA conversion kinetics and off-target metabolites.
- Deliverable: tunable BA output with induction curves mapping inducer dose → BA speciation.
4.3 Stage C (then) P. copri implementation with explicit engineering plan
- Loci selection: prioritize validated BA transformation genes identified by comparative genomics among P. copri strains correlated with BA phenotypes; shortlist 2–4 loci (e.g., candidate bsh-like hydrolase, HSDH candidates) with in vitro activity evidence from Stages A/B.
- Delivery/editing approach: specify conjugation-based plasmid delivery or electroporation optimized for Prevotella (to be developed), using anaerobe-active promoters; integrate dCas9 (CRISPRi/a) with guide RNAs targeting promoter regions; include plasmid retention/stability strategy (chromosomal integration if feasible; otherwise selection-free stability via toxin–antitoxin or periodic selection in vitro only).
- Stability and off-target assessment: passage engineered strains ≥20 generations; whole-genome sequencing for stability; untargeted metabolomics to detect unintended shifts beyond BA panel; growth-rate matching to control for biomass effects.
4.4 Preparation of “microbiome-conditioned BA” input
- Culture under standardized anaerobic conditions with defined BA substrate mix; harvest supernatant; sterile filter; normalize to total BA; verify BA speciation by LC–MS prior to chip dosing.

Step 5 — Causal testing in the drained biliary chip: BA speciation → FXR→SHP → stromal LOX/crosslinking
5.1 Experimental matrix (factorial design)
- Architecture: drained duct-connected chip vs matched no-drain (duct outlet blocked / static bile-side) as mandatory control.
- Injury: ±DDC (plus standardized BA overload if used).
- Inputs: vehicle BA vs enzyme-/chassis-/P. copri-conditioned BA with matched total BA.
- Pathway perturbations: FXR agonism (OCA), FXR antagonism (guggulsterone) and/or FXR knockdown; LOX inhibition (BAPN) as endpoint convergence control; TGF-β receptor inhibitor (e.g., SB431542) as a specificity probe to separate FXR-dependent from TGF-β-driven LOX.
5.2 FXR axis readouts
- FXR reporter line (FXRE-driven luciferase/fluorescent reporter) in hepatocytes and/or cholangiocytes; time-resolved reporter under flow.
- qPCR/RNA-seq for NR0B2/SHP, ABCB11/BSEP, SLC51A/B (OSTα/β), and bile acid synthesis/handling genes (CYP7A1 repression as supporting evidence in hepatocyte-like cells).
5.3 LOX and matrix crosslink outcomes
- LOX mRNA/protein and activity assay (Amplex Red-based) with compartment-specific sampling where possible.
- Collagen deposition: second harmonic generation (SHG) imaging and hydroxyproline.
- Crosslinks: pyridinoline/deoxypyridinoline quantification by LC–MS.
- Cell-state linkage: scRNA-seq/proteomics to connect FXR activation state to stromal activation programs and LOX module expression.
5.4 Transport/flux measurements as mechanistic mediators (not just QC)
- LC–MS of bile-side effluent over time to compute BA clearance rates and residence time.
- Establish whether identical BA inputs produce different intracellular stress/LOX outputs depending on bile drainage (decoupling composition vs accumulation).

Step 6 — Analysis plan
- Multivariate/mediation modeling: BA species features (input + bile effluent kinetics) → FXR reporter (AUC) → stromal transcriptional activation (TGF-β/HIF modules) → LOX activity → crosslink density.
- Compare mediated effect sizes across drained vs no-drain architectures; primary claim requires that drainage increases interpretability by preserving FXR pharmacology at matched total BA while reducing non-specific toxicity signatures.

Feasibility: 1) Canalicular-to-lumen credibility addressed by ‘duct-first’ design rules and quantified integrity testing. Rather than asserting that hepatocyte canaliculi can be directly routed into a fabricated outlet, the revised architecture uses a positive-control hepatocyte–cholangiocyte conduit in which cholangiocyte-lined ducts serve as the collectable biliary lumen. This is biologically aligned with how bile is transported (canaliculi → ductules → ducts). Structural plausibility and stability are enforced with (i) 3D continuity mapping of canaliculi-to-duct junctions, (ii) leakage assays with size-selective tracers, (iii) TEER/permeability monitoring under flow, and (iv) longitudinal canalicular network metrics to detect polarity collapse. These criteria directly satisfy the directive to quantify connectivity, leakage, and time-stability rather than relying on inferred transport.

2) LOX/crosslink interpretability is restored by adding the minimal fibrogenic unit and attributing cell-of-origin. LOX-mediated collagen crosslinking is primarily a stromal output in vivo; therefore iPSC-derived HSCs/portal fibroblasts are incorporated at controlled ratios and spatially patterned to a portal-like niche. Single-cell RNA-seq and targeted proteomics, combined with compartment-selective LOX perturbation, pre-specify how LOX origin and causality will be assigned, preventing ambiguous interpretation of ECM endpoints in an epithelial-only organoid.

3) DDC model limitations are explicitly managed. Because DDC injury in vivo involves porphyrin plugs and immune/stromal interplay, the proposal (i) uses DDC as one component of a cholestatic stress regimen, (ii) adds BA overload as a mechanistically aligned driver of epithelial stress and FXR engagement while the drain prevents artifactual accumulation, and (iii) incorporates macrophage cues optionally to capture inflammatory modulation of LOX. This makes the injury paradigm more faithful to cholangiopathy/fibrogenic signaling within an in vitro platform.

4) P. copri engineering risk is reduced via staged deliverables and metabolomics validation before committing to dCas9 in P. copri. The plan first reproduces BA transformations using purified enzymes, then heterologous expression in a tractable anaerobe with tunable induction curves, and only then implements CRISPRi/a in P. copri with explicit locus selection, delivery/stability assays, whole-genome sequencing, and untargeted metabolomics to detect off-target metabolic shifts. This sequencing converts a high-risk microbial engineering dependency into a stepwise pipeline where each stage yields usable ‘conditioned BA’ inputs for the chip.

5) Mouse–human BA mismatch is removed by restricting mechanistic claims to a human BA panel and human FXR pharmacology controls. Muricholates are excluded from primary inference in the human organoid system, and FXR activation is benchmarked against CDCA/OCA and blocked genetically/pharmacologically. This ensures that BA-species shifts are interpreted within the correct receptor-ligand space for the proposed human model.

6) FXR→LOX causality is tested against known alternative LOX drivers. Because LOX is also regulated by TGF-β, hypoxia, and inflammatory pathways, the revised plan includes orthogonal perturbations (TGF-β receptor inhibition, optional macrophage cues, LOX inhibition convergence) and mediation analysis linking BA speciation to FXR activity to stromal activation modules to LOX/crosslinks. This makes it possible to determine whether FXR signaling directly mediates LOX suppression, or whether observed LOX changes are secondary to broader changes in injury/inflammation—resolving the reviewer’s concern about indirectness.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and technically sophisticated proposal that directly engages prior reviewer concerns rather than bypassing them. The engineering resolution is very strong: the duct-first biliary architecture, quantitative leakage criteria, polarity stress-testing, and explicit BA flux measurements demonstrate physical credibility well beyond standard liver-on-chip or organoid systems. Logical consistency is also high; the proposal carefully separates bile-acid pharmacology from bile retention toxicity and builds a testable FXR→SHP→stromal LOX suppression pathway with orthogonal perturbations and mediation analysis. Minor deductions arise from residual biological uncertainty rather than conceptual flaws: (i) the degree to which Prevotella copri–conditioned BA pools in vitro will recapitulate in vivo FXR agonism remains inferential, even with staged de-risking, and (ii) DDC remains an imperfect cholangiopathy surrogate despite thoughtful mitigation. Evidence grounding is strong and stays within hepatic, biliary, microbial, and fibrogenic domains, though the microbial-to-host causality still relies on engineered metabolite inputs rather than direct host–microbe co-culture. Rationale quality is high because the proposal does not merely apply existing methods but restructures the biliary interface to solve a recognized interpretability bottleneck (canalicular drainage and LOX attribution). Overall, this is a top-tier mechanistic platform proposal with only modest translational uncertainty.

original_chain: Biomaterial -> Electrophoresis -> Hydroxyproline -> Farnesoid X receptor -> 3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: In 3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine (DDC)-induced cholestasis, sustained antifibrotic efficacy is limited primarily by *cell-type and zonal pharmacokinetic mismatch* (mis-targeting + intracellular access), not by intrinsic FXR agonist potency. Specifically, cholestasis-driven remodeling of sinusoidal transport and bile-acid handling increases hepatocyte and canalicular exposure while *reducing free intracellular agonist in activated hepatic stellate cells (HSCs)* via (i) transporter/efflux capture (MRP2/3/4, BCRP, OATPs/NTCP shifts), (ii) bile-acid–rich microenvironmental partitioning that favors hepatobiliary sequestration, and (iii) endolysosomal trapping in non-parenchymal sinks (Kupffer cells/LSECs). We hypothesize that an HSC-directed, pH-switchable bile-acid–mimetic polymer–lipid nanoparticle (FXR-PLN) with *architecturally segregated dual payloads*—FXR agonist in a hydrophobic core and SHP (Nr0b2) mRNA in an ionizable, endosomolytic sub-compartment—will overcome these barriers by (a) improving perisinusoidal retention while avoiding premature membrane FXR activation, (b) enforcing endosomal escape and nuclear delivery in HSCs, and (c) producing a temporally ordered mechanism: rapid SHP protein “pulse” to establish corepressor tone followed by sustained intracellular agonist to stabilize an FXR transcriptional complex that represses profibrotic signaling and reduces collagen deposition (hydroxyproline). Because FXR activity depends on receptor microstates (isoform/PTM/nuclear localization), we further hypothesize that a cIEF-defined “FXR functional microstate score” can be made a *validated* surrogate for on-target engagement when hard-anchored to orthogonal assays (FXR ChIP, targeted phospho-MS, nuclear translocation imaging) and used to guide formulation tuning only after three feasibility gates demonstrate: (1) the proposed barrier exists and is HSC-specific in vivo, (2) the dual-payload FXR-PLN has stable architecture and sequential bioactivity in bile-acid–rich conditions, and (3) cIEF peaks reliably map to active vs inactive FXR states.

Mechanistic rationale linking to endpoints: Restoring FXR→SHP repression in the DDC model reduces fibrogenic drive and collagen burden (hydroxyproline), consistent with published evidence that enhanced FXR signaling reduces fibrosis markers and hydroxyproline in cholestatic injury. The proposal’s core advance is to convert this pathway logic into a *cell-resolved, state-resolved* delivery-and-readout system that explicitly tests and corrects the distribution/efflux barrier that likely prevents free agonist from achieving sufficient nuclear FXR engagement in HSCs.
Plan: OVERVIEW: The project is explicitly hard-gated. Only if Gates 1–3 pass do we proceed to closed-loop optimization. All uptake and cIEF analyses will include hepatocytes, HSCs, Kupffer cells, and LSECs to prevent misattribution.

A. MODEL + CELL-TYPE RESOLVED SAMPLING (common to all gates)
A1. DDC model: C57BL/6J mice fed 0.1% (w/w) DDC for 6 weeks; planned collections at wk2 (cholestasis dominant), wk4 (transition), wk6 (established fibrosis). Include age/sex matching and randomization.
A2. Liver zonation framework: Map central vein (CV) to portal triad (PT) zones using glutamine synthetase (pericentral) and E-cadherin/CK19 (periportal) markers on adjacent sections.
A3. Multicell sorting panel (fresh livers):
- Hepatocytes: ASGPR1+ (or hepatocyte gate by size/granularity + ASGPR1)
- HSCs: PDGFRβ+ LRAT+ Desmin+ (activated HSC enrichment)
- Kupffer/macrophages: F4/80+ CLEC4F+ (separate infiltrating macrophages: CD11b+)
- LSECs: CD31+ Lyve1+ (or Stabilin-2+)
Preserve matched aliquots for: (i) LC–MS, (ii) RNA, (iii) protein (cIEF), (iv) imaging (confocal/IHC), (v) hydroxyproline and ECM fraction.

HARD-GATED DECISION EXPERIMENT 1 (GATE 1): Demonstrate the proposed barrier (zonal + transporter/efflux) and show free agonist fails specifically in HSCs
G1.1 Quantify intralobular agonist distribution (free drug):
- Administer a representative intracellular FXR agonist (tool compound or obeticholic acid) at a dose matched to later PLN studies; collect livers at 0.5h, 2h, 6h.
- Readout A (spatial): MALDI-MSI on fresh-frozen liver sections to map agonist intensity vs CV/PT zones; co-register with fibrosis markers (αSMA) and bile duct markers.
- Readout B (microdissection LC–MS): Laser capture microdissection (LCM) of CV and PT regions followed by LC–MS quantification of agonist and major bile acids (TCDCA, T-α-MCA, LCA where detectable) to quantify zone-dependent partitioning.
- Pass criterion (distribution barrier): a statistically significant zone bias indicating pericentral/periportal mismatch with HSC activation regions and/or a steep concentration drop in perisinusoidal compartments relative to hepatocyte-rich zones.
G1.2 Quantify cell-type drug exposure (free drug):
- Following the same dosing, isolate hepatocytes/HSCs/Kupffer/LSECs; quantify intracellular agonist by LC–MS (normalized to cell number/protein).
- Pass criterion (HSC exposure deficit): intracellular agonist in HSCs is ≤20% of hepatocyte level and/or is dominated by Kupffer/LSEC signal (sink behavior).
G1.3 Transporter/efflux landscape and functional contribution in DDC:
- Expression: qPCR + targeted proteomics (PRM) for NTCP (Slc10a1), Oatp1b2 (Slco1b2), Mrp2/3/4 (Abcc2/3/4), Bcrp (Abcg2), Bsep (Abcb11) in whole liver and sorted cells at wk2/wk4.
- Function: ex vivo transporter inhibition panel on freshly isolated cells:
  • Inhibitors (examples): MK-571 (MRPs), Ko143 (BCRP), rifampicin (OATPs; mouse-appropriate controls), plus bile-acid transport modulation as appropriate.
  • Measure change in intracellular agonist accumulation (LC–MS) and FXR reporter readouts (see G3) after short incubation.
- Pass criterion (efflux contribution): inhibitor(s) significantly increase HSC intracellular agonist and/or shift agonist distribution away from efflux-dominant compartments.
G1 Go/No-Go decision: Proceed only if data support that free agonist exposure and/or functional engagement is comparatively deficient in HSCs and linked to transporter/efflux/partitioning. If not supported, pivot: optimize hepatocyte-targeted FXR modulation and revise antifibrotic mechanism accordingly (predefined contingency).

HARD-GATED DECISION EXPERIMENT 2 (GATE 2): De-risk dual-payload FXR-PLN with explicit architecture, bile-acid challenge, sequential release, and endosomal escape
G2.1 FXR-PLN architecture (explicit): Build a *core–shell polymer–lipid nanoparticle with segregated compartments*.
- Core (agonist): hydrophobic polymer/lipid core containing agonist; specify core components e.g., cholesterol + DSPC + ionizable lipid fraction minimized in core to preserve hydrophobe loading.
- Sub-compartment for mRNA: ionizable lipid/polymer complexed mRNA (N/P 4–8) forming an internal or shell-localized polyplex domain.
- Polymer design (bile-acid mimetic + pH switch):
  • Block A (hydrophilic stealth): PEG (2–5 kDa) or zwitterionic alternative.
  • Block B (bile-acid mimetic display): sparse cholic-acid analog substitution (2%, 5%, 10% of repeat units) on hydrophilic block to modulate hepatobiliary interactions while being non-agonist.
  • Block C (pH-switch): tertiary-amine–rich segment with tunable pKa 6.2–6.8 (target 6.5) to drive endosomal protonation; include membrane-inserting hydrophobes (e.g., butyl side chains) at controlled fraction.
- Targeting ligand: vitamin A/retinol analog or PDGFRβ-binding peptide attached via maleimide–thiol coupling to terminal functional groups; valency series (e.g., 0, 5, 15, 30 ligands/particle estimated).
- Target physical specs acceptance: size 70–120 nm; PDI <0.2; zeta near neutral at pH 7.4; stability in 10–20% serum.
G2.2 Encapsulation and localization verification:
- Agonist loading: quantify by LC–MS; target >70% encapsulation efficiency and reproducible drug:lipid ratio.
- mRNA integrity: capillary electrophoresis/RNA integrity post-formulation; quantify encapsulation by RiboGreen assay.
- Compartmentalization proof: cryo-TEM + fluorescence quenching/FRET strategy (agonist analog fluor + labeled mRNA) to show spatial segregation and lack of premature complexation.
G2.3 Bile-acid challenge and serum stability:
- Incubate FXR-PLN in physiologic bile-acid mixtures reflecting DDC (measured from G1; include TCDCA, T-α-MCA, LCA ranges) + 50% mouse serum.
- Readouts after 0, 1, 4, 24 h: size/PDI, leakage (agonist LC–MS in filtrate), mRNA integrity, surface ligand accessibility (ELISA or binding assay), and protein corona composition (LC–MS proteomics) to assess whether bile-acid mimetic corona disrupts targeting.
- Pass criterion: <20% agonist leakage and preserved mRNA integrity over 4 h; ligand accessibility retained ≥50% relative to no-bile-acid condition.
G2.4 Endosomal escape quantification + sequential bioactivity:
- Endosomal escape: Gal8 recruitment assay in HSC-like cells (e.g., LX-2) and primary mouse HSCs; quantify % Gal8+ puncta per cell vs controls.
- Sequential payload function in vitro:
  • Early SHP pulse: SHP protein increase by 4–8 h (immunoblot/cIEF) following FXR-PLN dual.
  • Later FXR program stabilization: by 12–24 h, demonstrate repression of Cyp7a1 (hepatocytes) and modulation of profibrotic markers in HSCs (Col1a1, Acta2, Tgfb1) where applicable.
  • Use formulations with disabled pH-switch (amines acetylated or pKa <5.8) to show dependence.
- Pass criteria: robust endosomal escape over non-switch control (≥2×), demonstrable SHP protein induction, and evidence of downstream transcriptional effects with correct temporal ordering.
G2 Go/No-Go decision: Proceed only if dual payload is stable in bile-acid conditions and shows endosomal escape + sequential bioactivity. If not, split into two nanoparticles with timed dosing (SHP-mRNA PLN then agonist PLN) as predefined fallback while retaining cIEF-guided loop.

HARD-GATED DECISION EXPERIMENT 3 (GATE 3): Validate cIEF “FXR functional microstate score” with orthogonal assays and define active vs inactive peaks
G3.1 Define cIEF peaks with perturbation standards (in cells):
- Use kinase/phosphatase perturbations in hepatocytes and HSCs: phosphatase treatment (λPPase) collapses phospho-peaks; kinase activators/inhibitors (e.g., ERK pathway modulators) shift peaks.
- Establish peak identities: map each cIEF peak to phosphorylation status using targeted phospho-proteomics (PRM) on immunoprecipitated FXR from pooled samples.
G3.2 Nuclear translocation imaging:
- In primary cells and liver sections post-dose, quantify FXR nuclear localization by immunofluorescence (nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio), linked to cIEF peak distributions from matched samples.
G3.3 FXR DNA occupancy (functional):
- Perform CUT&RUN or ChIP-qPCR (low-input compatible) for FXR at Nr0b2 (SHP) and Abcb11 (BSEP) regulatory regions in sorted hepatocytes and HSCs where feasible.
- Correlate occupancy with cIEF-derived active peak fraction and SHP protein AUC.
G3.4 Predefine the score (locked before optimization):
- FXR functional microstate score = w1*(active FXR peak fraction) + w2*(nuclear localization index) + w3*(SHP protein AUC 0–24h) − w4*(pSMAD2/3 fraction by cIEF)
Weights (w1–w4) pre-registered based on correlation with ChIP/CUT&RUN and phospho-MS in pilot datasets.
G3 Pass criteria: (i) active peak fraction correlates with FXR occupancy (R≥0.6) and nuclear localization, (ii) peaks are assignable to phospho-states by PRM, (iii) score predicts directionality of target gene changes.

B. ITERATIVE OPTIMIZATION (only after Gate 1–3 pass)
B1. Quantitative targeting acceptance criteria (hard constraints):
- Functional delivery selectivity: ≥5–10× (HSC vs hepatocyte) *for SHP protein induction and/or FXR active microstate shift*;
- Uptake selectivity: ≥3× HSC:Kupffer and ≥3× HSC:LSEC nanoparticle-associated fluorescence and/or LC–MS payload per cell;
- Systemic FXR activation constraint: intestinal FXR markers (e.g., Fgf15 induction) must not exceed a predefined threshold vs free agonist at equal molar dose.
B2. Design matrix:
- Factors: bile-acid mimic density (0/2/5/10%), pH-switch pKa (6.2/6.5/6.8), ligand valency (0/5/15/30), particle size (target 80 vs 120 nm via mixing conditions).
- Screen in vivo at wk2–wk4 (window of reversibility), short PK/PD dosing with 24–72 h readout.
- Objective: maximize microstate score in sorted HSCs while satisfying acceptance criteria and minimizing Kupffer/LSEC activation.
B3. Controls:
- Vehicle; free agonist; PLN agonist-only; PLN SHP mRNA-only; PLN dual; non-targeted dual; pH-switch-deficient dual; ligand-blocking control (excess free retinol peptide competitor where appropriate).
- On-target dependence: FXR antagonist arm and/or liver conditional Fxr knockout (if feasible); at minimum, pharmacologic blockade.

C. EFFICACY STUDY (lead formulation)
C1. Dosing: select regimen based on PK/PD from optimization; treat during wk4–wk6 or wk2–wk6 depending on observed reversal window.
C2. Primary endpoints:
- Hydroxyproline quantification (total collagen burden).
- Sirius Red morphometry (fibrosis area).
- COL1A1/ACTA2 protein and transcript.
- ECM remodeling signature: capillary gel electrophoresis (CGE) of ECM-enriched fractions for collagen I/III chain ratios and fragment/crosslink-associated patterns to distinguish reduced deposition vs altered remodeling.
C3. Mechanistic endpoints:
- cIEF microstate score in sorted cells (HSCs/hepatocytes/Kupffer/LSECs).
- BA pool (LC–MS) in serum/liver/SI; FXR program nodes (Nr0b2, Abcb11, Slc51a/b, Cyp7a1).
C4. Safety:
- Serum ALT/AST/ALP, lipids; cytokines; gallbladder/intestine histology; pruritus-relevant BA shifts.

D. DATA INTEGRATION
D1. Multivariate model (locked analysis plan): nanoparticle parameters → protein corona features → cell-type uptake → endosomal escape metric → cIEF microstate score → FXR occupancy → gene program → collagen CGE signature → hydroxyproline.
D2. Use model to select final design with maximal efficacy per unit systemic FXR activation and minimal Kupffer/LSEC sink uptake.
Feasibility: 1) Addresses the key premise risk (mis-targeting/efflux) with a mandatory Gate 1 that directly measures zonal and cell-type agonist exposure and transporter/efflux function in DDC. This converts the central barrier from an assertion into a quantified, falsifiable mechanism.
