  • C-terminus junction: at the end of the last repeat helix that packs against the native C-cap (define as Rn_H2_end). Graft end = start of native C-cap helix (Ccap_start).
For each junction, generate 2–3 alternative cut sites spanning ±1 helical turn to allow register correction while preserving helix capping hydrogen-bond patterns.
1.2 Cap candidate library (geometry-matched, not generic):
  • Build a small panel of engineered helical-repeat-like cap modules with compatible helix bundle topology (ankyrin/DARPin-like helical hairpins are used only if their terminal helices can be oriented to match TALE terminal helix vectors). Include: (A) native TALE caps (baseline), (B) minimal synthetic helical cap (de novo short helical bundle designed to cap the terminal repeat helices), (C) DARPin/ankyrin-derived cap variants whose terminal helices are re-oriented by design (not direct transplantation).
  • For each cap, enforce: (i) matching terminal helix directionality (vector alignment tolerance pre-specified, e.g., <15° angular deviation), (ii) no steric clash with DNA in a TALE–DNA complex, and (iii) preserved superhelical curvature at repeat 1 / repeat n.
1.3 Structure-guided modeling and ranking (Rosetta/MD):
  • Rosetta-based pipeline:
    - Use RosettaCM or RosettaRemodel to construct cap-grafted models at each junction option.
    - Apply constraints to keep the TALE repeat backbone and RVD helix geometry within tight RMSD bounds (e.g., backbone coordinate restraints on RVD-bearing helices; restraint weights pre-specified).
    - Score and rank by: interface ΔΔG (Rosetta InterfaceAnalyzer), buried surface area (BSA), shape complementarity (SC), and absence of unsatisfied buried polar atoms.
  • MD refinement (explicit solvent, short runs for ranking):
    - Run 100–300 ns explicit-solvent MD for top designs (e.g., 5–10) to assess terminal stability, helix fraying, and cap–repeat contact persistence.
    - Quantify: RMSF at terminal repeats, hydrogen-bond persistence across junction, and solvent penetration at the cap–repeat interface.
1.4 Interface rewiring (repeat–repeat packing) with explicit constraints:
  • Identify repeat-junction residues that contribute to inter-repeat packing but do not contact DNA (from the structure and contact maps).
  • Implement a constrained design: allow mutations only at boundary-facing residues with high SASA in partially unfolded ensembles (estimated from MD snapshots or computational unfolding proxies).
  • Redox-insulation rules:
    - Eliminate nonessential Cys in solvent-exposed or boundary positions (Cys→Ser/Ala) while keeping any structurally required disulfide-free context.
    - Reduce solvent-exposed Met/Trp at boundaries when not part of a stabilizing hydrophobic core (Met→Leu/Ile; Trp→Phe/Tyr only if aromatic stacking is required).
    - Treat Tyr/His as oxidation liabilities: only introduce Tyr if burial increases and if MS controls are planned; avoid paired Tyr/His “radical sinks” unless a specific buried, low-SASA environment is demonstrated computationally.
  • Output a minimal, justified mutation set (e.g., 6–20 total substitutions across the array) prioritized by: (i) high predicted oxidation risk (high SASA + known propensity), (ii) low predicted impact on DNA-contact geometry, and (iii) predicted ΔΔG stabilization.
1.5 Pre-register design success/failure criteria (structural):
  • Must meet thresholds: SC/BSA above pre-set cutoffs; no DNA steric clashes; RVD helix backbone RMSD within a strict bound vs template; and predicted interface ΔΔG improvement vs baseline.

Step 2 — Protein production and in vitro folding/oxidation characterization with orthogonal intermediate probes
2.1 Expression and purification (E. coli) with controls:
  • Express TALE DBD variants in E. coli with standardized induction conditions; include a parallel arm with chaperone co-expression as a controlled variable.
  • Purify under identical buffers; record yields, monomer fraction (SEC), and baseline oxidation (intact mass).
  • Variants panel (minimum):
    A) WT caps + WT interfaces
    B) Cap-grafted (best N-cap), WT interfaces
    C) Cap-grafted (best N- and C-cap), WT interfaces
    D) WT caps + interface redox/stability mutations
    E) Cap-grafted + interface mutations (lead candidates)
2.2 Equilibrium unfolding/refolding with realistic expectations (no overclaiming two-state):
  • Perform chemical denaturation (urea and/or guanidinium chloride gradients) monitored by far-UV CD and intrinsic/label fluorescence.
  • Fit to: (i) two-state where justified, and (ii) multi-state/Ising-like repeat unfolding models when residuals and hysteresis indicate intermediates.
  • Pre-registered readouts of “intermediate collapse” rather than strict two-state: reduced hysteresis, reduced slow refolding phases, increased cooperativity proxy (m-value changes interpreted with caution), and reduced baseline aggregation during refolding.
2.3 Orthogonal detection of intermediates and local unfolding (mandatory additions):
  • HDX-MS:
    - Compare WT vs engineered constructs in native, partially denaturing, and refolding timepoints.
    - Map protection factors across repeats; success = increased protection at terminal repeats and boundary segments, and reduced heterogeneous exchange indicative of locally unfolded subpopulations.
  • Stopped-flow kinetics:
    - Measure refolding/unfolding kinetics after denaturant jumps; fit multi-exponential phases.
    - Success = reduced amplitude of slow phases and reduced kinetic partitioning under ROS challenge.
2.4 Controlled ROS challenge with explicit dosimetry and interpretation constraints:
  • Apply ROS in both folded-state exposure and during refolding:
    - Hydroxyl radical flux: Fe2+/H2O2 (Fenton) with short exposure times; quench with chelators; include “no-Fe” and “no-H2O2” controls.
    - Superoxide-like flux: xanthine/xanthine oxidase; include catalase/SOD controls to parse species contributions.
  • Define ROS doses based on preserving interpretability: maintain ≥70% monomer for at least one dose to allow comparisons; pre-register stopping criteria if complete aggregation occurs.
2.5 Oxidation and aggregation mapping with controls for newly introduced Tyr oxidation:
  • Intact-mass MS and LC–MS/MS to identify oxidation sites; quantify oxidation stoichiometry per residue class.
  • If Tyr is introduced/retained, explicitly track Tyr oxidation products; compare to WT and to “Tyr-sparing” alternative designs.
  • SEC-MALS/DLS for oligomerization; DSF/DSC for stability shifts pre/post ROS.
2.6 DNA binding function beyond endpoint affinity (addresses specificity risk):
  • Measure binding kinetics (k_on, k_off) using biolayer interferometry (BLI) or SPR with cognate DNA and a panel of near-cognate sequences.
  • Competitive binding assays: cognate vs mismatched competitor DNA to quantify specificity under crowding.
  • EMSA/anisotropy retained as orthogonal confirmation, but not primary specificity proof.

Step 3 — Cellular validation with normalization of expression, quality control, and nuclease kinetics
3.1 Mammalian expression constructs:
  • Fuse optimized TALE DBDs to obligate heterodimeric FokI variants; keep linkers constant across constructs.
  • Include tags/reporters enabling quantification (e.g., epitope tag for immunoblot; optional fluorescent fusion with careful controls for folding impact).
3.2 Proteostasis-aware normalization (mandatory):
  • Match not only total expression but also soluble fraction:
    - Perform cellular fractionation (soluble vs insoluble) followed by quantitative immunoblot.
    - Use fluorescence-based aggregation reporters if applicable (e.g., split-reporter complementation) as an orthogonal readout.
  • Success criterion: engineered constructs maintain higher soluble/monomeric fraction under oxidative stress at matched total expression.
3.3 Controlled oxidative stress models:
  • Apply H2O2 pulses and/or menadione with ROS quantification (cell-permeant probes calibrated to avoid probe artifacts); measure viability to ensure editing differences are not dominated by cytotoxicity.
  • Include antioxidant enzyme controls (catalase/SOD expression or treatment) to confirm ROS-causality of performance differences.
3.4 Genome editing outcomes:
  • On-target: amplicon NGS for indel spectra; ddPCR for precise frequencies.
  • Off-target: GUIDE-seq or CIRCLE-seq under matched ROS conditions to test whether altered binding kinetics shifts specificity.
3.5 Mechanistic nuclease performance assays (beyond endpoints):
  • Single-turnover cleavage kinetics in cell extracts or purified TALENs (where feasible) to measure intrinsic catalytic competence.
  • Correlate in vitro k_on/k_off and cleavage rates with cellular editing under ROS.
3.6 Integrated causality model (pre-registered):
  • Multivariate regression/SEM linking: cap/interface design scores (ΔΔG/BSA/SC) → HDX protection + stopped-flow kinetic phases → oxidation burden (MS) + aggregation (SEC-MALS) → binding kinetics (BLI/SPR) → cellular soluble fraction → on-target editing under ROS.

Step 4 — Go/no-go decision points and risk mitigation
4.1 If cap swaps disrupt DNA binding kinetics: revert to minimal de novo helical cap that only stabilizes terminal helices without introducing foreign repeat curvature; or use partial cap reinforcement (N-cap only) as an intermediate.
4.2 If long arrays resist cooperative folding collapse: restrict to shorter repeat arrays (still functional) or introduce internal “stabilization stitches” at sparse positions (every ~4–5 repeats) chosen by HDX hotspots, rather than global redesign.
4.3 If redox substitutions reduce activity: roll back mutations at positions that alter k_on or k_off disproportionately; prioritize burying oxidizable residues through packing rather than introducing new aromatic/His liabilities.

Success criteria (explicit)
• Structural/modeling: top designs pass geometric constraints (no DNA clash; RVD helix RMSD within bound; improved interface scores).
• Biophysics: reduced hysteresis and slow refolding phases; HDX shows increased protection at terminals/boundaries; reduced ROS-induced oxidation at mapped hotspots; reduced aggregation under ROS.
• Function: preserved or improved binding specificity measured by kinetics and competitive assays; ≥2–3× improved editing under ROS at matched soluble expression; no increased off-target burden.
Feasibility: 1) Structural integration is made testable and low-ambiguity by (a) anchoring design on specific TALE–DNA crystal structure geometries, (b) pre-defining graft junctions at helix boundaries with alternative cut sites to maintain register, and (c) ranking cap candidates using quantitative structural metrics (shape complementarity, buried surface area, interface ΔΔG) while enforcing invariant RVD helix geometry. This directly addresses the prior under-specification of how ankyrin/DARPin-like modules are integrated without distorting TALE curvature.

2) The folding claim is reframed to match known repeat-protein behavior: rather than assuming strict two-state unfolding for long arrays, the proposal pre-registers measurable criteria for “intermediate collapse” and adds orthogonal intermediate probes (HDX-MS and stopped-flow kinetics). This prevents overinterpretation of equilibrium denaturation curves and enables detection of local unfolding/near-degenerate states typical of repeat arrays.

3) Specificity preservation is treated as a dominant failure mode and is experimentally de-risked by moving beyond endpoint affinity/off-target lists: kinetic binding measurements (k_on/k_off by BLI/SPR), competitive binding, and (where feasible) single-turnover cleavage kinetics ensure that terminal/interface remodeling has not subtly altered the binding energy landscape, dwell time, or cleavage competence.

4) The ROS-mitigation chemistry is narrowed to a justified, oxidation-aware substitution set guided by computed SASA and established oxidation propensities (Met/Trp/Cys prioritized), explicitly controlling for newly introduced Tyr oxidation rather than relying on speculative “radical-scavenging microenvironments.” This converts a conceptual idea into a conservative, testable mutation strategy with clear MS-based validation.

5) Differences between E. coli production and mammalian proteostasis are explicitly normalized by quantifying soluble vs insoluble fractions in cells under ROS, not merely matching total expression. This ensures that improved editing is attributable to improved folding/quality control rather than expression artifacts, aligning the biophysical causality chain with cellular reality.

Collectively, these changes preserve the original mechanistic throughline (cap nucleation/interface packing → fewer oxidizable intermediates → preserved DNA binding → improved TALEN activity under ROS) while converting key weak points into explicit structural constraints, orthogonal measurements, and pre-registered decision points.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually strong in execution specificity: it pre-defines graft junction logic, quantitative geometric filters (angular deviation, DNA clash checks), and orthogonal intermediate readouts (HDX-MS + stopped-flow) with ROS dosimetry controls. The main deductions are: (i) the central mechanistic claim that ROS sensitivity is dominated by edge-repeat fraying/aggregation-competent intermediates is plausible but not tightly parameterized—there is no explicit kinetic/thermodynamic model predicting how much terminal stabilization must reduce intermediate population to measurably reduce oxidation/aggregation, nor clear separation of folded-state oxidation vs intermediate-state oxidation beyond two exposure modes; (ii) the cap strategy risks introducing new immunogenicity/proteostasis liabilities and altered global curvature that could change DNA residence time in ways not fully anticipated by RMSD constraints on the RVD helices alone (long-range allostery/helix register slippage could still occur without large local RMSD changes); (iii) computational screening (Rosetta + short MD) may not reliably discriminate subtle repeat-array multi-basin folding differences—MD timescales and force-field bias could yield false positives unless calibrated against known TALE cap variants or empirical benchmarks; (iv) the interface “minimal mutation set” is described qualitatively but would benefit from explicit per-repeat design rules (e.g., how many positions per junction are mutable, how to avoid creating periodicity-breaking strain) to avoid combinatorial drift and underpowered statistical comparisons across variants.

original_chain: Pluripotency maintenance -> GATA4 -> MAPK/ERK signaling pathway -> MYC-binding partner MAX -> GATA6 -> Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition -> WNT
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A WNT-synchronized, cis-regulatory “enhancer replay” at the endogenous Dusp2/7 loci can constrain ERK time-above-threshold during EMT without flattening basal ERK signaling, thereby preventing ERK-contingent opening of Gata4/Gata6 regulatory elements and subsequent endodermal priming. The mechanistic refinement explicitly separates two mutually exclusive operating regimes and makes them falsifiable: (Regime A: MAX-dependent rescue) the edited enhancer increases the probability of productive MYC/MAX occupancy (E-box grammar + local acetylation) so that, even when MAX is partially limiting (but not absent), Dusp2/7 transcriptional bursting is restored specifically during WNT-high windows; (Regime B: MAX-bypass) if MAX falls below a defined threshold, a WNT-induced, short-lived co-activator tethered only to the edited enhancer can substitute for the missing activation function while preserving endogenous locus control and WNT-phase restriction. The key mechanistic claim is not “ERK inhibition” but “ERK waveform shaping”: DUSP2/7 pulse-like transcription increases phosphatase availability with kinetics tuned to truncate ERK excursions (reduce dwell time above a GATA-priming threshold) while maintaining baseline ERK pulses needed for proliferation/patterning. To address the reviewer concern that WNT/EMT may prime Gata4/6 independently of ERK, the proposal explicitly tests whether Gata4/6 enhancer accessibility and transcription track ERK time-above-threshold under orthogonally controlled ERK waveforms at fixed WNT, and conversely whether β-catenin perturbation affects Gata4/6 when ERK waveforms are held constant. The refined approach overcomes limitations of global MEK inhibition or constitutive DUSP expression by operating at the endogenous cis layer (native mRNA/protein stoichiometry, feedback integration, and chromatin context) and by synchronizing Dusp2/7 reinforcement only to the WNT-high EMT interval where ERK excitability rises.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-specify a mechanistic decision framework (mandatory branching) and quantitative success criteria.
0.1 Define MAX titration axis: introduce an auxin-inducible degron (AID2) or dTAG degron on endogenous Max in the reporter EpiLC line, enabling graded depletion. Calibrate 5–7 MAX abundance levels spanning ~100% to ~0% (quantified by tagged MAX fluorescence and western blot).
0.2 Define the two regimes and go/no-go criteria:
  • Regime A (MAX-dependent rescue): edited enhancer must increase Dusp2/7 burst frequency and/or burst amplitude compared to WT enhancer at intermediate MAX (e.g., 20–60% of baseline), and must lose most of its gain when MAX approaches ~0% (i.e., effect collapses with near-complete MAX depletion). Occupancy requirement: CUT&RUN/Tag shows MAX enrichment at edited enhancer during WNT-high windows.
  • Regime B (MAX-bypass): if MAX <~5–10%, edited enhancer retains inducibility and Dusp2/7 bursting only when the WNT-triggered tethered co-activator is present; CUT&RUN/Tag confirms loss of MAX occupancy but retention of β-catenin/TCF and co-activator recruitment at the edited enhancer.
0.3 Define waveform outcome metrics: ERK-KTR time-above-threshold (TAT), peak amplitude, pulse frequency, and integral (AUC). Primary success: reduced TAT above a pre-defined GATA-priming threshold (set empirically in Step 1.4) without a >30% reduction in basal ERK pulse frequency or complete loss of spatial mesoderm patterning markers in micropatterns.

Step 1 — System setup and disambiguation of causal chain (ERK vs WNT/EMT direct effects).
1.1 Reporter platform (single-cell, time-resolved):
  • ERK activity: ERK-KTR nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio + periodic pERK IF validation.
  • WNT activity: TCF/LEF fluorescent reporter.
  • Dusp2 and Dusp7 transcription: MS2/PP7 knock-in (preferred for burst kinetics) or intronic fluorescent tagging if MS2/PP7 is not feasible.
  • Fate/state: Nanog/Rex1, Gata4, Gata6 knock-in reporters; EMT reporters (E-cadherin, Vimentin).
1.2 Establish micropattern EMT differentiation (Asset 2 conditions) with controlled WNT pulse schedules (e.g., continuous vs pulsed CHIR) and FGF titration. Acquire radial time courses with live imaging for ERK-KTR, WNT reporter, Dusp2/7 bursting, and Gata4/6 onset.
1.3 Establish causal baseline with MAX depletion (Asset 1 reproduction): graded MAX degron in micropattern EMT; quantify Dusp2/7 bursting collapse, ERK TAT increase, and Gata4/6 induction.
1.4 Orthogonal ERK waveform control to test ERK→GATA priming necessity/sufficiency:
  • Implement optoRAF or optoMEK (light-inducible RAF/MEK) or chemically inducible MEK/ERK activation to impose defined ERK pulse trains under constant WNT (fixed CHIR).
  • Map a “GATA-priming boundary” by varying ERK pulse width/frequency and measuring: (i) time-resolved ATAC at Gata4/Gata6 enhancers, (ii) Gata4/6 reporter activation.
  • Success criterion for ERK dependence: Gata4/6 enhancer accessibility and transcription must correlate with ERK TAT across imposed waveforms even when WNT is constant.
1.5 Orthogonal β-catenin/WNT perturbation to test WNT direct effects at matched ERK:
  • At fixed imposed ERK waveforms (from 1.4), perturb β-catenin/TCF (e.g., β-catenin degradation, dominant-negative TCF, or porcupine/WNT secretion inhibition as applicable) while maintaining ERK waveform.
  • If Gata4/6 priming persists with matched ERK, WNT-independent ERK causality is supported; if priming collapses, WNT direct gating is implicated. This explicitly disambiguates attribution.

Step 2 — Define native “MAX-centered enhancer logic” at Dusp2/7 and preserve 3D topology.
2.1 Map cis-regulatory architecture across PSC→EpiLC→EMT time course:
  • CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN: MAX, MYC, H3K27ac, H3K4me1, p300/CBP, BRD4, and TCF7L1/TCF7L2.
  • ATAC-seq for accessibility dynamics.
  • Nascent transcription (PRO-seq or TT-seq) on key timepoints to quantify enhancer RNAs and Dusp2/7 initiation rates.
2.2 3D topology risk mitigation (mandatory):
  • Micro-C or HiChIP (H3K27ac and/or cohesin/RAD21) focusing on the Dusp2 and Dusp7 domains to identify enhancer–promoter loops and CTCF boundaries.
  • Explicit rule: edits must not delete/transpose CTCF motifs or boundary elements; if an enhancer overlaps architectural elements, use augmentation rather than replacement.
2.3 Identify “minimal necessary” enhancer segments: select enhancer(s) with (i) strong MAX/MYC occupancy in PSC/EpiLC, (ii) WNT/EMT time-dependent modulation, and (iii) physical contact with Dusp2/7 promoters. Prioritize elements whose activity drops upon acute MAX depletion.

Step 3 — Cis-regulatory enhancer replay designs (locus-integrated) with explicit parameters and controls.
3.1 Two editing strategies (run in parallel to de-risk topology disruption):
  • Strategy R (Replacement): precise substitution of a defined enhancer core (≤300–600 bp) that lacks CTCF/boundary motifs.
  • Strategy A (Augmentation “landing pad”): insert a compact synthetic enhancer module into a permissive site within the same TAD and within mapped enhancer hub proximity (validated by Micro-C/HiChIP), leaving endogenous enhancer intact.
3.2 Synthetic enhancer grammar (explicit and testable):
  • E-box cluster: 3–5 canonical E-boxes (CACGTG) with defined spacing (e.g., 10–14 bp periodicity to favor cooperative binding), plus 1–2 lower-affinity E-box variants to tune dynamic range.
  • TCF/LEF motifs: 2–4 TCF motifs positioned to enable WNT-phase amplification without constitutive activation (tested via motif deletion arms).
  • Chromatin cofactor compatibility: include a short acetylation-favoring sequence context (validated by p300/H3K27ac readouts) without introducing new CTCF motifs.
3.3 Mandatory motif/grammar control arms (installed at Dusp2 only, Dusp7 only, and both):
  • WT enhancer (unedited).
  • TCF-only (E-boxes mutated).
  • E-box-only (TCF motifs mutated).
  • Scrambled spacing/orientation (same motif counts, altered grammar).
  • Neutral sequence insertion control (length-matched).

Step 4 — Specify the WNT-triggered co-activator: explicit recruitment route, half-life, and off-target tests.
4.1 Design principle: enhancer-local recruitment without dCas9 targeting (preferred) to avoid genome-wide binding. Use a β-catenin/TCF-dependent recruitment mechanism that acts only at the edited enhancer.
4.2 Concrete, testable architecture (two alternatives; choose based on off-target performance):
  • Option 1 (TCF-tethered activator, enhancer-restricted): knock-in a minimal, inducible TCF-interacting co-activator module expressed only during WNT-high windows, engineered to be recruited through TCF bound at the edited enhancer. The activator domain is compact and defined (e.g., p300 HAT core mini-domain or a BRD4/Mediator-recruiting domain), fused to a strong degron.
  • Option 2 (β-catenin-interacting activator): a degron-tagged, β-catenin-binding peptide fused to a defined activation domain that enhances local transcription only where β-catenin/TCF is DNA-bound; recruitment is mediated by β-catenin interaction.
4.3 Degron kinetics (explicit): implement AID2 or dTAG for rapid clearance; target protein half-life ≤1–2 hours after WNT withdrawal, verified by live fluorescence decay. Expression is under a TCF/LEF-responsive promoter with destabilized mRNA (e.g., AU-rich element) to reduce carryover.
4.4 Specificity/off-target profiling (mandatory):
  • During WNT-high windows, perform RNA-seq (bulk and/or scRNA-seq) and nascent transcription (PRO-seq/TT-seq) to detect global activation at other WNT or E-box loci.
  • CUT&Tag for the activator fusion (epitope-tagged) to confirm enrichment at edited Dusp2/7 enhancers and quantify genome-wide binding.
  • Pre-specified acceptance: minimal activation of non-target MYC/MAX or WNT targets beyond expected WNT program; any broad hyperacetylation signatures triggers fallback to Strategy A only (augmentation without co-activator) or lower-activity domains.

Step 5 — Quantitative DUSP→ERK dynamical modeling to tune enhancer strength and predict waveform shaping.
5.1 Build an ODE/state-space model incorporating: ERK activation (FGF/MAPK), Dusp2/7 transcriptional bursting (from MS2/PP7), DUSP protein turnover, and ERK dephosphorylation kinetics. Fit parameters using perturbation data (FGF titration, MAX titration, WNT pulses).
5.2 Use the model to choose motif number/affinity to achieve: (i) increased burst frequency during WNT-high, (ii) minimal change during WNT-low, (iii) predicted reduction in ERK TAT without abolishing basal pulses.
5.3 Validate model predictions experimentally by comparing motif variants and measuring ERK waveform metrics and fate outputs.

Step 6 — Validation in micropattern EMT with mechanistic endpoints and benchmarking.
6.1 Primary mechanistic readouts:
  • Dusp2/7 transcription bursting statistics vs WNT phase.
  • ERK waveform metrics (TAT, amplitude, AUC) across micropattern radii.
  • MAX/MYC/TCF and co-activator occupancy at edited enhancers (CUT&RUN/Tag).
6.2 ERK vs WNT/EMT disambiguation endpoints:
  • ATAC-seq (or scATAC) at Gata4/Gata6 enhancers under: (i) imposed ERK waveforms at fixed WNT, (ii) β-catenin perturbation at matched ERK.
  • Requirement: edited enhancer reduces Gata4/6 enhancer accessibility specifically when ERK TAT is constrained.
6.3 Developmental competence and specificity:
  • Spatial fate markers (BRACHYURY, CDX2, definitive endoderm markers upon protocol switch) to ensure patterning competence.
  • Compare against: global MEK inhibition, constitutive Dusp2/7 transgene, and generic CRISPRa (if included).
6.4 Redundancy/compensation risk management:
  • Measure other DUSPs and feedback nodes (e.g., Dusp1/5/6) by scRNA-seq; test whether compensation undermines the intended ERK shaping.
  • If redundancy blunts effect, iterate by including additional MYC/MAX-responsive phosphatase enhancer replay only if modeling predicts necessity (pre-specified threshold for iteration).

Feasibility: 1) Mechanistic coherence and falsifiability (addresses ‘MAX-centered logic’ ambiguity): The proposal now enforces a decision framework that distinguishes MAX-dependent rescue from MAX-bypass with explicit MAX titration, occupancy assays, and pre-specified success/failure criteria. This directly resolves the reviewer’s concern that an E-box enhancer cannot function when MAX is absent without contradicting the stated mechanism.

2) Explicit co-activator design and off-target containment: The β-catenin/WNT-triggered co-activator is no longer a vague peptide; it has (i) a defined recruitment route (via TCF/β-catenin interaction at the edited enhancer), (ii) a defined activation mechanism (Mediator/BRD4/p300-recruitment option), (iii) enforced rapid turnover (AID2/dTAG; ≤1–2 h half-life), and (iv) mandatory genome-wide binding/transcriptional off-target profiling (CUT&Tag + PRO-seq/RNA-seq) during WNT-high windows. This makes specificity testable and provides clear fallback logic (drop co-activator; use augmentation-only) if promiscuity is detected.

3) Disambiguation of ERK-dependent vs WNT/EMT-direct GATA priming: By orthogonally imposing ERK waveforms (opto/chemogenetic RAF/MEK) under constant WNT and performing β-catenin perturbations under matched ERK, the causal attribution “ERK TAT → Gata4/6 enhancer opening” becomes experimentally isolatable rather than assumed.

4) Enhancer editing feasibility and topology protection: The plan explicitly maps 3D contacts (Micro-C/HiChIP) and prohibits disruption of CTCF/boundary elements. It also de-risks multi-locus editing by running a safer enhancer-augmentation (landing pad) arm in parallel with replacement, preserving native locus architecture if replacement perturbs looping.

5) Dynamic shaping is quantitatively engineered rather than hoped: A DUSP→ERK dynamical model is incorporated to tune motif number/affinity and predict the degree of ERK excursion truncation achievable from burst-frequency modulation, accounting for feedback kinetics and potential redundancy in the DUSP network. This directly addresses concerns about achieving “prevent excursions without flattening” and about compensatory phosphatase networks.

6) Alignment with Assets 1–2 and comparative advantage: Asset 1 provides the mechanistic anchor (MYC/MAX→Dusp2/7→low ERK for pluripotency), while Asset 2 provides the relevant high-excitability WNT/EMT context where ERK excursions and GATA6-linked progression are likely. The revised intervention remains cis-logic-driven at endogenous loci and is benchmarked against MEK inhibition and constitutive DUSP expression to demonstrate preserved developmental fidelity and competence.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually strong in engineering resolution: it specifies endogenous editing strategies (replacement vs augmentation), mandatory topology protection via Micro-C/HiChIP, quantitative single-cell burst/ERK waveform metrics, and a falsifiable decision framework around MAX dependence. The main score deductions are for (i) mechanistic overreach in the MAX-bypass regime: a WNT-triggered activator recruited via β-catenin/TCF is likely to act broadly at many TCF-occupied loci, and the claim of enhancer-restricted action without a locus-unique recruiter is not fully justified; CUT&Tag/PRO-seq will detect off-targets, but the design premise itself is precarious. (ii) Causal chain complexity: Dusp2/7 are not the only ERK phosphatases shaping ERK dwell time; redundancy (Dusp5/6, Sprouty, etc.) may dominate ERK TAT, and the proposal’s success criteria risk being unattainable from Dusp2/7-only edits unless effect sizes are demonstrated early. (iii) Practical throughput: combining micropattern live imaging, MS2/PP7 at two loci, graded MAX degron, optoERK, ATAC time series, and multiple enhancer edit arms is an exceptionally heavy integration burden; prioritization/critical-path reduction is not fully enforced despite the stated branching logic.

original_chain: Obeticholic acid -> Leptin -> Resistin -> Ursodeoxycholic acid -> Wnt signalling pathway -> All-trans retinoic acid
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) establishes a hepatobiliary Wnt/β-catenin chromatin state that gates FXR genomic occupancy and transcriptional output at bile-acid metabolic and secretome loci, thereby reprogramming the liver’s endocrine signals that control adipokine balance (resistin vs leptin) in a coupled liver–adipose axis. The key mechanistic refinement is that FXR activation requires intracellular ligand; therefore, ECM ‘tethering’ is not assumed to directly activate FXR. Instead, we will explicitly discriminate (i) true intracellular delivery from (ii) purely extracellular presentation that cannot enter cells, using a mandatory ligand triad: (A) cell-impermeant, non-cleavable ECM-tethered UDCA/OCA; (B) matched soluble UDCA/OCA; and (C) ECM-tethered but cleavable UDCA/OCA (photocleavable or esterase-cleavable) engineered to release native ligand in a quantifiable, localized, slow-release manner under flow. We hypothesize that only conditions that produce measurable intracellular UDCA/OCA (soluble and cleavable-tether) will generate FXR nuclear translocation/occupancy and canonical target induction, while the non-cleavable cell-impermeant tether will not—thereby converting the tethering concept into a controllable intracellular-kinetics module rather than an assumed ‘receptor-proximal’ activator. Within those verified intracellular-exposure regimes, we further hypothesize that ATRA-induced Wnt chromatin priming is necessary for the differential FXR cistrome/transcriptome induced by UDCA versus OCA potency (clinical divergence), such that Wnt suppression (β-catenin knockdown/CRISPRi, PORCN inhibition, or TCF/LEF blockade) will ablate ATRA-dependent differences in FXR occupancy and downstream endocrine outputs (e.g., FGF19/cytokines) that drive resistin-linked inflammation versus leptin-linked energy homeostasis. This framework directly addresses the reviewer’s physical/biochemical concern (intracellular ligand requirement) and adds decisive causality tests for Wnt→FXR coupling.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registration, success criteria, and experimental design
0.1 Pre-register primary outcomes and quantitative success criteria:
  (i) Intracellular ligand: LC–MS/MS in hepatocytes/cholangiocytes must show >5× above LLOQ and >3× over non-cleavable tether condition for ‘intracellular-exposure-positive’ conditions.
  (ii) FXR activation: ≥2-fold induction (qPCR and RNA-seq concordant) of ≥3 canonical FXR targets (NR0B2/SHP, ABCB11/BSEP, SLC51A/B/OSTα/β) plus FXR nuclear translocation (immunofluorescence time series) and FXR chromatin occupancy gain (CUT&Tag) at target enhancers/promoters.
  (iii) Wnt-dependence: ATRA-driven differences in FXR occupancy/transcriptome between UDCA vs OCA must be reduced by ≥70% (effect-size shrinkage in differential binding and DE genes) under Wnt suppression (β-catenin CRISPRi or PORCN inhibitor) compared with Wnt-intact controls.
  (iv) Endocrine/adipokine coupling: liver module secretome changes must predict adipose resistin/leptin shifts with pre-specified directionality (reduce resistin and normalize leptin) and meet a minimum explained variance R² ≥ 0.5 in the pre-registered ODE/PK-PD model.
0.2 Power/replication structure: ≥3 independent hepatocyte donors; within-donor triplicate chips per condition; randomization of chip assignment; blinded sample processing for omics.

Step 1 — Build the coupled human liver–adipose microphysiological system (MPS) with defined transport/metabolism capabilities
1.1 Liver module cellular architecture:
  - Primary human hepatocytes (PHH) co-cultured with cholangiocytes and hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) in a tunable ECM hydrogel (e.g., PEG-based or gelatin methacrylate variant) optimized for hepatocyte polarity.
  - Confirm canalicular function and bile acid transport competence: BSEP/ABCB11 localization, MRP2, NTCP/SLC10A1; functional assays with fluorescent bile acid analog transport.
1.2 Adipose module:
  - Mature adipocytes plus stromal vascular fraction cells to capture inflammatory/adipokine responsiveness.
1.3 Fluidic coupling:
  - Recirculating medium to permit endocrine cross-talk; define flow rates and shear (report actual µL/min; maintain hepatocyte-appropriate shear ranges).
  - Document what “metabolism/transport confounds” remain operative: quantify bile-acid uptake (NTCP), efflux (BSEP/OSTα/β), and metabolic conversion (CYP/phase II if present) using targeted LC–MS/MS.

Step 2 — Establish disease-relevant cholestatic stress context with explicit controls
2.1 Induce cholestatic-like stress in the liver module:
  - BSEP inhibition (tool compound) plus bile acid overload; add inflammatory cues to mimic PBC/PSC-like environment.
2.2 Baseline readouts (pre-intervention):
  - FXR axis: NR0B2/SHP, ABCB11/BSEP, SLC51A/B.
  - Wnt axis: AXIN2, LGR5.
  - Fibrosis: COL1A1, ACTA2; HSC activation markers; ECM stiffness mapping.
  - Adipokines in shared circulation: resistin, leptin.

Step 3 — Engineer and validate the mandatory ligand triad to resolve the ‘intracellular ligand’ requirement
3.1 Chemistry design (three ligand formats per bile acid; both UDCA and OCA):
  A) Non-cleavable, cell-impermeant ECM-tether:
    - Install a high-polarity, PEGylated linker and a permanent covalent attachment to hydrogel (SPAAC click: azide–DBCO).
    - Add a charged moiety on the linker (e.g., sulfonate) to prevent membrane permeation and minimize passive uptake after any incidental release.
  B) Soluble ligand controls:
    - Native UDCA and OCA at matched nominal concentrations and exposure time.
  C) Cleavable ECM-tether (two options; implement at least one):
    - Photocleavable linker (e.g., o-nitrobenzyl-based) enabling spatial/temporal release; quantify release rate under defined illumination dose.
    - Esterase-cleavable linker (e.g., self-immolative ester) enabling slow enzymatic release; quantify release kinetics in conditioned medium.
3.2 Hydrogel functionalization parameters:
  - Functionalize hydrogel with DBCO at a defined mol% relative to polymer repeat units; create a tether-density series (e.g., low/medium/high) and directly quantify immobilized ligand density by using a fluorescently tagged analog in parallel or by exhaustive hydrogel digestion followed by LC–MS/MS.
3.3 Validation assays (must pass before proceeding to mechanistic omics):
  - Intracellular UDCA/OCA quantification (LC–MS/MS) in hepatocytes/cholangiocytes for each condition (A/B/C) under flow at multiple timepoints.
  - FXR reporter assay (in hepatocyte reporter line) using released fractions from cleavable tethers to verify preserved agonism.
  - FXR nuclear translocation time course (immunofluorescence) and early target gene induction kinetics.
Decision gate:
  - If non-cleavable tether (A) yields negligible intracellular ligand and no FXR activation (expected), proceed using condition (C) as the engineered ‘controlled intracellular kinetics’ modality.
  - If (A) unexpectedly yields intracellular ligand, perform additional permeability/leak testing (hydrogel release, linker instability) to rule out unintended cleavage.
  - If (C) fails to generate controllable intracellular exposure, pivot (pre-specified) to an alternative intracellular-kinetics controller: albumin-bound slow-release formulation or nanoparticle/prodrug delivery with matched kinetics, retaining the same causal Wnt→FXR tests.

Step 4 — ATRA priming and hard Wnt-causality interventions (necessary/sufficient tests)
4.1 ATRA priming schedule:
  - Apply ATRA during a defined priming window; washout to separate priming from direct ligand cross-effects.
4.2 Wnt perturbation panel (implement at least two orthogonal approaches):
  - β-catenin (CTNNB1) CRISPRi or siRNA knockdown in hepatocytes (and optionally cholangiocytes).
  - PORCN inhibition to block Wnt ligand secretion.
  - TCF/LEF transcriptional blockade (dominant-negative or small-molecule where appropriate).
4.3 Necessity criterion:
  - Require that ATRA-induced changes in FXR cistrome/transcriptome (and endocrine outputs) are abolished or markedly reduced under Wnt suppression.
4.4 Sufficiency test (optional but recommended):
  - Activate Wnt (e.g., Wnt3a or GSK3β inhibition) without ATRA to test whether Wnt activation alone can reproduce the primed FXR response profile.

Step 5 — Map Wnt→FXR chromatin coupling with mechanistic resolution
5.1 ATAC-seq (or low-input ATAC) in hepatocytes/cholangiocytes:
  - Compare accessibility changes induced by ATRA priming ± Wnt blockade.
5.2 CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN:
  - FXR occupancy mapping under intracellular-exposure-positive conditions (soluble vs cleavable-tether) with and without ATRA priming.
  - β-catenin/TCF occupancy mapping to identify co-occupied or sequentially primed regions.
5.3 Causal linkage readouts:
  - Identify loci where ATRA increases accessibility/β-catenin occupancy and enables subsequent FXR binding (or alters binding strength), particularly at bile-acid transport/metabolism genes and secretome/cytokine genes.

Step 6 — Endocrine coupling to adipose module and adipokine outcomes (resistin/leptin)
6.1 Liver secretome profiling:
  - Targeted and unbiased: cytokines, FGF19, lipoprotein-related factors, bile-acid composition (LC–MS/MS).
6.2 Adipose response:
  - Resistin and leptin secretion; STAT3/AMPK signaling; NF-κB activation; insulin signaling and glucose uptake.
6.3 Mediator dissection:
  - Neutralization/antagonism: FGFR4 blockade (FGF19 axis), TGR5 controls, and selective inhibition as needed to attribute adipose changes to defined liver outputs.

Step 7 — Disease-relevant endpoints
7.1 Fibrogenesis and cholangiopathy:
  - HSC activation, collagen deposition, and stiffness mapping; cholangiocyte injury markers.
7.2 Metabolic endpoints:
  - Hepatic steatosis imaging, β-oxidation flux; adipose insulin sensitivity.

Step 8 — Quantitative ODE/PK-PD model with identifiability tied to measured variables
8.1 Define state variables:
  - Effective FXR activation E_FXR(t) explicitly parameterized by measured intracellular ligand concentration C_intra(t), nuclear FXR fraction N_FXR(t), and residence/occupancy O_FXR(t).
  - Wnt chromatin priming parameter P_Wnt derived from ATAC-seq accessibility metrics at pre-defined FXR target loci and β-catenin occupancy.
8.2 Identifiability analysis:
  - Use the tether-density series and release kinetics measurements (for cleavable-tether) to ensure parameters governing C_intra(t) are identifiable from LC–MS/MS timecourses under flow.
  - Pre-specify acceptance: parameters must have bounded confidence intervals and low collinearity; otherwise simplify model or add measurements.
8.3 Predictive objective:
  - Predict intervention combinations (ATRA timing + UDCA/OCA potency + intracellular exposure kinetics) that minimize resistin, normalize leptin, and improve cholestatic injury markers; prospectively validate in held-out donor chips.
Feasibility: 1) Directly resolves the reviewer’s core biochemical concern (FXR is intracellular): The proposal no longer assumes ECM-immobilized bile acids ‘activate FXR at the membrane.’ Instead, the mandatory ligand triad (non-cleavable cell-impermeant tether vs soluble vs cleavable-tether) combined with intracellular LC–MS/MS and FXR occupancy readouts provides a decisive feasibility test. If tethering cannot produce intracellular exposure, the design contains a pre-specified pivot to alternative intracellular-kinetics control (albumin-bound slow-release or nanoparticle/prodrug), preserving the central aim (controlling ligand kinetics under flow) without violating FXR biology.
2) Establishes Wnt causality (not correlation): Orthogonal Wnt suppression (β-catenin CRISPRi/knockdown, PORCN inhibition, and/or TCF/LEF blockade) is explicitly required to abolish ATRA-dependent differences in FXR cistrome/transcriptome and downstream endocrine outputs. This meets the necessity criterion demanded by reviewers and directly tests the hypothesis that an ATRA-set Wnt chromatin state gates FXR transcriptional programs.
3) Retains and strengthens the UDCA vs OCA divergence logic: Asset 1 supports bile-acid receptor modulation (FXR) affecting metabolic/inflammatory outputs and adipokines (resistin/leptin), while Asset 2 supports cholestasis/fibrosis pathway dysregulation involving Wnt and highlights ATRA as an emerging modulator. The refined proposal connects these by (i) verifying intracellular exposure and FXR pathway fidelity under controlled-release conditions, and (ii) mapping how Wnt priming shifts FXR occupancy at metabolic/secretome loci that plausibly drive adipose resistin/leptin responses.
4) Quantitative rigor and definitional clarity: The “effective FXR activation” variable is no longer an inferred proxy from tether density alone; it is explicitly anchored to measurable tether/release parameters, intracellular ligand concentration, nuclear FXR dynamics, and chromatin occupancy, with pre-registered success criteria and identifiability analysis. This prevents overreach about eliminating metabolism/transport confounds and instead quantifies which transport/metabolic pathways remain active and how controlled-release changes intracellular kinetics.
5) Implementability within an MPS: Each critical step has concrete, testable parameters (tether density series; cleavable linker option; LC–MS/MS timecourses; decision gates). The approach leverages established bioorthogonal hydrogel chemistry and established omics assays (ATAC-seq, CUT&Tag) while adding the specific controls necessary to make the mechanistic claims physically and biochemically valid.
final_critique: The proposal is strongest where it converts a prior conceptual weakness (FXR requires intracellular ligand) into a falsifiable engineering module: the triad, quantitative intracellular LC–MS/MS criteria, and explicit pivot plan are technically grounded and reviewer-responsive. The Wnt→FXR causality plan is also materially improved by orthogonal Wnt suppression and explicit effect-size shrinkage thresholds. Key score deductions: (i) biological plausibility and specificity of the endocrine bridge to adipose remains underdetermined—resistin/leptin shifts are plausibly multi-mediator and donor/context dependent, and the proposal does not pre-specify a minimal mechanistic set of liver-derived mediators beyond broad secretome profiling; this risks post hoc attribution even with neutralization tests. (ii) The cholestatic stress model (BSEP inhibition + BA overload + inflammatory cues) may confound FXR readouts by altering transport, toxicity, and nuclear receptor cross-talk; while the proposal acknowledges transport/metabolism confounds, it does not clearly define how it will disentangle injury-driven transcriptomic shifts from bona fide FXR cistrome reprogramming (e.g., viability thresholds, stress-response covariates, or orthogonal FXR antagonism controls). (iii) The ATRA→Wnt “chromatin priming” claim is ambitious: the design includes ATAC-seq and β-catenin/TCF occupancy, but it lacks a crisp definition of the primed state at pre-specified loci (beyond general accessibility metrics) and does not include an explicit temporal ordering test (ATRA/Wnt occupancy preceding FXR binding) with adequate time resolution. (iv) The ECM-tether chemistry is plausible, but the non-permeant/non-cleavable condition could still yield intracellular ligand via hydrogel erosion, bile-acid transporter-mediated uptake of trace released ligand, or adsorption to proteins—controls are mentioned but not fully enumerated (mass balance, hydrogel integrity under shear, protein corona effects). Overall: high engineering rigor and a coherent mechanistic narrative, with remaining risk centered on endocrine-coupling specificity and confounding stress biology in the disease context.

original_chain: Neurotoxic ibotenic acid -> Cerebral cortex -> Dendritic spine -> Rabies-based trans-synaptic tracing -> Dendritic spine -> Cerebral cortex -> Couptf1 -> Pyramidal glutamatergic cortical neuron
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Post-lesion circuit reintegration of pyramidal glutamatergic cortical neurons is governed by a non-canonical, post-translational function of Couptf1 that regulates dendritic spine competency for stable trans-synaptic coupling. Specifically, we hypothesize that activity-dependent nuclear–cytoplasmic shuttling of Couptf1 controls a spine-localized transcriptional memory program via interaction with chromatin-associated RNAs, thereby biasing which spines become permissive for long-range cortical inputs. A structurally novel methodological adaptation—nanobody-mediated, light-controllable Couptf1 sequestration combined with barcoded, self-inactivating rabies-based trans-synaptic tracing—will causally reveal how Couptf1-dependent spine states dictate cortical connectivity after ibotenic-acid–induced lesions.
Plan: Step 1: System setup and lesion paradigm.
- Induce focal excitotoxic lesions in adult mouse visual cortex using neurotoxic ibotenic acid to selectively ablate local pyramidal glutamatergic neurons while preserving afferent axons and cortical lamination.
- Use wild-type mice (no Cre/driver lines) to avoid developmental confounds and ensure post-lesion specificity of all manipulations.

Step 2: Methodological adaptation – post-translational Couptf1 control and spine-state encoding.
- Engineer an intracellular anti-Couptf1 nanobody fused to a light-sensitive LOV2 domain and a nuclear export signal (NES). Under blue-light illumination, the LOV2 domain uncages the NES, acutely exporting Couptf1 from the nucleus; in darkness, Couptf1 remains nuclear. This enables reversible, temporally precise manipulation of Couptf1 function without altering its gene expression.
- Co-express a spine-targeted RNA barcoding module: an MS2-tagged immediate-early RNA scaffold (localized to dendritic spines via Arc 3′UTR elements) that recruits an RNA-binding protein fused to a histone-modifying enzyme (e.g., SETD1A catalytic core). This creates a Couptf1-dependent ‘epigenetic imprint’ reflecting prior spine activity.
- Implement a self-inactivating, glycoprotein-deleted rabies virus library carrying unique synaptic barcodes (but with rabies glycoprotein supplied transiently in trans via a destabilized protein). This limits viral spread temporally and allows quantitative mapping of presynaptic partners to individual starter neurons without sustained toxicity.
- Optical manipulation of Couptf1 nuclear availability is performed during defined post-lesion windows (e.g., days 5–10) to test causality between Couptf1 state, spine imprinting, and connectivity.

Step 3: Validation and analytical framework.
- Perform longitudinal two-photon imaging to track dendritic spine formation, elimination, and stabilization under different Couptf1 shuttling regimes.
- Recover rabies barcodes from presynaptic neurons using single-cell RNA sequencing, reconstructing input maps to individual pyramidal neurons and correlating them with prior spine-state imprints.
- Use electrophysiology to assess synaptic strength and input specificity (visual vs non-visual cortical afferents).
- Apply causal mediation modeling to test whether Couptf1-dependent spine imprints statistically mediate the relationship between lesion-induced activity and trans-synaptic partner selection.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Couptf1 is classically viewed as a transcription factor, but emerging evidence indicates that several nuclear receptors exert rapid, non-genomic effects through regulated nuclear shuttling and RNA interactions. Dendritic spine stabilization is known to depend on activity history and local RNA regulation, providing a plausible mechanistic bridge.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): This proposal adapts rabies-based trans-synaptic tracing from a static connectivity map into a temporally gated, barcode-resolved assay integrated with post-translational protein control—an approach squarely within advanced bioengineering and biomedicine.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike genetic enhancer logic or permanent gene perturbation, this strategy achieves reversible, time-resolved control of Couptf1 function and links it to a physical spine-state memory. It disentangles transcriptional versus post-translational roles of Couptf1 and provides a mechanistic explanation for selective cortical rewiring after excitotoxic injury.
final_critique: This is an ambitious and largely well-integrated proposal with strong bioengineering innovation. The nanobody–LOV2 strategy for post-translational Couptf1 control is technically plausible and appropriately matched to the hypothesis. However, several mechanistic links remain speculative: (i) the existence of a spine-localized, Couptf1-dependent chromatin/RNA ‘memory’ program is asserted without sufficient intermediate validation steps; (ii) recruiting a histone-modifying enzyme via spine-localized RNAs risks nuclear off-target effects and dilution of spatial specificity; and (iii) performing barcode-resolved rabies tracing in wild-type mice without genetic targeting introduces ambiguity in starter-cell identity and cell-type specificity. These issues do not invalidate the proposal but reduce confidence in causal interpretability.

original_chain: Retinitis pigmentosa -> Regenerative medicine -> Embryonic hematopoietic ontogeny -> Human pluripotent stem cell -> Regenerative medicine -> Embryonic stem cell -> Diabetes mellitus -> Pdx1 gene
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A minimal, lineage-relevant, enhancer-gated CRISPR editing framework—restricted to definitive endoderm (for pancreas) and photoreceptor progenitor (for retina) competence windows—will achieve superior on-target precision, reduced stress signaling, and improved functional maturation compared to constitutive hPSC editing, without invoking a mesodermal HE/EHT detour. Mechanistically, transient editor activation during these lineage-appropriate windows exploits (i) cell-cycle states enriched for S/G2, (ii) locally open chromatin at fate-defining loci (PDX1 or RP-associated genes), and (iii) a balanced DNA repair milieu characterized by increased RAD51/BRCA1 recruitment and restrained 53BP1 occupancy. A narrowly defined, short-duration modulation of the p53–PUMA axis during editing further enhances cell survival while preserving post-edit genomic surveillance. The hypothesis explicitly predicts that HE/EHT-like states are not generically transferable for genome conditioning across lineages; instead, genomic stability and editing fidelity are maximized when editor activity is aligned with lineage-intrinsic competence states that naturally coordinate chromatin accessibility, DNA repair pathway usage, and differentiation trajectory.
Plan: Minimal Viable Architecture (shared across both arms):
1) Editor modality: a single high-fidelity SpCas9-HF1 (or PEmax for RP if point mutation requires) fused to an FKBP12-derived destabilization domain, allowing rapid small-molecule-controlled clearance (Shield-1 on/off kinetics <6 h).
2) Gating logic: one recombinase system (CreERT2) driven by lineage-specific enhancers only—SOX17/FOXA2 enhancer for definitive endoderm; CRX or NRL enhancer for photoreceptor progenitors. No HE/EHT enhancers are included in the base design.
3) Leakiness thresholds: editor expression <1% of cells outside reporter-positive gate (quantified by Cas9 immunostaining and amplicon sequencing); failure triggers removal of recombinase gating and fallback to inducible promoter-only control.

Step A: System setup and reporters.
A1) Generate patient-derived iPSCs with (i) a defined RP point mutation and (ii) a diabetes-relevant genetic background; insert fluorescent reporters at SOX17 (definitive endoderm) and CRX (photoreceptor progenitor) loci.
A2) Integrate a single safe-harbor cassette (AAVS1) containing: Cre-activated editor + degron + negative selection marker (HSV-TK) expressed only if editor persists beyond 72 h.

Step B: Lineage-relevant gated editing.
B1) Pancreatic arm: Differentiate iPSCs to definitive endoderm. Upon SOX17-reporter positivity, activate CreERT2 for a 24 h window to induce Cas9 or dCas9-VP64. Apply CRISPRa to endogenous PDX1 promoter/enhancer cluster with a defined pulse (24–48 h), then withdraw Shield-1 to clear editor.
B2) Retinal arm: Generate retinal organoids. Upon CRX/NRL-reporter positivity, induce CreERT2 for 24 h to activate base or prime editor correcting the RP allele. Allele-specific guides are used where possible.

Step C: p53 modulation and safeguards.
C1) p53 strategy: transient CRISPRi or siRNA targeting PUMA (BBC3), not TP53, applied only during the 24 h editing window. Recovery criterion: restoration of PUMA expression within 48 h post-edit; failure triggers HSV-TK-mediated ablation.
C2) Clone-level safeguards: negative selection against cells retaining editor beyond 72 h; release criteria include normal karyotype, absence of large SVs by optical genome mapping, and <0.5% residual editor transcript by qPCR.

Step D: Mechanistic causality tests.
D1) DNA repair assays during gated window: RAD51 and BRCA1 foci formation, 53BP1 displacement kinetics, HDR/NHEJ reporter ratios, and cell-cycle profiling.
D2) Necessity test: parallel arms with (i) ungated constitutive editing and (ii) attempted HE/EHT-gated editing; compare repair metrics, lineage fidelity, and stress-response programs.

Step E: Functional validation.
E1) Beta-like cells: glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, transcriptomic maturity index, and in vivo glycemic rescue.
E2) Photoreceptors: outer segment formation, electrophysiology, and light-response rescue in organoid assays.

Fallback logic: If recombinase gating shows >1% leakiness or incomplete clearance, revert to small-molecule-inducible editor without enhancer gating; if CRISPRa of PDX1 underperforms, substitute short mRNA-based PDX1 pulse for benchmarking only.
Feasibility: This revised design directly addresses reviewer concerns by eliminating the HE/EHT detour unless explicitly reintroduced as a controlled comparator. Causality is de-risked through defined mechanistic endpoints linking lineage-gated editing to DNA repair pathway usage (RAD51/BRCA1 vs 53BP1), cell-cycle state, and chromatin accessibility at target loci. The system is intentionally minimal—one editor, one recombinase, one safe-harbor cassette—with quantified leakiness thresholds and explicit fallback options. By separating shared infrastructure (editor, degron, safeguards) from arm-specific biology (PDX1 CRISPRa vs RP allele correction), the proposal clarifies essential versus optional components. Safety is strengthened by targeting the p53–PUMA apoptotic node rather than TP53 itself, tightly constraining duration, and enforcing clone-level negative selection and genomic release criteria compatible with GMP translation. Overall, the approach leverages established principles from pluripotent stem cell biology and developmental gene regulation while avoiding unnecessary architectural complexity, making the proposal technically feasible, mechanistically testable, and translationally credible.
final_critique: This is a technically sophisticated and conceptually disciplined proposal. Engineering resolution is high: the use of enhancer-driven CreERT2 gating, FKBP-based destabilization, safe-harbor integration, and clone-level negative selection reflects careful architectural minimalism rather than gadget accumulation. The mechanistic logic—aligning editor activity with lineage-specific chromatin accessibility, S/G2 enrichment, and RAD51/BRCA1-biased repair—is internally consistent and experimentally testable. The explicit rejection of HE/EHT as a generically transferable genome-conditioning state is a strength, not a weakness, and the inclusion of HE/EHT as a comparator arm strengthens causal inference. Minor deductions arise from feasibility risk at the margins: enhancer specificity and timing precision in organoids (CRX/NRL windows) are nontrivial, and the reliance on PUMA-only modulation assumes uniform decoupling of apoptosis from other p53-dependent stress responses. Evidence grounding is strong but slightly overextended by the inclusion of embryonic hematopoietic ontogeny, which, while justified as a falsified alternative, is still peripheral to the core regenerative endpoints. Overall, the rationale is creative and addresses a real bottleneck—editing-induced stress and loss of maturation in hPSC derivatives—through a structurally novel yet restrained solution.

original_chain: Mitochondrial disorder -> Neurological disorder -> Human pluripotent stem cell -> Catalytic domain of histone demethylase JMJD3 -> HNF1A -> Hepatic cell
concept_chain: Catalytic domain of histone demethylase JMJD3
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: In mitochondrial-disorder hPSCs, an altered αKG-dependent dioxygenase environment during hepatic specification (low effective nuclear αKG, elevated succinate/2-HG competition, and ROS-linked depletion of labile Fe2+) slows the *kinetic turnover* of H3K27me3 at hepatic lineage enhancers/promoters, particularly at the HNF1A regulatory landscape, thereby sustaining PRC2/Polycomb repression long enough to miss the developmental “opening” window in which FOXA2/HNF4A pioneer activity normally stabilizes a hepatoblast-to-hepatocyte trajectory. This yields low-fidelity hepatocyte programs with impaired nitrogen/aromatic amino-acid handling and metabolite buffering, which can secondarily exacerbate neuronal oxidative stress and metabolic instability.

To overcome the reviewers’ feasibility concerns, we replace the abstract succinate/αKG + redox logic gate with a build-testable, quantitatively benchmarked, dual-control system that converts mitochondrial/metabolic state into a *closed-loop, stage-restricted JMJD3 catalytic permission signal* using only validated molecular parts:

(1) A validated NADH/NAD+ proxy biosensor (nuclear-targeted SoNar) provides a quantitative readout of “ETC-reduced” vs “ETC-permissive” states that correlates with mitochondrial dysfunction and differentiation-stage metabolic transitions. SoNar’s ratiometric signal is used to drive an external, calibrated actuator (optogenetic or chemical inducer) rather than relying on an unvalidated metabolite-binding NLS switch.

(2) A validated redox-responsive nuclear export control (Keap1–Nrf2 ETGE/DLG degron logic or an H2O2-responsive OxyR-based switch) is used only as a *safety interlock* (blocks activation under high nuclear oxidative stress), explicitly acknowledging that nuclear redox may not be monotonic with mitochondrial ROS and therefore is not used as the primary quantitative gate.

(3) Locus selectivity is not asserted via promiscuous IDRs; instead, catalytic JMJD3 is recruited by a minimal, defined-affinity interaction module to endogenous hepatic TF/cofactor hubs (e.g., MED1- or BRD4-associated enhancer assemblies) using short, characterized binding motifs and direct measurements of nuclear partitioning and JMJD3 occupancy at HNF1A.

Mechanistically, this refined system addresses the key limitation: the mitochondrial disorder creates a transient but decisive mismatch between (i) required JMJD3 demethylation kinetics and (ii) differentiation timing. By enforcing *only-in-window* JMJD3 activity with quantitatively bounded leakiness and direct occupancy verification, we test (a) necessity of αKG/Fe2+-limited JMJD3 kinetics for HNF1A unlocking and (b) sufficiency of temporally localized JMJD3 activity to restore the HNF1A regulon even when metabolic defects persist.
Plan: Step 0 — Define quantitative success criteria (go/no-go) upfront
0.1 Gate leakiness: in “non-permissive” conditions (mitochondrial-disorder baseline; early DE stage), <5% of cells show reporter-positive JMJD3 activation; protease/actuator off-state cleavage <2% over 24 h.
0.2 Epigenome safety: global H3K27me3 signal change (genome-wide CUT&Tag spike-in normalized) must be ≤10% relative to matched controls; locus-focused effect required: ≥30% reduction at pre-specified hepatic loci (HNF1A, HNF4A targets, PROX1 enhancers) during the permission window.
0.3 Lineage fidelity: off-lineage transcriptional programs (neuronal/mesodermal/intestinal) must remain ≤5% of total UMIs in scRNA-seq at hepatoblast stage; hepatocyte marker module score must increase ≥1 SD over baseline mitochondrial-disorder differentiation.
0.4 Recruitment specificity: JMJD3 occupancy enrichment at HNF1A regulatory elements ≥3-fold over genomic background and ≥2-fold over non-hepatic super-enhancers (CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN for JMJD3).

Step 1 — Establish causality of the metabolic→JMJD3→Polycomb→HNF1A chain (epistasis-grade)
1.1 Cell panels and differentiation: mitochondrial-disorder iPSCs spanning nuclear-encoded ETC (Complex I/IV) and mtDNA variants; isogenic corrected controls where feasible; healthy donors. Use identical passage windows and synchronized hepatic differentiation (DE → hepatic specification → hepatoblast → HLC). Sample every 24 h days 0–10, with denser sampling (every 12 h) during hepatic specification (e.g., days 3–6 depending on protocol).

1.2 Quantify the putative dioxygenase constraint with direct nuclear relevance:
  - Targeted metabolomics (LC–MS): αKG, succinate, fumarate, 2-HG in whole-cell and nuclear-enriched fractions (validate fraction purity by Lamin A/C enrichment).
  - Labile Fe2+: nuclear and cytosolic labile Fe2+ using FerroOrange (plus orthogonal ICP-MS for total iron if needed).
  - Redox: nuclear H2O2 with nuclear HyPer7; mitochondrial superoxide with MitoSOX; NADH/NAD+ proxy with SoNar targeted to nucleus and cytosol.
  - Bioenergetics: Seahorse OCR/ECAR; lactate release.

1.3 Measure endogenous JMJD3 behavior directly (not only histone marks):
  - JMJD3 occupancy: CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN for JMJD3 at timepoints spanning the permission window; focus on HNF1A enhancers/promoter and hepatic super-enhancers.
  - JMJD3 abundance/turnover: quantitative Western + targeted proteomics; optional FRAP if fluorescently tagged endogenous JMJD3 via knock-in.
  - Demethylase functional readout: H3K27me3 and H3K27ac CUT&Tag with spike-in normalization; ATAC-seq for accessibility.

1.4 Decisive epistasis experiments (necessity and sufficiency):
  A) Necessity of JMJD3 for αKG/Fe2+-mediated rescue
   - Acute metabolic restoration during hepatic specification:
     * αKG restoration: cell-permeable dimethyl-αKG titration (e.g., 0.1–2 mM; determine non-toxic range).
     * Fe2+ restoration: low-dose ferrous ammonium citrate or holotransferrin supplementation with iron chelation controls.
     * ROS buffering: mitoTEMPO or NAC as supportive, not primary, perturbation.
   - In parallel: JMJD3 CRISPRi knockdown (inducible dCas9-KRAB) or JMJD3 KO (if viable) introduced into corrected controls and/or disease lines.
   - Readout criterion: αKG/Fe2+ interventions reduce H3K27me3 at HNF1A and activate HNF1A mRNA/protein only when JMJD3 is present; under JMJD3 knockdown/KO, metabolic restoration fails to clear H3K27me3 and fails to induce HNF1A (formal epistasis).

  B) Sufficiency of JMJD3 activation despite persistent metabolic defects
   - Maintain mitochondrial dysfunction (e.g., low-dose rotenone/antimycin or hypoxia within viability bounds) while enforcing localized JMJD3 activation (Step 2 actuator). If HNF1A unlocking and downstream hepatocyte programs recover, this supports JMJD3 sufficiency for the chromatin barrier even when metabolism remains impaired.

1.5 Rule out alternative explanations quantitatively (parallel tracks)
  - PRC2 activity: EZH2 occupancy (CUT&Tag) and H3K27me3 writer activity markers; test EZH2 inhibition (tazemetostat) as a comparator and epistasis partner.
  - HDAC state: H3K27ac dynamics and HDAC inhibitor comparator (e.g., low-dose TSA) with careful lineage-fidelity monitoring.
  - Pioneer factor access: FOXA2/HNF4A occupancy (CUT&Tag), and ATAC footprinting at HNF1A enhancers.

Step 2 — Build-testable control system replacing the abstract metabolite/redox gate
2.1 Core actuation strategy: externalized, biosensor-informed “metabolic permission” controller
  - Use nuclear-targeted SoNar (validated ratiometric NADH/NAD+ proxy) to *measure* permissive vs non-permissive metabolic states. Because direct intracellular succinate/αKG ratio sensing is not robustly established, SoNar serves as a quantitative proxy for ETC redox imbalance that tracks mitochondrial pathology and differentiation-stage metabolic remodeling.
  - Controller implementation:
    Option A (preferred for quantitative benchmarking): optogenetic split protease reconstitution (blue-light inducible split TEV or split Tobacco Etch Virus protease variants where available). Light dose sets activation amplitude; enables precise response-time and leak measurement.
    Option B (chemical): split protease dimerization using a clinically used heterodimerizer (FKBP–FRB with rapalog) for on-demand activation.
  - Closed-loop concept in practice: during differentiation, SoNar ratio is monitored; activation is applied only when SoNar indicates “permissive” range (threshold set empirically from Step 1 controls). This satisfies the directive: an experimentally demonstrated biosensor coupled to an optogenetic/chemical inducer.

2.2 Quantitative specs to benchmark (per reviewer directive)
  - SoNar dynamic range target: ≥1.5–2.5-fold ratiometric change between permissive vs non-permissive states (to be empirically calibrated per line); response time <2 min for sensor readout; photobleaching-corrected stability over differentiation imaging.
  - Actuator response time: protease reconstitution to cleavage reporter half-time <10–20 min; reversibility (optogenetic) within 30–60 min after light-off.
  - Off-state leak: <2% cleavage/24 h in darkness/no drug.

2.3 MS-J3Switch v2 architecture (buildable parts)
  - Autoinhibited JMJD3 catalytic module: JMJD3 catalytic domain fused to a TEV-cleavable inhibitory linker that sterically blocks the active site (validated via catalytic-dead and cleavage-null controls).
  - Protease cleavage unlock: TEV cleavage releases the inhibitory segment to permit catalysis.
  - Stage restriction: hepatic specification promoter/enhancer (e.g., HHEX or FOXA2 enhancer-driven, validated by reporter kinetics) + degron-based shutdown (dTAG system) to terminate activity after specification.

2.4 Recruitment/selectivity module without promiscuous IDRs
  - Replace multivalent IDRs with minimal, measurable-affinity docking:
    * Use a short, characterized cofactor-binding motif to enrich at hepatic enhancer assemblies (e.g., BRD4-binding peptide or MED1 interaction motif if available) OR a direct TF interaction peptide validated by co-IP (FOXA2 or HNF4A cofactor interface).
    * Include an IDR-free baseline design and a “minimal low-complexity” design (short, defined length) as a controlled comparison, not the default.
  - Measure binding affinity in vitro (MST or SPR) for the motif–target interaction; target Kd in low µM to high nM range to favor enrichment without irreversible sequestration.

2.5 Genomic integration
  - Single-copy safe-harbor integration (AAVS1 or CLYBL) for: (i) MS-J3Switch v2, (ii) cleavage reporter, (iii) SoNar sensor, with matched expression across genotypes.

Step 3 — Demonstrate selectivity, occupancy, and functional rescue (with quantitative thresholds)
3.1 Gate validation
  - Live-cell cleavage reporter (fluorescent TEV substrate) to quantify activation kinetics, leakiness, and cell-to-cell variability.
  - Correlate activation with SoNar ratio in single cells; define permissive threshold based on control differentiation trajectories.

3.2 Direct demonstration of locus engagement
  - CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN for JMJD3 (endogenous and/or tagged MS-J3Switch) during activation vs non-activation.
  - Quantify occupancy at HNF1A regulatory elements and hepatic enhancers; compare to off-target loci and to IDR-free vs IDR-containing variants.
  - Imaging: co-localization/partitioning assays with FOXA2/HNF4A and enhancer markers (MED1/BRD4) using confocal + quantitative co-localization metrics; additionally check partitioning into nucleoli/speckles (fibrillarin/SC35 markers) to rule out promiscuous nuclear body localization.

3.3 Chromatin and transcriptome outcomes
  - CUT&Tag time course: H3K27me3 and H3K27ac with spike-in normalization; acceptance: global change ≤10% with on-target hepatic loci reduction ≥30%.
  - ATAC-seq: accessibility gain at HNF1A enhancers/promoter and hepatic super-enhancers.
  - RNA-seq time series + scRNA-seq at hepatic specification and hepatoblast stages; quantify trajectory correction and HNF1A regulon restoration (SCENIC/CellOracle).

3.4 Functional hepatocyte competence linked to systemic neuro-metabolite buffering
  - Core hepatic functions: albumin secretion, urea cycle flux/ammonia clearance (challenge assay), bile acid transport, glycogen storage.
  - Metabolic stress tests: fatty acid oxidation challenge with OCR/ROS monitoring; CYP inducibility (CYP3A4/2C9).
  - Neuro-metabolite handling outputs: ammonia, lactate, aromatic amino acids, cytokine panels in conditioned media.

3.5 Liver–brain relevance assays (ties to neurological phenotype logic)
  - Conditioned media and/or transwell co-culture with iPSC-derived NPCs/neurons (leveraging established PSC neurological modeling): assess neuronal oxidative stress (HyPer7/ROS), neurite outgrowth, synaptic markers under metabolic stress. Test whether hepatocyte rescue reduces neuronal stress signatures.

Step 4 — Controls and benchmarking (expanded per reviewer)
4.1 Mechanistic controls
  - Catalytic-dead JMJD3 (active-site mutant) with intact cleavage/recruitment.
  - Cleavage-null inhibitory cage (TEV site mutated) to quantify leak.
  - Always-on JMJD3 catalytic domain (no cage) to quantify global H3K27me3 erosion risk.
  - Recruitment-null minimal module.
  - JMJD3 knockdown/KO epistasis across metabolic rescue.

4.2 Comparators
  - Global JMJD3c transient overexpression (Asset 3 comparator) versus MS-J3Switch v2.
  - EZH2 inhibition benchmark (extent of H3K27me3 loss vs lineage fidelity).

4.3 Safety
  - Karyotype, pluripotency marker re-emergence, stress-response transcriptomic signatures, proliferation/apoptosis profiling; long-term stability after dTAG shutdown.

Deliverables
  - A quantitative “permission map” linking SoNar state and external actuation dose to: (i) cleavage %, (ii) JMJD3 occupancy at HNF1A, (iii) H3K27me3 kinetics, (iv) hepatocyte function, with defined go/no-go boundaries for leak and global epigenome disruption.
Feasibility: Addresses critique (1): We remove the unvalidated succinate/αKG NLS sensor. Instead, we use a validated, ratiometric NADH/NAD+ proxy biosensor (SoNar) to *measure* metabolic state and couple it to a calibrated, externally controllable protease actuator (optogenetic or chemical). This is build-testable immediately, with explicit dynamic-range, response-time, and leak targets and a direct cleavage reporter.

Addresses critique (2): Nuclear redox is not assumed to monotonically reflect mitochondrial ROS. Redox sensing is demoted to a safety interlock (blocks activation under high nuclear oxidative stress) rather than a primary quantitative gate, reducing confounding by compartment buffering and differentiation-stage redox shifts.

Addresses critique (3): Locus selectivity is no longer predicated on broadly phase-separating IDRs. We adopt minimal, affinity-characterized docking motifs and explicitly compare IDR-free versus minimal-IDR variants, while directly measuring nuclear partitioning and JMJD3 occupancy (CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN for JMJD3) at HNF1A and control loci. We set quantitative acceptance criteria for global H3K27me3 change to prevent genome-wide erosion.

Addresses critique (4): Step 1 is upgraded from correlational to epistasis-grade causality: αKG/Fe2+ restoration is tested for rescue *only when JMJD3 is present* (JMJD3 CRISPRi/KO), and enforced JMJD3 activation is tested for rescue *despite persistent metabolic defects* (sufficiency). Parallel measurements of PRC2 (EZH2 occupancy), HDAC state, and pioneer factor binding explicitly evaluate alternative mechanisms.

Addresses critique (5): We add genome-wide and locus-specific engagement assays beyond histone marks: JMJD3 CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN, quantitative cleavage/leak reporters, and pre-registered go/no-go thresholds for global H3K27me3 change, off-lineage transcriptional burden, and activation leakiness.

Grounding in assets: Asset 3 supports that JMJD3 catalytic activity can unlock hepatic programs including HNF1A; our approach constrains this activity temporally and spatially to avoid global demethylation. Assets 1–2 motivate the PSC-based modeling framework and the broader mitochondrial/neurological disease linkage, while our added liver–brain co-culture tests provide a mechanistic bridge from hepatic rescue to neuronal stress phenotypes relevant in mitochondrial disorders.
final_critique: The engineering plan is unusually concrete (quantified leak targets, spike-in normalized CUT&Tag thresholds, cleavage reporter kinetics, safe-harbor integration, and explicit control constructs) and directly addresses prior feasibility critiques. However, several high-risk assumptions remain insufficiently deconvolved: (i) SoNar (NADH/NAD+) is an indirect proxy for the relevant nuclear αKG/succinate/2-HG/Fe2+ dioxygenase constraints; closed-loop actuation based on SoNar may misclassify the true JMJD3-permissive window across genotypes and stages, undermining the central ‘permission’ concept. (ii) The proposed locus-selective recruitment via short MED1/BRD4-associated motifs is under-specified and plausibly non-selective at the genome scale (MED1/BRD4 hubs are widespread); without a pre-registered panel of off-target loci and quantitative occupancy selectivity metrics beyond “2-fold over non-hepatic super-enhancers,” the risk of broad chromatin perturbation remains. (iii) The autoinhibitory ‘cage’ for the JMJD3 catalytic domain is described at a schematic level; steric blocking that is tight enough to meet <2%/24h leak yet fully reversible with fast TEV kinetics is non-trivial and will require extensive protein engineering that is not fully scoped. (iv) The mechanistic claim that slowed H3K27me3 turnover at HNF1A causes a missed pioneer-factor stabilization window is plausible but not uniquely supported; alternative drivers (PRC2 recruitment dynamics, chromatin remodelers, DNA methylation, or impaired FOXA2/HNF4A expression/activation) could generate the same phenotype, and the current ‘rule-out’ set does not yet include the strongest competing causal nodes (e.g., DNMT/TET balance, SWI/SNF/BAF occupancy, enhancer RNA output). Overall, the proposal is strong and testable, but its core control variable (SoNar-defined permissivity) and its specificity mechanism (BRD4/MED1 docking) remain the primary logical and technical liabilities.

original_chain: Thermal stability -> BioMOFs -> Encapsulation yield -> Biocatalysis -> Metal nanoparticle -> Nano-silica -> Enzyme immobilization
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A “silica-templated, metal-nanoparticle crosslinked BioMOF nanoreactor” will achieve simultaneously higher encapsulation yield, higher thermal stability, and longer biocatalytic lifetime than conventional MOF-only or silica-only immobilization by replacing post-synthetic silica coating with an orthogonal, inside-out formation route: (i) in-situ enzyme encapsulation within a cystine–cobalt BioMOF is performed in the presence of sacrificial nano-silica that acts as a hard, diffusion-defined porogen; (ii) after MOF crystallization around the enzyme, ultrasmall metal nanoparticles are grown in a spatially confined manner at the BioMOF–silica interface to create multi-point ‘nano-anchors’ (coordination/thiol affinity to cystine motifs + silanol affinity to silica); and (iii) selective removal or partial etching of the nano-silica yields a mechanically stabilized, mesoporous ‘BioMOF aerogel-like’ network in which the enzyme remains confined, while the MNP crosslinks suppress framework slippage/fragmentation and preserve hydration, producing a quantifiable reduction in thermal unfolding and leaching. Mechanistically, the improvement arises from coupling (a) confinement-driven stabilization (reduced conformational entropy of unfolding) within BioMOF cages with (b) interfacial MNP crosslinking that increases framework shear modulus and reduces defect propagation under heat/flow, and (c) silica-templated mesoporosity that shortens diffusion path length without requiring any external silica armor that can block pores or expose the enzyme to sol–gel reagents.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Choose a primary biomedically relevant synthesis reaction and enzyme: nitrile hydratase (NHase) for nicotinamide production (Asset 1 continuity) and a secondary orthogonal enzyme (lipase) to test generality (Asset 2 continuity). Establish baseline kinetics (kcat, Km) and deactivation parameters (T50, t1/2 at 55–80 °C), including solvent tolerance if relevant to process.
