1.2 Prepare monodisperse nano-silica templates (two size regimes): (A) 20–50 nm solid Stöber silica for interparticle mesoporosity templating; (B) 80–150 nm mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNs) with controlled pore sizes (3–10 nm) for diffusion tuning. Functionalize silica minimally with amines (APTES, low density) to modulate local pH/ion adsorption without strong enzyme binding.
1.3 Define quantification pipelines: encapsulation yield by protein mass balance (BCA/Bradford) + fluorescently tagged enzyme tracking; activity assays (NHase product quant by HPLC; lipase pNP-ester assay); and leaching assays (protein in supernatant/effluent + activity-in-supernatant).

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Silica-templated BioMOF formation with in-situ enzyme encapsulation (structural adaptation vs standard MOF synthesis): Disperse nano-silica templates in buffered aqueous solution containing enzyme (NHase) under conditions that preserve activity. Add cystine ligand and cobalt salt to nucleate Co–Cys BioMOF while silica colloids act as a hard space-filler. Control the silica:MOF precursor ratio to drive formation of an intergrown BioMOF network around silica particles, while the enzyme is captured during nucleation/growth. Systematically vary (i) ionic strength and (ii) ligand:metal ratio to maximize encapsulation yield while preserving enzymatic activity.
2.2 Spatially confined metal nanoparticle (MNP) growth as an interfacial crosslinker (methodological adaptation): After BioMOF formation, introduce a low concentration of metal precursor (e.g., Au(III) or Pd(II)) under conditions where ions preferentially localize at cystine-rich MOF surfaces and silica interfaces. Reduce using an enzyme-benign reductant (ascorbate or glucose oxidase–mediated mild reduction) to form 1–3 nm MNPs. Critical design rule: tune precursor dosing to achieve sub-percolation MNP coverage that acts as multi-point ‘rivets’ at the MOF–silica boundary, rather than forming a continuous metallic layer. Include controls: (a) no MNP; (b) MNP grown without silica present; (c) MNP pre-formed then mixed (to demonstrate the necessity of interfacial nucleation).
2.3 Generate the final mesoporous, crosslinked BioMOF architecture via selective silica removal/partial etch: Remove sacrificial silica by mild dissolution (e.g., buffered ammonium fluoride at low concentration) or partial etching to retain a fraction of silica (creating a MOF–silica composite if full removal compromises integrity). This step creates an interconnected mesoporous network and exposes diffusion pathways previously occupied by silica. Optimize extent of removal to balance mass transfer with mechanical robustness.
2.4 Optional biomedical-process adaptation: Incorporate a thin zwitterionic polymer (e.g., sulfobetaine) adsorbed post-etch (no covalent chemistry) to reduce nonspecific fouling in complex bioprocess streams while maintaining pore access.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structure and composition: PXRD to confirm BioMOF crystallinity retention pre/post silica removal; SEM/TEM to visualize templated porosity and MNP localization; N2 sorption (BET, pore size distribution) to quantify mesoporosity introduced by templating; XPS/FTIR to confirm cystine coordination environment and silica removal; ICP-MS to quantify Co and noble metal content plus leaching under operating conditions.
3.2 Encapsulation yield and localization: Determine encapsulation yield via protein mass balance and confirm enzyme location by protease-accessibility mapping (surface-exposed vs protected), confocal imaging (fluorescent enzyme), and fractionation after gentle framework disruption.
3.3 Biocatalysis metrics and mass-transfer diagnostics: Measure specific activity and apparent kinetics (Km, Vmax) across particle sizes and pore architectures. Quantify internal diffusion limitations using effectiveness factor and Weisz–Prater analysis. Compare to: free enzyme, BioMOF-only (no silica, no MNP), silica-immobilized enzyme (nano-silica only), templated BioMOF without MNP, and non-templated BioMOF with MNP.
3.4 Thermal/mechanical stability and reuse: Assess T50 and t1/2 at 55–80 °C; repeated-batch recycle tests (≥20 cycles) and continuous-flow packed-bed operation (pressure drop monitoring). Track activity retention, framework attrition (particle size distribution), and enzyme leaching over time.
3.5 Mechanistic tests (explicitly probing the proposed stabilization mechanism): (a) Nanoindentation/AFM modulus measurements or rheology of packed beds to quantify mechanical reinforcement by interfacial MNP crosslinks; (b) DSC/CD (or nanoDSF) to quantify unfolding temperature shift and unfolding cooperativity; (c) hydration sensitivity tests (controlled water activity) to assess whether the templated porosity + crosslinking preserves a stabilizing hydration shell; (d) defect-propagation assay: thermal cycling + agitation with quantification of crystallinity loss (PXRD peak broadening) comparing MNP-crosslinked vs non-crosslinked.
3.6 Biomedicine-adjacent safety/compatibility window: Evaluate metal leaching in physiological-like buffers (pH 7.4, ionic strength) and cytocompatibility screens of leachates (if the catalyst is intended near biological matrices). Establish operating envelopes where leaching is below predetermined thresholds.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 1 demonstrates that Co–Cys BioMOFs can deliver very high encapsulation yield (~92.7%) and major thermal stability gains for NHase with strong recyclability, validating BioMOF confinement as a stabilizing mechanism. Asset 2 establishes nano-silica and metal nanoparticles as well-studied supports/modifiers that enhance operational and thermal stability in enzyme immobilization. The proposed approach integrates these elements but changes the construction logic: silica is used as a sacrificial porogen/template (not an external shell), and MNPs are used as interfacial crosslinkers to reinforce the MOF network.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): In bioengineering/biomedicine-scale biocatalysis, failure modes include thermal unfolding, framework attrition under flow, and diffusion limitations. Silica templating directly engineers mesoporosity to reduce diffusion barriers, while MNP crosslinking targets mechanical integrity and defect resistance—both are major determinants of long-term reactor performance. The approach avoids exposing enzymes to sol–gel silica growth chemistry (a common denaturation risk) and avoids dense external coatings that can throttle mass transfer.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with BioMOF-only encapsulation, the templated-and-crosslinked architecture is expected to (i) increase operational lifetime by suppressing heat/flow-induced framework fragmentation via MNP ‘rivets’, and (ii) improve apparent activity at high loading by introducing controlled mesoporosity that reduces diffusional limitation. Compared with nano-silica immobilization alone, BioMOF confinement yields higher encapsulation yield and a protective microenvironment, while avoiding random multi-point surface attachment that often reduces activity. Compared with any post-coating strategy, the method eliminates the core risk of pore-blocking or enzyme exposure to coating reagents by generating porosity through sacrificial templating and stabilizing the resulting network through interfacial MNP crosslinking.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely well-reasoned proposal with strong methodological resolution. The silica-templated, in-situ encapsulation strategy is clearly articulated, and the interfacial MNP growth as a mechanical crosslinking mechanism is both original and experimentally testable. Validation plans are unusually rigorous, especially the explicit mechanistic probes (modulus, defect propagation, hydration sensitivity), which elevates the logic score. Minor deductions arise from (i) residual uncertainty around the chemical stability of Co–Cys BioMOFs under even mild fluoride etching conditions, which could complicate interpretation of post-etch effects, and (ii) potential overloading of variables (silica size, MNP identity, partial vs full etch, polymer adsorption) that may dilute statistical power in early phases. Evidence grounding is strong and remains within the bioengineering/biocatalysis domain, though reliance on noble metal nanoparticles for biomedical-adjacent systems introduces translational considerations that are acknowledged but not fully bounded quantitatively. Overall, this is a high-merit proposal with only modest risks related to executional complexity rather than conceptual soundness.

original_chain: Coevolution -> dRAF complex -> posttranslational histone modification -> Drosophila -> Tumor
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a subset of Drosophila Polycomb group proteins—specifically the PRC2 catalytic subunit E(z)—has evolved latent, phosphorylation-sensitive regulatory micro-elements that can be repurposed to quantitatively couple Ras–dRAF signaling strength to intrinsic enzymatic output, rather than to chromatin recruitment. By explicitly identifying RAF-correlated phospho-regulatory motifs using phylogenetically controlled coevolution analyses and orthogonal phosphosite validation, and by inserting these motifs into structurally permissive regulatory loops of the E(z) SET domain under defined constraints, we can engineer a phosphorylation-gated PRC2 whose catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM for H3K27) scales with dRAF activity. This design overcomes key limitations of prior approaches by (i) avoiding nonspecific protein–protein rewiring, (ii) preserving native PRC2 assembly and targeting logic, and (iii) enabling a tunable signal-to-epigenetic transfer function. In follicle stem cell (FSC) tumor contexts driven by aberrant Wnt self-renewal, such a gated enzyme will selectively amplify H3K27me3 deposition at transcriptionally primed Wnt target loci—where PRC2 is already poised—thereby enforcing differentiation and tumor suppression without inducing global Polycomb hypermethylation or catastrophic stem cell loss.
Plan: Step 1: Statistically rigorous identification of RAF-linked phospho-regulatory motifs.
We will perform a phylogenetically corrected coevolution analysis across ≥12 Drosophila species, focusing on E(z), Su(z)12, Esc, and associated PcG regulators alongside the Ras–RAF–MEK–ERK kinase module. Evolutionary rate covariation will be quantified using phylogenetic generalized least squares (PGLS) and independent contrasts to control for shared ancestry. To de-risk spurious correlations, we will include: (i) a negative control set of unrelated serine/threonine kinases (e.g., AMPK, CK2, GSK3) matched for expression level and evolutionary rate; (ii) permutation-based null models (10,000 permutations) to estimate empirical false discovery rates; and (iii) kinase-family covariation controls to ensure specificity to RAF rather than generic MAPKs. Candidate motifs must satisfy all of the following go/no-go criteria: enrichment for RAF consensus sequences (minimal S/T–P motif with +1 proline bias), proximity to predicted intrinsically disordered regions adjacent to SET-I or post-SET loops, conservation within the melanogaster–obscura clade, and significant covariation with dRAF but not with negative-control kinases. Orthogonal validation will be obtained by in vivo phosphoproteomics (TMT-labeled LC–MS/MS) of native PRC2 components under genetically induced dRAF hyperactivation (RasV12 or optogenetic Ras) versus kinase-dead controls, requiring detection of the same phosphosite(s) in endogenous E(z).

Step 2: Structurally constrained phospho-switch engineering of E(z).
Using available PRC2 cryo-EM structures and AlphaFold2/RosettaFold models of Drosophila E(z), we will define three candidate insertion sites within the SET-I and post-SET regulatory regions that (i) are solvent-exposed, (ii) tolerate insertions of 6–12 amino acids without steric clash, and (iii) are predicted to allosterically couple to the conserved Tyr/Phe switch network governing SET-domain catalysis. The phospho-switch will consist of the minimal validated motif flanked by flexible glycine–serine linkers (GSGx2) to minimize structural perturbation. For each site, we will generate phospho-dead (S/T→A), phospho-mimetic (S/T→E), and wild-type variants. In silico stability and assembly predictions (ΔΔG thresholds <2 kcal/mol) will serve as an initial filter. In vitro reconstitution of recombinant PRC2 complexes will then assess: (i) preservation of stoichiometric binding to Su(z)12 and Esc (SEC-MALS and co-immunoprecipitation), and (ii) catalytic parameters (kcat, KM for H3K27) on recombinant nucleosomes ± active dRAF kinase. Only variants showing ≥2-fold phosphorylation-dependent changes in kcat/KM without loss of complex integrity will advance.

Step 3: Decoupling catalytic gating from chromatin recruitment.
To explicitly disentangle enzymatic activation from targeting, we will deploy a chromatin tethering control. Engineered E(z) variants will be recruited to a defined genomic reporter via dCas9 or a minimal DNA-binding module, allowing measurement of H3K27me3 deposition as a pure function of phosphorylation state. Parallel genome-wide CUT&Tag for H3K27me3 and PRC2 occupancy will quantify whether increased catalytic activity produces global spreading or preferential amplification at pre-bound sites. Viability, proliferation, and differentiation markers will be assessed to ensure that observed effects are not due to nonspecific Polycomb toxicity.

Step 4: Quantitative signaling-to-epigenetic input–output mapping in vivo.
In FSC tumor models, we will introduce the engineered E(z) alleles into graded dRAF activity backgrounds using (i) a Ras/dRAF allelic series and (ii) optogenetic ERK activation with tunable light intensity. This will enable construction of a quantitative transfer function linking dRAF activity → E(z) phosphorylation → local H3K27me3 gain at Wnt target loci → transcriptional repression (single-cell RNA-seq) → phenotypic outputs (epithelial extrusion frequency, FSC lineage commitment, and proliferation indices). Critically, these experiments will be staged in both wild-type and Psc/Su(z)2 mutant backgrounds, allowing epistasis analysis to determine whether tumor suppression requires intact PRC1, is enhanced by PRC2 gating, or is independent of PRC1 perturbation.
Feasibility: This refined proposal directly addresses reviewer concerns by embedding explicit de-risking at every stage. The coevolutionary discovery phase now uses phylogenetically rigorous statistics, negative kinase controls, permutation-based FDR estimation, and mandatory orthogonal phosphosite detection, minimizing false positives and ensuring RAF specificity. The engineering strategy is constrained by defined structural boundaries, multiple parallel insertion sites, and quantitative go/no-go criteria based on PRC2 assembly and enzymatic kinetics, reducing the risk of nonspecific destabilization or constitutive dysfunction. By incorporating chromatin tethering and genome-wide profiling, we explicitly separate catalytic gating from recruitment effects, allowing causal attribution of phenotypes to phosphorylation-dependent enzymatic tuning rather than altered targeting. Finally, the use of dRAF activity titration establishes a quantitative, systems-level link between oncogenic signaling and epigenetic output, transforming a qualitative concept into a testable input–output framework. Together, these elements preserve the original conceptual innovation—signal-gated epigenetic writing—while grounding it in rigorous evolutionary logic, structural biophysics, and mechanistic chromatin biology.
final_critique: The proposal is technically ambitious and unusually well-structured with clear go/no-go criteria, orthogonal phosphosite validation, and separation of catalytic gating from recruitment. However, the central mechanistic premise remains under-justified in two key places: (i) the evolutionary logic—ERC/PGLS covariation between dRAF and PRC2 components across ~12 Drosophila species is likely underpowered and vulnerable to shared lineage- or life-history-driven rate shifts, and does not directly localize to specific phospho-microelements (rates are typically gene- or domain-level, not site-level); (ii) the biophysical plausibility—short linear RAF motifs inserted into SET-I/post-SET loops may be phosphorylated yet fail to allosterically couple to catalysis in a scalable, approximately monotonic manner (risking binary disruption or nonspecific electrostatic effects). The RAF specificity criteria are also loose: the minimal S/T-P motif is common to many proline-directed kinases (ERK/CDK/JNK), and in vivo the phosphorylation state may reflect downstream MAPKs rather than dRAF directly. Finally, the tumor-suppression model assumes that selectively increasing PRC2 catalytic efficiency at “poised” Wnt targets will enforce differentiation without global H3K27me3 increases; this selectivity is not yet mechanistically secured, because increased kcat/KM could still enhance spreading wherever PRC2 transiently samples chromatin, and PRC2 targeting/feedback (e.g., EED-like allostery; in flies, analogous mechanisms) could amplify beyond intended loci.

original_chain: calypso -> dRAF complex -> Drosophila melanogaster -> Lymph gland -> Toll/NF-κB pathway -> Lamellocyte -> Serpent -> Hematopoiesis
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Emergency hematopoiesis in the Drosophila lymph gland is governed by a **looping-threshold gate** in which Toll/NF-κB-driven ROS signaling can only execute a Serpent-linked lamellocyte program when specific NF-κB-responsive enhancers form sufficiently **stable enhancer–promoter (E–P) proximity episodes** (dwell) to support productive transcriptional bursting at lamellocyte fate genes. We posit that the calypso–dRAF Polycomb-associated module does not primarily set fate by static histone-mark abundance, but by tuning the **conversion efficiency from physical proximity to transcription** (transcription-per-contact) and/or the **stability distribution** (dwell-time tail) of E–P proximity episodes, thereby shifting the **EC50 of NF-κB activity** required to trigger lamellocyte commitment while preserving maximal transcriptional capacity when signaling is saturating.

This revised approach directly addresses reviewer concerns by explicitly and orthogonally measuring and manipulating three separable state variables at the same loci and in the same cells: (A) **contact frequency** (ensemble conformation capture), (B) **contact dwell/proximity dynamics** (dual-color live/quasi-live locus tracking), and (C) **per-contact transcriptional productivity** (nascent transcription reporters/smFISH). The Synthetic Chromatin Bridge (SCB) is retained, but is operationalized as a tool to **clamp proximity** (raise A and extend B) while we quantify whether calypso/dRAF changes (i) B at fixed A (stability modulation) or (ii) C at fixed A and B (productivity modulation). Falsifiable outcomes are predefined to discriminate true looping-threshold gating from non-physiologic forced activation: SCB must (1) shift EC50 under matched NF-κB nuclear entry, (2) require intact enhancer NF-κB motifs and promoter Serpent sites, and (3) preserve maximal output under saturating signaling rather than creating ectopic maximal activation.
Plan: SCOPE REDUCTION AND LOCUS SELECTION (Go/No-Go at end of Phase 0)

Phase 0 — Choose 1–2 high-confidence enhancer–promoter pairs (4–6 weeks)
1) Candidate compilation (in silico + targeted validation):
   - Start with lamellocyte markers and effectors implicated in emergency hematopoiesis and lamellocyte differentiation (e.g., msn, Atilla/L1, eater) and intersect with published Toll/NF-κB-responsive gene sets in lymph gland/hemocytes (Assets 2–3) and known lamellocyte specification circuitry (Asset 4).
   - Select 1–2 loci meeting all criteria:
     i) inducible by wasp parasitism and benzene exposure (Assets 2–3),
     ii) shows Serpent dependence (promoter occupancy motif presence + genetic dependence by RNAi/heterozygosity),
     iii) contains a discrete enhancer with predicted NF-κB motifs (Dif/Dorsal binding motifs) and accessible chromatin upon challenge.
2) Minimal empirical screening:
   - Dissect lymph glands from unchallenged vs challenged larvae; perform targeted RT-qPCR for ~8 candidate genes plus NF-κB targets.
   - Perform low-cost targeted ATAC-qPCR at candidate enhancers to confirm challenge-induced accessibility.
Go/No-Go criteria Phase 0:
   - Proceed only if ≥1 locus shows (i) ≥3× induction in challenged glands and (ii) enhancer ATAC accessibility increase (≥2×) with interpretable cell-type localization by reporter/marker staining.

PHASE 1 — Build measurement stack to decouple A/B/C at the same locus

Phase 1A: Measure A (ensemble contact frequency) with explicit benchmarks
1) Targeted Capture-C (primary) + optional ultra-low-input Micro-C (secondary/risk-mitigated):
   - Primary conformation assay: **NG Capture-C** (or equivalent targeted 3C capture) for the chosen 1–2 loci.
   - Tissue input benchmark per replicate:
     - 40–60 lymph glands/replicate (estimated ~1–3×10^5 nuclei total depending on stage and dissection yield).
     - 3 biological replicates per condition (unchallenged, wasp, benzene; plus SCB/anti-bridge as below).
   - Restriction strategy and capture design:
     - Use DpnII/MboI 4-cutter for high fragment density.
     - Design 2–3 viewpoints per locus (promoter + enhancer + a nearby constitutive promoter control) and tiled capture oligos across the 200–500 kb surrounding region to quantify local compaction changes.
   - Resolution/success criteria:
     - Success = reproducible promoter–enhancer contact enrichment peak at <5 kb binning around the known enhancer (Pearson r ≥ 0.8 between replicates for interaction profiles across the 200–500 kb window).
2) Micro-C (optional only after Capture-C success):
   - Implement ultra-low-input Micro-C only if Capture-C supports the locus interaction and if nuclei yield consistently exceeds benchmark.
   - Micro-C success criterion: detectable nucleosome-resolution periodicity and stable contact decay curves across replicates.

Phase 1B: Measure B (proximity dwell distributions) in PSC vs progenitors
1) Dual-color locus tagging (two options; choose based on feasibility):
   Option 1 (preferred, quasi-live): **dCas9 imaging**
   - Express two orthogonal dCas9/dCas12a systems with distinct fluorescent tags:
     - Enhancer-bound: dCas12a–HaloTag (JF549 ligand) + 6–10 crRNAs tiled across enhancer.
     - Promoter-bound: dCas9–SNAP-tag (JF646 ligand) + 6–10 sgRNAs tiled across promoter.
   - Cell-type specificity:
     - PSC: col-GAL4; progenitors: dome-GAL4.
   - Imaging modality:
     - Spinning-disk confocal or lattice light-sheet (if available) on ex vivo cultured lymph glands (short-term culture 2–6 h) to preserve physiology.
   - Quantification:
     - Define proximity event as enhancer–promoter distance <250 nm for ≥2 consecutive frames.
     - Extract dwell-time distributions (Kaplan–Meier survival curves), event frequency per minute, and fraction time-in-proximity.
2) Controls:
   - Non-targeting guides; single-locus labeling only; swapped fluor pairs.
Go/No-Go criteria Phase 1B:
   - Achieve ≥50 trackable nuclei/condition with two resolvable puncta and stable labeling; proximity events detectable above non-targeting background.

Phase 1C: Measure C (per-contact transcriptional productivity) at the target promoter
1) Nascent transcription quantification (two-tier):
   Tier 1 (robust): **intron smFISH**
   - Design intronic probe sets for the target gene(s) to quantify active transcription sites per nucleus and intensity (burst size proxy).
   - Perform in the same gland preparations used for locus imaging (fixed after imaging) or in matched cohorts.
   Tier 2 (higher precision, if feasible): **MS2/PP7 reporter knock-in**
   - CRISPR knock-in of MS2 or PP7 stem loops into 5’ UTR/intron of target gene to report transcription bursts in live glands.
2) Conditional analysis “productivity per proximity”:
   - For each nucleus: pair proximity state metrics (B) with transcription site intensity/count (C).
   - Primary metric: P(active transcription | proximity) and burst intensity conditional on proximity vs non-proximity.

PHASE 2 — Causal perturbation with SCB/anti-bridge while preserving enhancer logic

Phase 2A: Refined SCB architecture with explicit parameters and physiological safeguards
1) DNA targeting layer:
   - Use dCas12a for enhancer and dCas9 for promoter (minimize guide crosstalk; distinct scaffolds).
2) Inducible bridging layer:
   - Primary: rapalog-inducible FRB/FKBP dimerization.
   - Secondary (orthogonal validation): temperature-switch coiled-coil zipper pair.
3) Mechanical linker series (explicit):
   - Insert elastin-like polypeptide (ELP) linkers of 3 defined contour lengths (approx. 15 nm, 40 nm, 80 nm equivalents; implemented as 60 aa, 160 aa, 320 aa ELPs) between dCas and docking domain.
   - Goal: vary effective capture radius and (hypothesized) dwell stabilization without changing binding site occupancy.
4) Anti-bridge blockade:
   - Two dCas constructs recruited to the intervening region that multimerize (e.g., engineered oligomerization domain) to sterically hinder close approach.
5) Physiologic-topology safeguards (to address “forced activation” concern):
   - Use minimal dCas occupancy: titrate guide number to lowest that yields reliable targeting (typically 3–5 guides per site).
   - Include “bridge-dead” dimerization mutants and “single-anchor only” constructs.
   - Verify no global chromatin compaction: ATAC-seq (targeted) at ±50 kb around locus; control loci unaffected.

Phase 2B: Matched signaling regimes to isolate looping gate from pathway dose
1) NF-κB activity matching:
   - Use an NF-κB nuclear translocation reporter (Dif/Dorsal localization or NF-κB response reporter) to match pathway activation across genotypes/conditions.
   - For each stress paradigm, titrate exposure to yield a mid-range NF-κB activation (~EC30–EC50) to maximize sensitivity to gate shifts.
2) Two paradigms retained but controlled:
   - Wasp parasitism and benzene exposure performed under matched NF-κB reporter readouts; if matching fails, prioritize one paradigm (wasp) for mechanistic claims and use the other only for limited generalization.

Phase 2C: Pre-registered falsifiable tests distinguishing gating vs forced activation
1) Threshold shift test (core claim):
   - Under graded NF-κB activation (dose series): quantify lamellocyte fraction and target gene nascent transcription.
   - Prediction for looping-threshold gate: SCB increases proximity dwell (B) and/or frequency (A), producing a left-shift in EC50 for transcription and lamellocyte commitment while preserving maximal response at saturating NF-κB.
   - Forced-activation signature to reject: SCB produces near-maximal transcription even at minimal NF-κB activity and/or activates when enhancer NF-κB motifs are mutated.
2) Enhancer logic requirement:
   - Mutate NF-κB motifs in the enhancer (CRISPR base editing) and Serpent-binding sites in the promoter (or partial Serpent knockdown) and test SCB.
   - Gate model prediction: SCB cannot rescue motif-dead enhancer; SCB effect is reduced/abolished with Serpent site disruption.

PHASE 3 — Operationalize calypso/dRAF mechanisms with orthogonal assays

Phase 3A: Define separable mechanistic predictions
We explicitly discriminate:
(A) Contact probability changes: calypso/dRAF perturbation changes Capture-C interaction frequency and/or locus proximity event rate.
(B) Contact stability changes: calypso/dRAF perturbation changes dwell-time distribution (B) at similar contact frequency.
(C) Transcription-per-contact changes: at clamped proximity (SCB induced to saturate B), calypso/dRAF perturbation changes P(transcription|proximity) and burst intensity (C) without altering B.
(D) Enhancer competence changes: calypso/dRAF perturbation alters enhancer accessibility (ATAC), NF-κB occupancy (CUT&Tag for Dif/Dorsal), or H3K27ac at enhancer independent of proximity.

Phase 3B: Experiments
1) Genetic perturbations:
   - Tissue-specific RNAi/heterozygous loss of calypso and selected dRAF subunits (prioritized based on viability and expression in lymph gland).
2) Readouts under two proximity regimes:
   - Native regime (no SCB): measure A (Capture-C), B (imaging), C (intron smFISH/MS2).
   - Clamped regime (SCB on, fixed inducer dose and linker length that yields high proximity): measure B and C; interpret changes primarily as productivity (C) if B is unchanged.
3) Molecular correlates (competence/productivity):
   - CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN in low-input format for:
     - NF-κB (Dif/Dorsal) at enhancer,
     - Serpent at promoter,
     - H3K27ac (enhancer activation), H3K27me3 (Polycomb), and H2Aub (PRC1 proxy) if feasible.

PHASE 4 — Outcome readouts and integration
1) Fate outcomes:
   - Lamellocytes: Atilla staining, msn-lacZ.
   - Lymph gland dispersal and larval survival.
2) Integrated model fitting (explicit):
   - Fit a hierarchical model where:
     - NF-κB activity (reporter) is input S,
     - proximity features (frequency and dwell) are P,
     - transcription burst metrics are T,
     - fate probability is F.
   - Test whether SCB primarily alters S→P, P→T, or S→T mappings; test whether calypso/dRAF alters P→T at fixed P (productivity tuning).

DECISION POINTS / RISK MANAGEMENT
- If Phase 1B imaging cannot robustly extract dwell distributions, proceed with fixed-cell distance mapping (Oligopaint DNA FISH for enhancer/promoter distance distributions) + intron smFISH for conditional transcription, acknowledging reduced temporal resolution.
- If MS2/PP7 knock-in is too slow/risky, intron smFISH remains the primary productivity readout.
- If benzene paradigm cannot be matched to wasp in NF-κB activity without confounding toxicity, restrict full mechanistic claims to wasp and use benzene only as a qualitative replication at one matched dose point.
Feasibility: 1) Directly addressing the reviewer’s A/B/C decoupling requirement
- Contact frequency (A): Targeted Capture-C provides reproducible ensemble contact probability at predefined loci with explicit replicate and input benchmarks. This is lower-risk than whole-genome Micro-C in tiny tissue and is sufficient for the 1–2 locus scope.
- Contact dwell/proximity dynamics (B): Dual-color locus tracking (dCas-based imaging) yields proximity event rates and dwell-time distributions—information not accessible from Capture-C/Micro-C. If live imaging is limiting, fixed-cell enhancer/promoter distance distributions (DNA FISH/Oligopaints) provide an interpretable fallback.
- Per-contact productivity (C): Intron smFISH (robust, low input) and/or MS2/PP7 nascent reporters quantify transcription bursting. Conditioning transcription on proximity state directly tests “transcription-per-contact.”

2) Benchmarked feasibility and explicit success criteria
- Tissue input: 40–60 lymph glands/replicate for Capture-C with 3 biological replicates is realistic for Drosophila larval dissections and provides enough material for targeted assays. Success is defined by replicate reproducibility (r ≥ 0.8) and locus-specific interaction peaks.
- Imaging: Success requires ≥50 trackable nuclei/condition with resolvable dual puncta and measurable proximity events above background; otherwise switch to fixed-cell distance mapping.
- Go/No-Go points are embedded after Phase 0 (locus induction/accessibility) and Phase 1B (dwell measurement capability).

3) Minimizing interpretation confounds from non-physiologic topology
- The proposal pre-registers rejection criteria for “forced activation,” including dependence on intact enhancer NF-κB motifs and promoter Serpent sites and preservation of maximal response at saturating NF-κB.
- SCB dosage is titrated (guide number, inducer concentration) and includes bridge-dead and single-anchor controls to separate proximity from steric/compaction artifacts.
- Local chromatin state is monitored (targeted ATAC; CUT&Tag for enhancer/promoter competence marks) to detect and account for unintended compaction or ectopic activation.

4) Operationalizing calypso/dRAF mechanism with discriminating predictions
- By using SCB to clamp proximity (fixing A/B), we can test whether calypso/dRAF alters transcription-per-contact (C) versus contact stability (B) versus enhancer competence (ATAC/CUT&Tag). This directly addresses the reviewer’s request for crisp separation among (a) altered contact probability, (b) altered transcription per contact, and (c) altered enhancer competence.

5) Controlling variance from two stress paradigms
- The plan explicitly matches NF-κB activity across wasp and benzene using a reporter-based calibration and restricts mechanistic claims to the paradigm(s) where matching is achieved. Locus scope is reduced to 1–2 pairs to preserve power and interpretability.

6) Strong biological grounding
- Assets 2–3 support that ROS activates Toll/NF-κB in the PSC and drives emergency hematopoiesis/lamellocyte differentiation under wasp and benzene stress.
- Asset 4 grounds lamellocyte specification in a defined transcriptional program and niche signaling logic, making conditional (proximity → burst → fate) tests mechanistically meaningful.
- Asset 1 supports that Polycomb-associated modules (including components tied to calypso/dRAF networks) evolve under interaction constraints, motivating a role in tuning regulatory coupling rather than only static marks—here made testable via productivity-versus-contact partitioning.
final_critique: This is a materially stronger, more falsifiable mechanistic proposal than a typical “looping causes expression” narrative: it operationalizes a looping-threshold gate into separable observables (A/B/C) and uses SCB as an intervention with defined rejection criteria (motif dependence, EC50 shift under matched NF-κB, no ectopic max at saturation). Engineering detail is generally high (replicate numbers, input benchmarks, viewpoint design, imaging definitions, linker series), and the logic connecting NF-κB dose → proximity dynamics → transcriptional bursting → lamellocyte fate is coherent. The main weaknesses are (i) feasibility/interpretability risk in the B–C coupling at single-cell resolution: ex vivo gland culture plus dCas imaging plus subsequent smFISH “same preparation” is nontrivial, and the proposal does not fully specify registration/segmentation strategy to align proximity state with nascent transcription per nucleus without bias; (ii) SCB is still vulnerable to confounds beyond proximity (steric hindrance, local chromatin remodeling by multivalent dCas occupancy, altered enhancer scanning kinetics), and the current safeguards (ATAC ±50 kb, guide titration) may not detect subtle promoter loading artifacts; (iii) calypso/dRAF is treated as a functional unit, but the biochemical link to Polycomb outputs is underspecified—without a sharper molecular prediction (e.g., which chromatin feature mediates “transcription-per-contact”), Phase 3 could remain correlational even with SCB clamping; (iv) the ‘EC50 shift’ claim hinges on robust NF-κB activity matching in the relevant cells (PSC vs progenitors), yet the plan does not specify how nuclear-entry readouts will be quantified cell-type specifically and integrated with the locus-level A/B/C measurements. Overall, the proposal is well-grounded in the target concept chain and has strong methodological ambition, but several critical implementation and interpretability details remain underdefined relative to the central promise of single-cell per-contact productivity inference.

original_chain: Polycomb group protein -> Chromatin structure -> Polycomb repressive complex 1 -> transcriptional repression -> RING1
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Engineered, allosterically switchable PRC1 (“Opto-PRC1”) that couples a light-gated conformational clamp to RING1A/B E3 ligase positioning will enable causally separable control of (i) PRC1 chromatin-compaction/remodeling antagonism and (ii) H2AK119 ubiquitination, thereby producing tunable and reversible transcriptional repression with defined chromatin-structural trajectories. Mechanistically, forcing a controllable geometric proximity between RING1 (E2~Ub-loaded active site) and the H2A N-terminus on nucleosomes while independently modulating CBX/PHC-mediated chromatin bridging will allow us to disentangle and optimize two repression modes: steric inhibition of SWI/SNF-type remodeling (as suggested by PRC1/PCC effects on nucleosome organization) and enzymatic deposition of H2AK119ub that stabilizes Polycomb occupancy and propagates silencing. The methodological adaptation is a structural re-engineering of PRC1 subunit architecture: (a) insertion of an optogenetic dimerization module (iLID/SspB or CRY2/CIBN) between RING1 and a nucleosome-anchoring reader (CBX chromodomain or a minimal H3K27me3-binding module) to light-control RING1 residence time and orientation on chromatin; and (b) incorporation of a mechanically stiff, length-tunable helical linker (“molecular ruler”) plus a leucine-zipper clamp to bias the RING1–E2~Ub trajectory toward H2A Lys119, increasing catalytic efficiency only when the clamp is engaged. This guarantees superiority over constitutive recruitment because repression will be achieved at lower PRC1 abundance with fewer off-target chromatin interactions, and because the two mechanisms (compaction vs ubiquitination) can be orthogonally gated to determine which is necessary/sufficient for stable repression in mammalian cells.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a human cell model with Polycomb-dependent lineage programs (e.g., hESCs or AML cells with high PcG dependence) and generate a safe-harbor landing pad (AAVS1) for single-copy integration of Opto-PRC1 components under doxycycline control.
1.2 Establish dual reporters: (i) a PRC2-primed, H3K27me3-marked synthetic Polycomb response element upstream of a destabilized fluorescent gene; (ii) an endogenous locus readout (e.g., HOX cluster gene) tagged with MS2/PP7 nascent RNA imaging for real-time transcription.
1.3 Create RING1A/B-null or degron lines (auxin-inducible degron) to remove endogenous RING1 activity, ensuring repression arises from engineered complexes.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Build modular Opto-PRC1 variants:
- Variant A (Orientation-gated ubiquitination): RING1B fused to SspB; CBX7 (or CBX4) fused to iLID; between RING1B and SspB insert a rigid ER/K helical linker of defined length (e.g., 10, 20, 30 nm) and a conditional leucine-zipper clamp that engages only upon iLID/SspB binding, constraining the active-site approach to H2A.
- Variant B (Compaction-gated remodeling antagonism): PHC1/PHC2 SAM domain polymerization module fused to CRY2 for light-inducible oligomerization to enhance chromatin bridging independent of RING1 catalytic gating.
- Variant C (Orthogonal control): Combine A and B with distinct wavelengths (e.g., blue-light iLID; near-IR bacterial phytochrome BphP1/QPAS1) to independently toggle ubiquitination vs compaction.
2.2 Quantitatively map structure–function:
- Measure H2AK119ub kinetics at targeted loci using CUT&Tag time courses (minutes to hours) after light pulses; use catalytically dead RING1B (Cys-to-Ala in RING) as a control for compaction-only effects.
- Assay chromatin structure changes using Micro-C (nucleosome-level contacts), ATAC-seq (accessibility), and live-cell single-locus compaction via CRISPR-dCas9 fluorescent tagging.
- Challenge remodeling directly: recruit a defined SWI/SNF ATPase module (e.g., BRG1 tethered via dCas9) and quantify whether Opto-PRC1 compaction mode blocks remodeling without requiring H2AK119ub (inspired by PCC/PSC inhibition of hSWI/SNF).
2.3 Engineer catalytic efficiency and specificity:
- Perform focused mutagenesis on RING1B–BMI1/PCGF interface residues that tune E2 (UBCH5/UBCH6) engagement and test variants under the same light-gated geometry to identify combinations that maximize on-target H2AK119ub while minimizing global ubiquitination.
- Compare CBX paralogs (CBX2/4/6/7/8) as anchoring readers (reflecting distinct PRC1 compositions) to test how reader choice alters repression potency and off-target binding.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Causality decomposition: Use factorial designs (ubiquitination ON/OFF; compaction ON/OFF) and quantify transcriptional repression onset time, depth, and memory (persistence after light-off), separating immediate steric remodeling inhibition from longer-term epigenetic stabilization.
3.2 Proteomic validation: Use proximity labeling (TurboID fused to engineered subunits) during light ON vs OFF to confirm assembly states and to identify unintended interactors (e.g., 14-3-3 effects on CBX4-like behavior).
3.3 Off-target and safety profiling: Genome-wide CUT&Tag for H2AK119ub and CBX occupancy plus RNA-seq to quantify collateral repression; assess DNA damage and replication stress markers to ensure chromatin perturbation does not induce toxicity.
3.4 Translational test: In a cancer-relevant model (e.g., Polycomb-addicted lymphoma), evaluate whether transient Opto-PRC1-mediated silencing of a driver enhancer network induces differentiation/apoptosis more selectively than global PRC1 inhibition, using xenograft-compatible red-shifted gating modules for in vivo feasibility.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: PRC1 components (including RING1/dRING1) can directly inhibit chromatin remodeling and alter nucleosome configurations, and mammalian PRC1 exists as CBX-mutually exclusive assemblies with distinct repression potencies. RING1’s E3 ligase activity (H2AK119ub) and CBX chromodomain-mediated recognition of H3K27me3 provide natural, modular handles for engineered recruitment and mechanistic separation.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Optogenetic proximity control and rigid-linker “molecular ruler” strategies are established in protein engineering for controlling enzyme–substrate geometry; adapting them to PRC1 directly addresses a key limitation in epigenetic therapy/biology—current perturbations (knockouts or inhibitors) are global, slow, and confound enzymatic and structural roles. The proposed architecture converts PRC1 from a constitutive, multi-factorial regulator into a tunable bioengineered actuator suitable for causal biomedicine.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with standard CRISPRi (which recruits generic repressors) or pharmacologic PRC1 inhibition (global loss of function), Opto-PRC1 offers (i) orthogonal control of compaction vs ubiquitination, (ii) reversible, time-resolved perturbations to infer mechanism, (iii) enhanced on-target catalytic efficiency via enforced geometry reducing required expression levels, and (iv) the ability to select CBX paralog-specific complexes to match disease context and minimize off-target repression.
final_critique: This is an unusually sophisticated and well-integrated bioengineering proposal that demonstrates deep command of PRC1 biology, chromatin mechanics, and protein-engineering principles. The engineering resolution is high: optogenetic modules, ER/K rigid linkers, factorial gating of compaction versus ubiquitination, and locus-resolved readouts are all specified with actionable detail. Logical consistency is strong—the hypothesis that geometric control of RING1 positioning can decouple enzymatic ubiquitination from steric remodeling inhibition is mechanistically defensible and well motivated by prior PRC1/PCC literature. Minor deductions arise from cumulative complexity: the simultaneous integration of multiple optogenetic systems, degrons, rigid-linker tuning, and chromatin assays increases the risk that failure modes (misfolding, impaired PRC1 assembly, altered nuclear dynamics) could confound interpretation, and contingency plans are not explicitly articulated. Evidence grounding is excellent, remaining tightly anchored to Polycomb biology and chromatin structure, with no conceptual drift. Rationale quality is very high, as the proposal directly targets a central bottleneck in the field—causal separation of PRC1’s structural versus enzymatic repression modes—via a genuinely novel structural re-engineering rather than incremental application of CRISPRi-like tools.

original_chain: Genome-wide association study -> HLA-C -> Cutaneous psoriasis -> Psoriatic arthritis -> Cutaneous psoriasis -> HLA gene -> HLA-DQA1 amino acid position 53
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Amino-acid variation at HLA-DQA1 position 53 (DQα53) changes the susceptibility of HLA-DQ to HLA-DM–mediated peptide editing under endosomal-like conditions, thereby re-shaping the *stability distribution* (surface half-life and kinetic persistence) of naturally selected DQ peptide–MHC (pMHCII) complexes on antigen-presenting cells (APCs). This edited kinetic landscape—rather than any single dominant peptide identity—biases CD4+ T-cell signaling toward a tissue-invasive inflammatory helper program (e.g., IL-17A/GM-CSF/IFN-γ with defined signaling dwell-time features). Those CD4-derived cytokines then *mechanistically* amplify HLA-C*06:02–restricted cytotoxicity by (i) upregulating HLA-C surface abundance and (ii) remodeling antigen-processing and peptide supply pathways (immunoproteasome/TAP/ERAP), increasing the density and durability of stimulatory HLA-C–peptide complexes on target cells. The refined approach overcomes prior assay-context limitations by explicitly reconstituting peptide exchange/editing with HLA-DM (±HLA-DO) at endosomal pH and by validating DQα53 effects in isogenic, full-length membrane HLA-DQ APCs with direct measurement of surface pMHC abundance/half-life. It further eliminates peptide-choice artifacts by first defining the natural DQ ligandome via DQ immunopeptidomics from DQA1-53–stratified APCs and/or psoriatic tissue and then testing whether kinetic-state metrics predict T-cell outputs *after controlling for peptide identity*. Finally, it replaces the indirect HLA-C “amplifier” concept with a necessity/sufficiency pathway test that identifies the precise CD4-derived cytokines responsible for HLA-C modulation and demonstrates that blocking them abrogates enhanced HLA-C*06:02–restricted CD8 activation on matched antigenic targets, integrating the GWAS architecture of HLA-DQA1 and HLA-C in the same mechanistic chain.
Plan: Tier 0 — Cohort integration and genotype anchoring (ties HLA-DQA1-53 to HLA-C risk architecture)
0.1 Recruit/biobank PsC-only and PsA subjects; HLA type at high resolution: HLA-DQA1 (resolve residue at position 53), HLA-DQB1 pairing, and HLA-C*06:02 status (and key MHC covariates if needed). Stratify into at minimum four genotype groups: (A) DQα53-risk / C*06:02+, (B) DQα53-protective / C*06:02+, (C) DQα53-risk / C*06:02−, (D) DQα53-protective / C*06:02−; match age/sex/therapy.
0.2 Define primary cellular sources: monocyte-derived DCs (moDCs) and B cells (high MHCII), plus keratinocytes and synovial fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) as HLA-C–bearing targets.

Tier 1 — Physiology-anchored peptide editing and kinetic-state definition (addresses DM/DO critique)
1.1 Produce recombinant soluble HLA-DQ heterodimers differing only at DQA1 residue 53 *and matched DQB1*: express in mammalian cells (e.g., HEK293) with controlled N-glycan state (include glycosidase trimming to homogeneous glycoforms if needed); confirm proper folding by conformational anti-DQ mAbs and size-exclusion profiles.
1.2 Reconstitute peptide exchange/editing under endosomal-like conditions:
  • Buffer: pH 5.0–5.5 (acetate/citrate), 150 mM NaCl, 1–2 mM reducing agent as appropriate, 0.01–0.05% mild detergent if required for stability.
  • Add recombinant HLA-DM at defined molar ratios (e.g., DM:DQ = 0.2, 1, 5) to map DM-susceptibility curves.
  • Add HLA-DO as an inhibitory modulator in select conditions (DO:DM ratio series) to test whether DQα53 effects persist across DM regulation states.
  • Include time-resolved exchange using either (a) fluorescent peptide tracers (FP/anisotropy) with DM present, or (b) BLI/SPR with DM in solution and DQ immobilized via oriented capture (anti-tag) to quantify effective kon/koff under editing conditions.
1.3 Replace sole reliance on photocleavable conditional ligands with a dual system:
  • Conditional ligand for synchronization (photocleavable), *plus* DM-catalyzed peptide exchange using competitive peptide pools that mimic endosomal peptide mixtures.
  • Quantify: (i) DM-catalyzed peptide release rate, (ii) DM-catalyzed peptide loading rate, (iii) resulting pMHC half-life at pH 7.4 (post-endosomal “surface stabilization” phase), explicitly separating endosomal editing from surface persistence.
1.4 Define “kinetic-state metrics” as a vector per peptide and genotype: DM-susceptibility (editing rate), exchangeability index (DM-dependent vs DM-independent), and surface half-life (t1/2 at neutral pH). These become the mechanistic intermediates used downstream.

Tier 2 — Isogenic membrane HLA-DQ validation in APCs with direct pMHC abundance/half-life (mandatory directive)
2.1 Generate isogenic APC lines (e.g., HLA class II–positive B-cell line or moDC-like line) via CRISPR knock-in editing of endogenous DQA1 to encode the alternative residue at position 53, maintaining identical genomic background and DQB1 pairing. Validate:
  • Genomic edit (amplicon sequencing),
  • Total HLA-DQ expression (flow cytometry),
  • DM/DO expression levels (qPCR/Western/flow) to ensure comparability.
2.2 Directly measure surface pMHCII abundance and half-life:
  • Use pan–HLA-DQ conformational antibodies to quantify total DQ.
  • Use peptide-receptive vs peptide-loaded DQ probes (where available) and/or pulse-chase with labeled peptides followed by acid wash/temperature shift assays.
  • Determine decay of specific pMHC on the surface using time-course staining after peptide pulse and endosomal loading, fitting exponential decay to estimate t1/2 for multiple ligands.
2.3 Quantify antigen presentation functionally with matched CD4 TCR reporters (primary clones or engineered Jurkat NFAT reporters) to infer effective pMHC density thresholds and dwell-time regimes on real APC membranes.

Tier 3 — Unbiased DQ immunopeptidomics to constrain natural ligand sets (eliminates peptide-choice artifacts)
3.1 Perform HLA-DQ immunoprecipitation from:
  • (i) isogenic APCs (DQα53-risk vs protective) under baseline and psoriatic cytokine milieu (e.g., IFN-γ/TNF-α/IL-17A stimulation), and
  • (ii) patient-derived APCs and/or lesional skin cell suspensions where feasible, stratified by DQA1-53 genotype.
3.2 LC–MS/MS with stringent controls:
  • Use allele-aware database searching, replicate IPs, and contaminant filtering; quantify peptide abundance (label-free quantification) and length/motif distributions.
3.3 Define a “natural ligand panel”:
  • Select (a) shared peptides presented in both genotypes, and (b) genotype-skewed peptides that differ in abundance.
  • Prioritize peptides derived from keratinocyte/joint-associated proteins and inflammatory pathways.

Tier 4 — Controlled kinetic-to-function mapping while explicitly controlling peptide identity
4.1 For each peptide in the natural ligand panel, measure Tier-1 kinetic-state metrics (DM-susceptibility + surface t1/2) on both DQα53 variants.
4.2 Present matched peptide–DQ complexes to CD4 T cells in two contexts:
  • (i) immobilized defined-density pMHC on microfluidic synapse devices (standardized pMHC density gradients) to isolate dwell-time effects,
  • (ii) isogenic APC presentation (Tier-2) to capture physiological co-stimulation and membrane dynamics.
4.3 Readouts (continuous variables): TCR dwell time (single-molecule or effective dwell via kinetic proofreading reporters where possible), Ca2+ flux kinetics, NFAT/NF-κB nuclear translocation timing, and cytokine outputs (IL-17A, GM-CSF, IFN-γ, IL-21) at single-cell level (e.g., intracellular cytokine staining + scRNA/protein panels).
4.4 Statistical framework to enforce peptide-identity control:
  • Mixed-effects models where peptide identity is a random effect and DQα53 genotype and kinetic-state metrics are fixed effects.
  • Test whether kinetic metrics mediate genotype → T-cell phenotype relationships (formal mediation analysis), quantifying variance explained beyond peptide identity.

Tier 5 — Mechanistically specific HLA-C amplification pathway (necessity/sufficiency; replaces indirect DC conditioning)
5.1 Identify candidate CD4-derived mediators:
  • From Tier-4 supernatants and single-cell data, nominate cytokines most associated with genotype-linked kinetic states (e.g., IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-17A, GM-CSF).
5.2 Test necessity/sufficiency for HLA-C modulation:
  • Treat keratinocytes and synovial FLS (and/or dendritic cells, depending on the intended target) with defined cytokine combinations at physiologic doses; quantify:
    – HLA-C surface abundance (flow),
    – antigen-processing gene programs (TAP1/2, PSMB8/9, ERAP1/2) by qPCR/proteomics,
    – HLA-C peptide repertoire changes via HLA-C immunopeptidomics if feasible.
  • Neutralization/perturbation: block nominated cytokines (neutralizing Abs or receptor antagonists) in CD4 supernatants; repeat HLA-C and processing measurements.
  • Demonstrate sufficiency by adding back single cytokines (or minimal combinations) to recreate the effect.
5.3 Demonstrate impact on HLA-C*06:02–restricted CD8 activation with matched antigenic targets:
  • Use HLA-C*06:02+ target cells loaded endogenously (via minigene expression) or exogenously with a defined HLA-C*06:02 peptide.
  • Use HLA-C*06:02–restricted CD8 T cells (clones or engineered TCR reporters).
  • Compare CD8 activation/cytotoxicity (degranulation, target killing, cytokines) across conditions: (i) CD4 supernatant from DQα53-risk vs protective kinetic states, (ii) with/without cytokine neutralization, (iii) cytokine add-back.
  • Include controls to ensure effects are not generic licensing: match total inflammatory cytokine load, include irrelevant cytokine blocks, and normalize HLA class I induction where possible.

Tier 6 — Clinical linkage and model integration (PsC vs PsA; joint operation of DQA1-53 and HLA-C)
6.1 In patient samples stratified by DQA1-53 and HLA-C*06:02, measure:
  • circulating/lesional CD4 cytokine signatures,
  • APC pMHCII stability proxies (e.g., peptide-receptive DQ proportions, where measurable),
  • HLA-C expression on keratinocytes/immune targets.
6.2 Build an integrated multivariate model:
  • Inputs: DQA1-53 genotype, HLA-C*06:02, DQ ligandome features, kinetic-state metrics, cytokine mediator levels.
  • Outputs: PsA status/progression indicators.
  • Explicitly test interaction terms (DQA1-53 × HLA-C*06:02) to align with GWAS architecture and assess whether the pathway is contingent on HLA-C risk background.

Deliverables/decision points
D1: Demonstrate DQα53-dependent differences in DM-mediated editing kinetics and/or surface pMHC half-life under endosomal-like conditions.
D2: Validate the same directionality in full-length, membrane DQ on isogenic APCs.
D3: Define a natural DQ ligand panel and show genotype-linked shifts are not artifacts of in silico peptide choice.
D4: Show kinetic-state metrics predict CD4 polarization after controlling for peptide identity.
D5: Identify cytokine mediator(s) that are necessary/sufficient for HLA-C modulation and demonstrate causal enhancement of HLA-C*06:02–restricted CD8 activation.
Feasibility: Physiological fidelity (addresses DM/DO concern): The proposal no longer infers exchange kinetics from purified DQ alone; it explicitly reconstructs peptide editing with HLA-DM (±HLA-DO) at endosomal pH and separates endosomal editing rates from post-editing surface half-life. This directly tests whether DQα53 changes *DM susceptibility*—a plausible mechanistic lever for a single α-chain residue—under conditions that govern real peptide selection.

Direct membrane validation (addresses assay-context dependence): CRISPR knock-in of DQA1-53 into an isogenic APC background provides a stringent test that any kinetic-state differences manifest in intact antigen processing compartments, with direct measurement of surface pMHC abundance and decay. This eliminates the criticism that soluble assays may not translate to cellular presentation.

Unbiased ligand identification (addresses peptide-choice artifacts): DQ immunopeptidomics in isogenic APCs and genotype-stratified patient material constrains testing to naturally presented peptides. Subsequent analyses explicitly model peptide identity as a factor, allowing the central claim—kinetic-state mediation beyond peptide identity—to be quantitatively evaluated.

Mechanistic specificity of the HLA-C bridge (addresses under-specified amplification): Rather than indirect DC conditioning, the revised plan identifies the precise CD4-derived cytokines linked to DQα53-dependent kinetic states and tests necessity/sufficiency for HLA-C upregulation and antigen-processing remodeling using neutralization and add-back. The downstream consequence is validated with matched HLA-C*06:02 antigenic targets and restricted CD8 effectors, ensuring the pathway is HLA-C–specific and not merely generic inflammatory licensing.

Alignment with GWAS architecture (integrates Assets 1–2): Fine-mapping implicates HLA-DQA1 position 53 as an independent MHC risk component (Asset 2), while HLA-C–linked variants are strongly associated with cutaneous psoriasis and risk architecture differs across PsC vs PsA (Assets 1–2). By stratifying cohorts and mechanistic experiments jointly by DQA1-53 and HLA-C*06:02, and by testing interaction terms, the proposal operationalizes how these genetic signals can co-act in the same individuals/cells to promote the PsA phenotype.

Technical practicality: Each tier uses established, high-success methodologies (recombinant HLA-DQ/DM/DO systems, endosomal pH exchange assays, CRISPR editing in APCs, DQ immunopeptidomics, cytokine perturbation, HLA-C*06:02 CD8 assays). The innovation lies in their integration around a single-residue genotype perturbation and in treating kinetic-state variables as formal mediators in a genotype→presentation→T-cell→HLA-C amplification chain.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually strong in methodological specificity and in explicitly closing known loopholes (DM/DO dependence, soluble-vs-membrane translation, peptide-choice artifacts). The main deductions are for (1) mechanistic overreach at two junctions that are not yet physically anchored: (i) the structural/biophysical basis by which a single DQα53 substitution alters DM susceptibility across peptide space (needs a priori structural rationale or targeted structural validation), and (ii) the downstream “HLA-C amplification” claim that cytokines remodel peptide supply to increase the *density/durability of specific HLA-C*06:02–peptide complexes*—which is plausible but not guaranteed, and will be confounded by broad class I induction and global inflammatory licensing. (2) Feasibility risk from scope: immunopeptidomics (DQ and potentially HLA-C), CRISPR isogenic APC engineering, single-cell functional phenotyping, and paired CD8 assays is a multi-lab program; success hinges on early go/no-go gating and reagent availability (high-quality HLA-DQ IP antibodies, sufficient starting material from patient tissue, robust DQ allele-specific MS assignment, and authentic HLA-C*06:02 CD8 effectors). (3) The statistical “control for peptide identity” is directionally correct, but mixed-effects/mediation will still be sensitive to peptide detection limits and missing-not-at-random abundance; without an explicit design for balanced peptide panels and power calculations, the mediation claim may remain underdetermined.

original_chain: Biophysics -> Tandem repeat protein -> Combinatorial evolution -> Secondary structure element -> Binary patterning -> Functional proteins
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Binary-patterned tandem repeat proteins can be made reliably foldable and *predictably* evolvable into high-affinity, developable binders by coupling (i) repeat-unit hydrophobic/polar (H/P) binary patterning that enforces a fixed secondary-structure registry and suppresses misfolded-state degeneracy, with (ii) an identifiability-controlled 1D Ising inference workflow that yields *credible intervals* for intrinsic repeat stability (h) and inter-repeat coupling (J), and (iii) a cap-templated, two-module diversification strategy whose sequence choices are scored by an explicit ΔJ–Δh objective function.

Mechanistically, binary patterning reduces conformational entropy by pre-organizing helix/turn (or β/turn) microstructures within each repeat, while engineered N/C terminal caps eliminate end fraying that otherwise confounds cooperativity measurements. The Ising model (fitted and validated across repeat-number series and orthogonal single-site perturbations) provides a quantitative decomposition of stability into h and J, enabling *predictive* selection/design: (a) “coupling-module” mutations at enumerated inter-repeat interface positions are chosen to increase J within a prespecified target band (ΔJ) while bounding destabilization (Δh), producing a more cooperative folding landscape (sharper transitions, higher barrier to partially unfolded intermediates); (b) “function-module” mutations are restricted to a geometrically defined paratope patch whose chemistries are broadened beyond the H/P alphabet via controlled introduction of polar-aromatic and charged residues, while negative design removes polyreactive/aggregation-prone motifs.

This architecture overcomes reviewer-noted limitations by (1) making h/J inference robust and identifiable (global fits across repeat counts, m-value scaling constraints, Bayesian/bootstrapped uncertainty), (2) operationalizing “J-increasing” as a structural/energetic rubric tied to measurable ΔJ thresholds and a ΔJ–Δh trade-off objective, (3) deconvoluting folding thermodynamics from expression/display artifacts using orthogonal purified-protein readouts and in-cell solubility kinetics, and (4) predefining a falsifiable mechanism: at fixed h, increasing J must expand tolerated functional-mutation load (mutational robustness) and improve developability metrics without increasing nonspecific binding.
Plan: Step 0 — Scaffold and blueprint selection (pre-registered design constraints)
0.1 Select a canonical repeat family with well-characterized modularity and therapeutic precedent: ankyrin-like (DARPin-like) or TPR-like. Start with a 4–6 internal-repeat construct plus consensus N- and C-terminal caps (cap sequences fixed across the entire study to suppress end effects).
0.2 Fix a single secondary-structure blueprint per family (e.g., ankyrin: helix–turn–helix–β-hairpin-like loop; TPR: helix–turn–helix). Lock repeat length and register using a consensus backbone template; do not vary insertions/deletions during inference.

Step 1 — Binary patterning with explicit chemical allowances (foldability + functional chemistry)
1.1 Define the per-repeat H/P map from the consensus structure: core positions (H) = buried packing sites; boundary/interface positions = split into (i) coupling-interface set and (ii) solvent-facing set; turn/capping positions fixed.
1.2 Amino-acid sets (explicit):
  • Core H positions: {V, L, I, M, F} with a hard constraint on aromatic frequency (≤1 F per repeat) to limit aggregation; no W in the core.
  • Solvent P positions (non-paratope): {E, D, K, Q, N, S, T} with a net-charge window per construct (e.g., −5 to +5 at pH 7.4) to prevent extreme polyelectrolyte behavior.
  • Turn/helix-cap constraints: glycine/proline only at predefined turn positions; enforce one N-cap motif per helix (e.g., Asn/Asp/Ser/Thr at i position) and one C-cap motif (e.g., Gly at i+1 if structurally appropriate) to reduce fraying; proline disallowed in helices.
1.3 Functional paratope chemistry expansion (while keeping the fold grammar): define a contiguous surface patch (e.g., 8–14 positions across 2–3 repeats) where allowed residues include {Y, W (sparingly), H, R, K, D, E, N, Q, S, T, A, G} plus limited hydrophobics {F, L} only if solvent-exposed by structure. Apply negative design filters: exclude motifs correlated with polyreactivity (e.g., excessive aromatic clusters, long Lys/Lys runs) and predicted aggregation hotspots.

Step 2 — Identifiability-first Ising inference (variant matrix, fit criteria, uncertainty)
2.1 Minimum variant matrix (predefined, required before any evolution decisions):
  A) Repeat-number series (global constraint on cooperativity): capped constructs with N repeats where N ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8}. (At least 6 points.)
  B) Orthogonal single-site perturbations (break degeneracy of h vs J):
     • Core perturbations (targeting h): ≥8 single substitutions at strictly buried core positions (one per repeat class position, distributed across repeats), chosen to be near-isosteric but destabilizing (e.g., L→A, I→V) to primarily affect intrinsic repeat stability.
     • Interface perturbations (targeting J): ≥8 single substitutions at enumerated inter-repeat boundary positions (e.g., salt-bridge disruption, packing relief) designed to primarily affect coupling (e.g., introduce/remove complementary charge pairs or adjust sidechain volume at the repeat boundary).
     • End-effect controls: 2 constructs with altered caps (one weakened cap, one strengthened cap) used only to quantify end-effect magnitude; caps otherwise fixed.
  Total minimal panel: repeat series (6) + core singles (8) + interface singles (8) + end controls (2) = 24 constructs (expandable).
2.2 Experimental unfolding dataset requirements (to detect non-two-state and m-value issues):
  • Chemical denaturation (urea or GdnHCl) monitored by far-UV CD and intrinsic fluorescence (two observables) for each construct; ≥3 technical replicates per construct.
  • DSF (thermal melt) on purified protein as an orthogonal stability proxy; record Tm and onset.
  • For a subset (≥6 constructs spanning stability range): kinetic folding/unfolding (stopped-flow or manual jump) to detect intermediates or hysteresis.
2.3 Two-state adequacy and acceptance thresholds (pre-registered decision gates):
  • Global fit across repeat counts must explain ≥95% variance for both CD and fluorescence simultaneously with shared h/J parameters and per-construct baselines.
  • m-value scaling: enforce a monotonic, approximately linear dependence of m on repeat number (within a predefined tolerance band, e.g., R^2 ≥ 0.9 for m vs N, allowing cap offset). If violated, switch to an extended model (e.g., N-dependent m or inclusion of a partially folded intermediate state) and re-evaluate identifiability.
  • Residual diagnostics: no systematic deviations near transition midpoints; replicate-to-replicate ΔG error ≤0.3 kcal/mol.
2.4 Identifiability and uncertainty quantification:
  • Fit the 1D Ising model using Bayesian inference (priors: h and J centered on literature-consistent ranges for repeat proteins; weakly informative) or bootstrap resampling (≥1,000 resamples). Report posterior/CI for h and J and their covariance.
  • Identifiability criterion: |corr(h,J)| < 0.8 in posterior samples and 95% CI widths below thresholds (e.g., CI(h) ≤ 0.3 kcal/mol per repeat; CI(J) ≤ 0.2 kcal/mol coupling unit). If not met, expand the perturbation set (additional core/interface singles) before proceeding.

Step 3 — Make “J-increasing” predictive (interface rubric + ΔJ–Δh objective)
3.1 Enumerate coupling-interface positions (fixed list): define residues at repeat boundaries that participate in (i) hydrophobic knobs-into-holes packing and (ii) inter-repeat electrostatic networks (salt bridges/H-bonds) based on the consensus backbone.
3.2 Structural/energetic rubric for candidate coupling mutations (screen before library build):
  • Packing metric: maintain shape complementarity at boundary (avoid cavities); prioritize conservative volume adjustments (e.g., V↔I↔L) only at interface-facing hydrophobics.
  • Electrostatics: introduce paired charges across the boundary (E–K, D–R) only if solvent-exposed enough to avoid burying unsatisfied charges; allow H-bond networks using Q/N/S/T at boundary-adjacent positions.
  • Cap compatibility: no coupling mutations in cap repeats.
3.3 Quantitative design objective (used to accept/reject coupling designs):
  • Predictive score S = wJ·ΔJ − wh·max(0, −Δh) − wagg·AggRisk − wpoly·PolyreactRisk, where ΔJ and Δh are estimated from the validated Ising model (or from calibrated mapping between in vitro readouts and inferred parameters), and AggRisk/PolyreactRisk are computed from sequence heuristics and chromatography behavior (see Step 5).
  • Target bands (predefined): ΔJ per boundary mutation set should be +0.3 to +1.0 kcal/mol (credible interval excluding 0), while Δh penalty must be ≥ −0.2 kcal/mol per repeat (i.e., not substantially destabilizing intrinsic repeats). Candidates outside this Pareto region are not advanced.

Step 4 — Library architecture and phased evolution with deconvoluted readouts
4.1 Library phases (each with explicit selection readouts and purified-protein confirmation):
  Phase I (cooperativity-first):
   • Build a coupling-module library: diversify only interface positions (from the enumerated list) with a small, chemically coherent alphabet (hydrophobic packing + designed salt-bridge pairs), keeping core H/P pattern fixed.
   • Primary selection: protease resistance challenge performed on purified proteins (not only display). Use standardized protease conditions and quantify intact fraction by SDS-PAGE/LC-MS.
   • Orthogonal gating: DSF (Tm threshold) and SEC monodispersity. Only variants passing all gates advance.
   • Refit Ising parameters on a representative subset (≥24 variants) to confirm ΔJ shifts with uncertainty.

  Phase II (binding evolution with negative design):
   • Build a function-module library: diversify the predefined paratope patch (8–14 positions) using an alphabet that includes polar aromatics and charged residues to enable high-affinity interactions.
   • Display/selection: phage, ribosome, or yeast display against a specific biomedical target (e.g., Hsp90 or VEGF-A), with decreasing antigen concentration and off-rate selection.
   • Negative selections (mandatory):
      (i) Polyreactivity screens: binding depletion against irrelevant proteins (e.g., BSA, IgG Fc, heparin) and sticky surfaces.
      (ii) Aggregation gate: SEC-based depletion or detergent sensitivity; remove variants with high hydrophobic surface exposure signals.
   • Purified confirmation: for top hits per round, measure affinity/kinetics by SPR/BLI and re-measure DSF/chemical denaturation to ensure stability is retained.

4.2 Deconvolution of folding vs expression artifacts (parallel readouts):
  • In-cell expression/solubility: pulse-chase or time-resolved soluble fraction quantification (e.g., split-GFP solubility reporter plus Western of total expression).
  • In vitro refolding: denature/refold assays to measure refolding yield and aggregation during refolding.
  • Protease challenge on purified protein (repeated from Phase I) to ensure protease resistance reflects intrinsic stability/cooperativity rather than display shielding.

Step 5 — Validation, developability, and mechanistic falsification (predefined metrics)
5.1 Structural validation:
  • Far-UV CD for secondary structure; near-UV CD (where applicable) for tertiary packing.
  • For 2–3 top candidates and key controls: solution NMR or crystallography to confirm repeat registry, cap integrity, and interface geometry.

5.2 Developability panel (pass/fail thresholds set before final downselect):
  • Expression yield in E. coli (mg/L) and solubility fraction.
  • SEC-MALS monodispersity (single dominant species) and DLS polydispersity.
  • Serum stability or protease stability in relevant biological matrices.

5.3 Mechanistic falsification via mutational robustness metric (core requirement):
  • Define mutational robustness R(N): for each scaffold class (high-J vs baseline-J at matched h), introduce N paratope mutations (N = 3, 6, 9; random within allowed paratope alphabet) and measure fraction that remains (i) soluble/monodisperse and (ii) maintains ≥X% of binding signal (or ≥threshold KD).
  • Prediction: at fixed h (matched within ±0.2 kcal/mol per repeat), higher J scaffolds must show higher R(N) and better retention of developability metrics.
  • Falsification criteria:
     (i) If ΔJ-increased variants do not improve R(N) vs baseline, the “J→evolvability” mechanism is rejected (even if binders are found).
     (ii) If R(N) improves but only with increased aggregation/polyreactivity, the mechanism is incomplete and negative design constraints must be revised.

5.4 Controls (decision-making, not just comparison):
  • Non-binary-patterned scaffold (matched length) subjected to the same evolution: tests necessity of binary patterning for foldability.
  • Binary-patterned but non-Ising-guided random mutagenesis: tests necessity of parameter-guided mutation masking.
  • Interface “anti-J” mutations (predicted to reduce coupling) at fixed h: should reduce cooperativity and R(N), providing causal directionality.

Step 6 — Iterative DBTL with parameter-aware stopping rules
6.1 After each cycle, update Ising posteriors (h/J with CI) on a representative panel and update mutation masks.
6.2 Stopping rule for scaffold optimization: stop increasing J when (i) additional ΔJ yields diminishing returns in R(N), or (ii) negative selection failures rise (polyreactivity/aggregation), indicating over-coupling or excessive surface hydrophobicity.
6.3 Final downselect: choose candidates that jointly satisfy (binding potency + specificity) AND (h/J within validated predictive regime) AND developability thresholds.
Feasibility: Empirical foundation: Consensus-designed repeat proteins (e.g., ankyrin/TPR/LRR scaffolds) are known to be highly stable, expressible in E. coli, and often display simplified folding behavior that is amenable to cooperative models. Binary patterning is a validated strategy for enforcing foldability by controlling core packing and secondary-structure formation, while repeat proteins’ modular architecture makes them well-suited to an Ising-like decomposition into intrinsic stability (h) and coupling (J).

Addressing identifiability/robustness concerns: The plan elevates rigor by predefining a minimal, orthogonal variant matrix (repeat-number series + core vs interface single perturbations + end-effect probes) and imposing explicit acceptance criteria for two-state adequacy and m-value scaling across repeat counts. Bayesian/bootstrapped inference provides uncertainty bounds and identifiability diagnostics (h–J covariance), with a predefined contingency (expand perturbation set / adopt an extended model) if criteria are not met.

Making “J-increasing” operationally predictive: The proposal replaces qualitative claims with (i) an enumerated interface-position set grounded in repeat-boundary geometry, (ii) a packing/electrostatic rubric for mutation choice, and (iii) a quantitative objective function trading ΔJ gains against Δh penalties and developability risks. A target ΔJ band with credible-interval exclusion of zero establishes what constitutes a meaningful coupling increase.

Deconvoluting folding from expression/display artifacts: Selection is not allowed to rely on display readouts alone. Purified-protein protease challenge, DSF, chemical denaturation, refolding yield, and pulse-chase solubility kinetics are executed in parallel so that improvements in cooperativity/stability are distinguished from expression level, protease accessibility, and display-context shielding.

Mechanistic falsifiability: The central mechanism—higher J at fixed h increases mutational robustness/evolvability of the paratope without sacrificing developability—is tested via a quantitative robustness function R(N) across controlled paratope mutation loads and compared to explicit baselines (non-Ising-guided and non-binary-patterned). Failure to increase R(N) under matched h conditions falsifies the hypothesized J-driven evolvability advantage, providing a clear go/no-go criterion rather than post hoc interpretation.
final_critique: Methodologically, the proposal is unusually well-specified (variant matrix, acceptance gates, uncertainty/identifiability criteria, falsification tests) and addresses known confounders in repeat-protein cooperativity measurements (end fraying, m-value scaling, display artifacts). The largest scientific risk is model mismatch: a 1D nearest-neighbor Ising decomposition into a single h and J may not remain valid once the paratope introduces heterogeneous chemistries (aromatics/charges) that can create long-range or repeat-specific effects, partially folded intermediates, or nonuniform m-values; the contingency plan mentions extended models but does not specify how parameter interpretability (and thus the ΔJ–Δh objective) will be preserved under heterogeneity. Second, the operational definition of ‘interface mutations primarily affect J’ vs ‘core mutations primarily affect h’ is plausible but not guaranteed—many boundary residues affect both intrinsic repeat stability and coupling, and without an explicit structural energy model (or direct structural constraints), ΔJ attribution could be overconfident even with good statistical identifiability. Third, the key mechanistic claim—higher J at fixed h increases tolerated functional-mutation load without increasing nonspecific binding—may be confounded because increased cooperativity can correlate with increased surface hydrophobicity or altered dynamics that also change polyreactivity; the negative design gates help but are not quantitatively tied back to the mechanistic metric R(N) (e.g., how to separate ‘robustness’ from selection biases introduced by the screens). Finally, several thresholds (e.g., ΔJ target band, CI widths, variance explained) are reasonable but somewhat arbitrary; power analysis/expected effect sizes are not provided, leaving uncertainty about whether the planned panel size can reliably detect ΔJ shifts of ~0.3 kcal/mol amid experimental noise and baseline drift.

original_chain: Embryonic stem cell -> Blastocyst complementation -> Retinal pigment epithelium -> Embryonic stem cell -> Somatic cell reprogramming -> Pluripotent stem cell -> Dissolved oxygen
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: RPE cells exhibit a reprogramming bottleneck that prevents generation of blastocyst-complementation–competent iPSCs because early epigenetic erasure is rate-limited by (a) insufficient pericellular/intracellular O2 availability for TET and JmjC dioxygenases during the replication-coupled demethylation window and (b) a redox/iron constraint in which reprogramming-associated ROS transiently oxidizes the labile Fe2+ pool and diverts α-ketoglutarate (αKG) to 2-hydroxyglutarate (2HG), competitively inhibiting dioxygenases. We hypothesize that a quantitatively calibrated, short-duration high-pericellular-O2 “epigenetic reset window” (days 2–6 post-OSK induction) will increase dioxygenase flux only if (i) intracellular O2 is verified to rise above Km(O2)-relevant ranges, (ii) nuclear αKG:succinate is increased and 2HG is reduced via minimal-perturbation metabolic routing, and (iii) ROS/Fe redox are actively managed in real time to avoid net loss of Fe2+ and DNA damage.
