Mechanistically, brief O2 pulses—validated at the pericellular and intracellular levels—should increase the effective velocity of TET1/2 and KDM2/4/6 reactions by raising [O2] relative to Km(O2) while improving the competitive substrate landscape (higher αKG, lower 2HG/succinate), accelerating removal of somatic DNA methylation and H3K9me3/H3K27me3 barriers at pluripotency loci. This will shorten the time RPE cells remain in stress-prone intermediate states, improving naïve-state entry, preserving imprint stability/mitochondrial integrity, and thereby increasing staged chimera competency culminating in organ-deficient blastocyst complementation.
Plan: A. System architecture and quantitative oxygen delivery
A1. Reprogramming inputs and baseline conditions
- Biological substrates: (i) mouse primary RPE (for chimera work), (ii) human and pig RPE (for mechanistic/translation concordance; no in vivo chimera endpoints).
- Reprogramming: non-integrating OSK (Sendai or episomal). Include a doxycycline-inducible OSK variant only if needed for synchronized kinetics; otherwise standard transient OSK.
- Culture: feeder-free matrix (e.g., laminin-511 or vitronectin) to minimize variability; defined medium matched across arms.

A2. Perfused, closed-loop DO platform (explicit control variables)
- Geometry: 24-well perfused plate with a gas-permeable membrane base (PDMS or equivalent) and low-shear recirculating perfusion (target wall shear stress <0.5 dyn/cm^2; verify with tracer-based CFD or manufacturer specs).
- Oxygen buffering: hemoglobin-alginate microbeads (diameter 100–300 µm; 0.5–2% v/v) with O2-binding tuned to smooth setpoint transitions; beads separated from cells by transwell insert or retained by micro-sieve to prevent bead-cell contact.
- Sensors and control:
  1) Bulk medium DO: optical lifetime DO spot sensor per well (calibrated two-point: 0% with sodium sulfite; 100% air saturation at 37°C; report DO in µM and % air saturation).
  2) Pericellular DO: planar luminescent O2 sensor film bonded to the culture surface (within ~50–200 µm of cells) to read pericellular DO separately from bulk.
  3) PID control actuators: gas-mixing module controlling O2/N2/CO2 to headspace + membrane feed; perfusion rate modulation as secondary actuator.
- Explicit setpoints:
  - Report and control (i) gas phase %O2, (ii) bulk medium DO (µM), and (iii) pericellular DO (µM). Primary controlled variable = pericellular DO.

A3. Intracellular O2 validation (mandatory)
- Intracellular O2 probe: phosphorescent intracellular O2 probe (e.g., nanoparticle-based or small-molecule compatible with live imaging) calibrated in situ using respiratory inhibition (antimycin/rotenone) and O2 clamp conditions.
- Spatial mapping: microelectrode O2 mapping (Clark-type) across boundary layer in representative wells during pulses to validate gradients and mass transfer.
- Acceptance criterion before biological experiments: demonstrate that a programmed pericellular step change yields a reproducible intracellular O2 increase with defined kinetics (t90 rise/fall) and amplitude.

B. Pulse regimen definition + quantitative enzyme-flux model
B1. Enzyme-flux model (pre-registered) linking O2 and metabolites to TET/JmjC velocity
- Model form: Michaelis–Menten with competitive inhibition for αKG-dependent dioxygenases:
  v = Vmax * [O2]/(Km,O2 + [O2]) * [αKG]/(Km,αKG + [αKG]) * 1/(1 + [2HG]/Ki,2HG + [succinate]/Ki,succ)
- Parameterization:
  - Use literature Km(O2) ranges for TET/JmjC where available; otherwise fit an empirical apparent Km,O2 using measured 5hmC gain rates vs intracellular O2 under fixed αKG/2HG.
  - Fit Vmax scaling using early timepoints of 5hmC accumulation and histone mark loss.
- Predicted effect sizes required for go-forward:
  - Intracellular O2 during pulse must exceed baseline by ≥2-fold and reach a regime predicted to increase v by ≥25% relative to baseline (from the fitted model).

B2. DO pulse regimen (controlled at pericellular DO; not only gas phase)
- Baseline: days 0–2 at pericellular DO corresponding to 5% O2-equivalent (report actual µM).
- Reset window: days 2–6 apply pulses raising pericellular DO to a level corresponding to 30% O2-equivalent (report µM), for 60–90 minutes, 2x/day.
- Rationale: short pulses to increase dioxygenase flux while limiting cumulative oxidative burden.
- Dose-finding sub-study (before main study): 3 amplitudes (20%, 30%, 40% O2-equivalent) × 2 durations (45, 90 min) with constant media, perfusion, cell density; pick regimen that maximizes 5hmC gain and H3K9me3 loss without exceeding ROS/DNA-damage thresholds (see Section C go/no-go).

C. Real-time ROS/Fe-redox risk management with pre-specified mitigation arms
C1. Real-time oxidative stress measurements during days 2–6 pulses
- ROS and redox:
  - mitoSOX (mitochondrial superoxide) live readout pre-, mid-, post-pulse.
  - Cytosolic ROS (H2DCFDA or equivalent) as orthogonal.
  - GSH/GSSG ratio (enzymatic assay) at defined timepoints.
  - Lipid peroxidation: BODIPY 581/591 C11 live readout + 4-HNE adducts by immunoassay.
- Iron redox:
  - Labile Fe2+ pool via FerroOrange (live) and total labile iron (Calcein-AM quench) where appropriate.
  - Ferritin, FPN1, TFRC expression (qPCR/protein) as longer-timescale iron handling indicators.
- DNA damage/stress response (during, not only endpoint):
  - γH2AX foci quantification, phospho-p53, and p21 expression during days 2–6.
  - Replication stress markers (RPA foci) if γH2AX rises.

C2. Pre-specified mitigation arms (to de-risk Fe oxidation/ROS without masking mechanism)
- Antioxidant timing arm: antioxidants administered only during the pulse (e.g., 15 min before to end of pulse) to reduce oxidative burst while preserving baseline signaling. Candidate(s): NAC or Trolox at titrated doses; exclude conditions that reduce reprogramming efficiency.
- Iron redox management:
  - If Fe2+ drops during pulses, test a paired arm with transient low-dose iron supplementation (bioavailable form) outside the pulse to restore labile Fe2+ without catalyzing Fenton chemistry during peak O2.
  - Add a chelation “safety” arm (deferoxamine/DFO at low dose) only if lipid peroxidation/ferroptosis markers rise; then replete iron after pulse window.
- Ferroptosis surveillance: GPX4 levels, ACSL4, PTGS2 induction; cell death mode assays.

C3. Go/no-go criteria (hard thresholds) for proceeding to chimera stages
- During pulse window:
  1) γH2AX: must not exceed 2× baseline median foci/cell sustained across >24 h.
  2) GSH/GSSG: must not drop >30% relative to baseline for >6 h.
  3) Lipid peroxidation: BODIPY shift must remain within a pre-defined non-lethal range; if exceeded, mitigation arm becomes mandatory and pulse amplitude reduced.
  4) Labile Fe2+: must not show sustained depletion (>25% drop at 6 h post-pulse) unless corrected by mitigation.
- If criteria fail at 30% pulses, step down amplitude/duration per the dose-finding matrix.

D. Replace “αKG exporter module” with minimal-perturbation, validated routing + isotope tracing
D1. Primary strategy (non-genetic): metabolite delivery to increase αKG and suppress 2HG
- Use cell-permeable αKG derivative (e.g., dimethyl-αKG) delivered only during days 2–6, titrated to raise nuclear αKG without altering pH/osmolality.
- Add glutamine control: keep glutamine constant across arms; include a tracer-only arm without supplementation.

D2. Secondary (genetically defined, minimal) strategy only if needed
- Use a defined mitochondrial carrier with evidence for αKG/malate exchange capacity and net export under high glycolytic flux; expression under tight, transient doxycycline control (days 1–7) with quantitative expression verification.
- Must pass a confounding test: in constant DO baseline, the carrier alone must not reproduce the full epigenetic reset signature; otherwise attribution to DO becomes ambiguous.

D3. Orthogonal isotope tracing to prove nuclear αKG source and routing
- U-13C5-glutamine and U-13C6-glucose tracing during pulse window.
- Readouts: LC–MS/MS of nuclear and cytosolic fractions for m+5 αKG (from glutamine) and related TCA intermediates; quantify labeling in 2HG to confirm whether pulses shift αKG→2HG routing.
- Fractionation QC: nuclear purity markers (Lamin A/C) and cytosolic contamination (GAPDH) by immunoblot.

E. Mechanistic readouts (epigenetic + cell-state) aligned to the causal chain
E1. Dioxygenase activity
- TET: global 5hmC (ELISA) plus oxidative bisulfite sequencing at key loci; time-resolved sampling (days 2, 4, 6).
- KDM: CUT&Tag for H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 (barrier marks) + H3K4me3 (activation) at pluripotency loci; quantify kinetics.

E2. Competing bottlenecks explicitly monitored
- Cell cycle: EdU incorporation; cell cycle phase distribution by flow.
- MET timing: E-cadherin, Vimentin, EPCAM dynamics.
- Stress/p53 pathway: phospho-p53, p21; include a documentation-only arm (no p53 suppression unless reviewers allow; if used, it must be a separate mechanistic add-on, not part of the core claim).

F. Functional endpoint ladder with powered, staged comparisons (pre-registered)
F1. Experimental groups (mouse RPE)
- G1: Standard reprogramming, constant baseline DO (5% O2-equivalent).
- G2: Constant normoxia DO control (e.g., 20% O2-equivalent pericellular DO).
- G3: DO-pulsed reset (selected amplitude/duration) with no antioxidant.
- G4: DO-pulsed reset + mitigation (if triggered by go/no-go rules; otherwise pre-specified secondary arm).
- Optional mechanistic controls:
  - G5: DO-pulsed + DMOG/succinate (necessity test).
  - G6: Baseline DO + αKG (sufficiency boundary test).

F2. Acceptance thresholds before any embryo work
- Naïve/ESC-like transcriptome: scRNA-seq naïve score within pre-defined distance to ESC reference; exclude lines with lineage priming signatures.
- Epigenome: demonstrable accelerated demethylation trajectory; imprint stability within acceptable deviation (define locus panel; exclude gross imprint erosion).
- Genome integrity: karyotype normal; mitochondrial heteroplasmy not substantially increased; oxidative damage markers not elevated beyond thresholds.

F3. Staged in vivo ladder (avoid all-or-nothing)
- Stage 1 (pre-implantation contribution): inject candidate iPSCs into 8-cell embryos or blastocysts; assess (a) survival, (b) ICM vs TE allocation at E3.5–E4.5 by lineage markers.
- Stage 2 (early post-implantation): assess contribution at E6.5–E9.5 (epiblast contribution; donor fraction by reporter and genotyping).
- Stage 3 (mid-gestation chimera): quantify chimerism at E12.5–E14.5 in multiple tissues to ensure no abnormal allocation patterns.
- Stage 4 (organ-deficient complementation endpoint): Pdx1−/− blastocyst complementation for pancreas niche (as validated in rodent complementation literature); quantify donor-derived pancreas formation and function where ethically/technically appropriate.

F4. Powering and success criteria (explicit)
- Pre-register primary endpoint for staged success:
  - Primary: Stage 1 ICM allocation rate and donor fraction compared to G1.
  - Secondary: Stage 2 epiblast contribution; Stage 4 pancreas complementation frequency.
- Sample sizes:
  - Stage 1: ≥50 embryos/group across ≥3 independent iPSC derivations.
  - Stage 2: ≥15 conceptuses/group (account for loss).
  - Stage 4: powered to detect a ≥2× increase in complementation frequency vs G1 (exact n refined from pilot rates; commit to interim analysis rules).
- Statistical plan: mixed-effects models with iPSC line as random effect; correction for multiple comparisons across endpoints.

G. Manufacturing/QbD mapping (DO as CPP; dioxygenase signature as CQA)
- CPPs: pericellular DO peak (µM), pulse duration, pulse rise time (t90), cumulative O2 exposure, perfusion rate, cell density.
- CQAs: (i) Δ5hmC during days 2–6, (ii) ΔH3K9me3/ΔH3K27me3 at pluripotency loci, (iii) naïve scRNA potency score, (iv) Stage 1 ICM allocation potency.
- Release rule (mouse): only batches meeting CQA thresholds proceed to embryo stages; track DO traces as batch records.

Feasibility: 1) Direct validation of the delivered oxygen signal (addresses critique iii)
The revised plan treats pericellular and intracellular O2 as the true controlled/validated variables, not “O2-equivalent” gas settings. A three-layer validation (bulk DO, pericellular planar sensors, intracellular probes) plus microelectrode mapping establishes that pulses actually reach the intracellular regime relevant to TET/JmjC kinetics. This directly mitigates the risk that nominal headspace O2 fails to translate into intracellular O2 changes.

2) Quantitative linkage from O2/metabolites to dioxygenase flux with predicted effect sizes (addresses directive 1)
A pre-registered kinetic model (O2 dependence + αKG/2HG/succinate competition) is fitted using time-resolved 5hmC and histone mark kinetics. This converts the central claim from qualitative plausibility to quantitative, falsifiable predictions (e.g., ≥25% predicted flux increase required). The model also guards against over-attributing outcomes to O2 if metabolite competition dominates.

3) ROS/Fe-redox de-risking with real-time monitoring and mitigation arms (addresses critique i and directive 2)
High O2 can increase ROS, oxidize Fe2+, and elevate DNA damage—each can negate dioxygenase benefits and impair chimera competence. The revised plan adds real-time readouts during the pulse window (mitoSOX, GSH/GSSG, lipid peroxidation, labile Fe2+, γH2AX/p53) and hard go/no-go thresholds. Pre-specified mitigation arms (pulse-timed antioxidants; iron chelation/repletion logic; ferroptosis surveillance) prevent proceeding under damaging conditions rather than relying on endpoint 8-oxo-dG alone.

4) Minimal-perturbation αKG strategy + isotope tracing (addresses critique ii and directive 3)
The underspecified “αKG exporter” is replaced by a primary non-genetic approach (cell-permeable αKG derivative restricted to days 2–6) to minimize confounding reprogramming effects. A secondary genetically defined carrier is only used if needed and is explicitly tested for confounding. Orthogonal U-13C tracing in nuclear fractions demonstrates whether increased nuclear αKG originates from intended routing and whether αKG→2HG diversion is altered by O2 pulses—directly answering the reviewer’s concern about unproven nuclear metabolite changes.

5) Functional endpoint ladder with powered, staged outcomes (addresses critique iv and directive 4)
Because full blastocyst complementation is a high bar, the plan introduces a staged ladder (ICM allocation → post-implantation epiblast contribution → mid-gestation chimerism → organ-deficient complementation) with explicit acceptance thresholds before embryo work and pre-registered primary endpoints, sample sizes, and mixed-effects statistics. This avoids an all-or-nothing endpoint and provides interpretable failure modes (e.g., epiblast entry failure vs later developmental attrition).

6) Competing rate-limiters monitored to prevent overcommitment to O2-substrate limitation (addresses critique)
The revised mechanism explicitly acknowledges and measures competing bottlenecks—cell cycle dynamics, MET timing, and p53/stress responses—during the pulse window. This allows attribution: if DO pulses improve dioxygenase signatures but stall cell cycle/MET or activate p53, the causal chain can be revised rather than assumed.

Overall, the revised proposal keeps the original concept chain (DO → dioxygenase kinetics → epigenetic erasure → ESC-like/naïve state → chimera competence) but upgrades it into a calibrated, risk-managed, quantitatively modeled, and staged-evaluation program that can convincingly support or refute the central hypothesis.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and technically mature proposal. Engineering resolution is very strong: oxygen delivery is treated as a controlled process variable with explicit sensing, validation, and acceptance criteria, rather than a nominal culture condition. The logical chain from dissolved oxygen to dioxygenase kinetics, epigenetic erasure, and chimera competence is internally consistent and stress-tested via competing bottleneck measurements. Minor deductions arise from residual biological uncertainty rather than proposal weakness: (i) the assumption that O2/Km limitations dominate over chromatin accessibility or replication timing across all RPE lines remains empirically unproven, and (ii) the complexity of the platform risks reducing throughput and increasing failure modes, particularly for intracellular O2 probes and iron redox readouts in reprogramming cells. Evidence grounding is strong, though some mechanistic inferences (e.g., nuclear αKG sufficiency for locus-specific demethylation) still rely on correlative rather than causal demonstrations. Overall, this proposal is closer to a systems-engineering program than a typical biological study, which is a strength but also raises execution risk.

original_chain: Dimethyloxalylglycine -> Human pluripotent stem cell -> Blastocyst complementation -> Interspecies chimerism -> Neonatal interspecies chimera -> Pluripotent stem cell -> Ganciclovir
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A dual-orthogonal, embryo-tunable human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC) engineering strategy will increase target-organ human contribution while preventing ectopic human expansion in neonatal interspecies chimeras generated by blastocyst complementation by (i) implementing an *orthogonal small-molecule-inducible metabolic–epigenetic compatibility governor* that buffers peri-implantation hypoxia/2-OG-dioxygenase stress (including DMOG-like background PHD inhibition) without using DMOG as the control input, and (ii) deploying a *hardened, multi-layer containment architecture* combining a constitutive failsafe suicide switch plus a small set of empirically validated, cross-species-conserved lineage-restricted thymidine kinase (TK) ablation elements with quantified leakiness and developmental timing.

Mechanistic rationale addressing prior fragilities:
1) **Input orthogonality and clampability**: Rather than sensing DMOG (which is intrinsically confounded by oxygen, αKG/succinate ratio, Fe2+/ascorbate, and embryo microenvironment), the governor is actuated by a ligand–receptor pair that is orthogonal to mammalian metabolism (e.g., rapalog-induced dimerization or trimethoprim-stabilized DD). DMOG is treated only as a *background perturbation* that the circuit buffers. This decouples the *control input* from embryo variable physiology and makes a bounded “compatibility state” achievable with a defined transfer function.
2) **Biologically implementable circuit dynamics**: The governor is engineered as a *two-loop controller* (fast induction + delayed negative feedback) with explicitly parameterized response time, amplitude, and noise, such that protective modules turn on within the embryo peri-implantation window while preventing sustained HIF-like maladaptive transcriptional states.
3) **Containment robustness**: Instead of complex multi-input CRISPR logic with high in vivo leakage risk, containment is simplified to (a) an always-available orthogonal failsafe suicide switch for catastrophic shutdown, and (b) a minimal number of lineage promoter/enhancer modules chosen for cross-species conservation and empirically characterized ROC/leak curves in pig embryos/ex vivo gastrulation models. Prohibited lineages are targeted at the earliest transcriptionally detectable stage *before colonization becomes effectively irreversible*, and early migratory escape is addressed by adding an early-window “germline/ectoderm sentinel” ablation layer.
4) **In vivo pharmacology and escape management**: Ganciclovir (GCV) timing, dosing, placental transfer, and on/off kinetics are explicitly mapped with PK sampling and linked to reporter-based real-time TK expression readouts; cassette silencing/escape is monitored by longitudinal ddPCR for integrity, single-cell reporter quantification, and enrichment checks for resistant clones.

Collectively, these modifications preserve the original concept chain—metabolic/epigenetic buffering to improve peri-implantation fitness plus post hoc ablation to prevent ectopic contribution—while removing the DMOG-sensor confound, quantifying circuit dynamics, hardening containment logic, and concretizing fetal drug exposure and escape surveillance.
Plan: Step 0 — Model choice, ethical boundary conditions, and baseline chimera performance mapping
0.1 Choose a stringent blastocyst complementation niche with established developmental constraint and measurable organ function endpoints:
  - Primary: porcine PDX1-/- (pancreas) or SALL1-/- (kidney).
  - Define prohibited tissues a priori: CNS (forebrain/midbrain/hindbrain), germline (gonadal ridge, PGC markers), and any ectopic epithelial/mesenchymal expansions.
0.2 Establish baseline with non-engineered primed hPSCs vs “chimera-competent” benchmark (e.g., naïve-like hPSC state if permitted) to quantify:
  - Early retention/apoptosis (24–120 h post-injection), spatial localization, and proliferation.
  - Mid-gestation tissue distribution (ddPCR human DNA; immunostaining; pilot scRNA-seq) to determine the earliest timepoint where prohibited lineages become transcriptionally detectable.

Step 1 — Build orthogonal compatibility governor (DMOG = disturbance, not input)
1.1 Genomic architecture (two safe-harbor sites; single copy; insulated):
  - Site A (e.g., AAVS1): Orthogonal actuator + governor program.
  - Site B (e.g., CLYBL): Containment modules + reporters.
  - Use strong insulators (e.g., cHS4 or equivalent) flanking each cassette; verify single-copy insertion by long-read sequencing spanning junctions.

1.2 Actuation modality (choose one and lock it early; both are orthogonal):
  Option 1: **Rapalog-inducible dimerization** (FRB/FKBP) controlling a synthetic transcription factor (synTF).
    - Architecture: synTF = DNA-binding domain (e.g., dCas9 to fixed gRNAs or a synthetic zinc-finger array) split into two halves fused to FRB and FKBP; rapalog drives assembly.
    - Advantage: rapid ON kinetics (minutes), tunable by ligand concentration, reversible.
  Option 2: **Trimethoprim (TMP)-stabilized degron (DHFR-DD)** controlling synTF abundance.
    - Architecture: synTF fused to DHFR-DD; TMP stabilizes; withdrawal yields rapid degradation.
    - Advantage: direct abundance control; simple dose-response.

1.3 Governor program (explicitly bounded “compatibility state”):
  - Outputs are modular and limited to a small, testable set with direct mechanistic ties to peri-implantation attrition:
    (i) Redox/anoikis protection: e.g., controlled expression of catalase/SOD2 or NRF2-axis activator (bounded).
    (ii) Mitochondrial support/anaplerosis: controlled expression of a mild anaplerotic enhancer (e.g., pyruvate carboxylase upshift) avoiding broad metabolic rewiring.
    (iii) Epigenetic flux buffering: increase availability of αKG equivalents via mild transporter/enzymatic tuning (bounded), with explicit monitoring of αKG/succinate ratio.
  - Add a *HIF-output limiter* without attempting to “sense DMOG”: implement repression of a small panel of maladaptive glycolytic/HIF targets (pre-identified in baseline embryos) via synTF-driven CRISPRi.

1.4 Dynamics shaping (quantitative, parameterized):
  - Implement a **two-loop controller**:
    Fast loop: ligand → synTF ON (tON target: 15–60 min in vitro; 1–2 h in embryo culture).
    Slow loop: synTF induces delayed negative feedback (e.g., inducible expression of a repressor or an shRNA targeting synTF mRNA) with delay τ set by using an intron-containing transcript and a weak promoter.
  - Design targets (to be achieved and verified):
    - Peak-to-baseline fold-change of key outputs: 2–5× (avoid supra-physiologic expression).
    - Pulse width: 6–18 h after a single ligand exposure; reversible to baseline within 24–36 h after withdrawal.
    - Cell-to-cell variability: CV < 0.35 for synTF reporter at peak (measured by flow cytometry).

Step 2 — Quantify transfer function, noise, and predictive minimal model (in vitro then ex vivo embryo)
2.1 In vitro disturbance-testing panel (DMOG as stressor; also hypoxia and succinate):
  - Conditions: normoxia vs 1–5% O2; ± DMOG (dose range chosen to mimic embryo-exposure stress), ± succinate elevation, low nutrient, dissociation/shear stress.
  - Readouts (time-resolved, single-cell where possible):
    - Metabolomics: αKG, succinate, 2-HG; compute αKG/succinate ratio.
    - Dioxygenase-linked epigenetics: global and locus-specific histone marks (e.g., H3K27me3/H3K4me3 panels) + DNA methylation proxies.
    - HIF program: targeted transcript panel and reporter.
    - Survival: caspase activation, anoikis assays, mitochondrial membrane potential.

2.2 System identification (explicit modeling requirement):
  - Fit a minimal ODE or state-space model linking ligand input → synTF abundance/activity → output modules → survival proxy under disturbances.
  - Extract: EC50 for ligand, Hill coefficient, t1/2 ON/OFF, hysteresis, and noise propagation (report as transfer curves and distributions).
  - Use the model to choose an embryo-compatible ligand dosing schedule that achieves a bounded protective pulse without sustained reprogramming.

2.3 Ex vivo embryo culture validation (predictive control):
  - Inject engineered hPSCs into host blastocysts; apply ligand pulse schedule predicted from 2.2 (not DMOG).
  - Add DMOG only as a controlled disturbance arm to show buffering.
  - Validate that measured embryo-level outputs match model predictions within pre-specified tolerance (e.g., ±20% on synTF reporter AUC; ±25% on apoptosis reduction).

Step 3 — Hardened containment: dual-layer safety + simplified lineage restriction with empirical ROC curves
3.1 Layer 1 (constitutive failsafe; orthogonal drug):
  - Introduce an independent suicide switch activated by a second drug distinct from GCV (e.g., inducible caspase-9 with AP1903/rimiducid), driven by a constitutive promoter active in all hPSC derivatives.
  - Purpose: absolute shutdown if unexpected widespread human contribution occurs.

3.2 Layer 2 (GCV/TK-based lineage containment; simplified and empirically validated):
  - Replace complex multi-input CRISPR logic with **a small panel of promoters/enhancers** selected for:
    (i) cross-species conservation of regulatory logic,
    (ii) early activation in prohibited lineages,
    (iii) low/quantifiable leak in target organ progenitors.
  - Proposed minimal set (to be empirically down-selected):
    - Prohibited ectoderm/CNS sentinel: early neural markers (e.g., SOX1/PAX6 enhancer elements validated in pig embryo context).
    - Prohibited germline sentinel: PGC-associated regulatory elements (e.g., PRDM14/DPPA3-associated enhancer logic—final choice contingent on pig embryo expression conservation).
    - Optional mesendoderm off-target sentinel if baseline shows diversion.
  - Each sentinel drives TK plus a bright reporter (e.g., nuclear fluorescent protein) via 2A, enabling direct leak quantification.

3.3 ROC/leak characterization before in vivo use:
  - In vitro differentiation series into target organ progenitors vs prohibited lineages; compute:
    - Sensitivity: fraction of prohibited-lineage cells that activate sentinel.
    - Specificity: fraction of on-target progenitors that remain sentinel-negative.
    - Determine thresholding strategy (e.g., minimal promoter variants, enhancer truncations) to achieve pre-specified operating point (e.g., >95% sensitivity at <1% leak into on-target progenitors).

3.4 Developmental timing map (detectability vs irreversibility):
  - Using baseline chimera and ex vivo embryo data, map:
    - t_detect: first time prohibited lineage transcripts/reporters become reliably detectable in human donor cells.
    - t_commit: earliest time when prohibited colonization becomes spatially established (migration/settlement markers).
  - Select GCV window(s) such that t_treat ≤ t_commit and after initial niche occupancy for on-target lineage.

Step 4 — In vivo blastocyst complementation with defined ligand and GCV regimens
4.1 Embryo procedure:
  - Inject equal numbers of engineered vs control hPSCs into niche-deficient blastocysts.
  - Apply orthogonal ligand pulse (rapalog or TMP) during pre-transfer embryo culture to induce compatibility governor; washout prior to transfer.
  - Include DMOG-disturbance arm (optional) to demonstrate buffering rather than control.

4.2 GCV pharmacokinetic (PK) and delivery plan (explicit):
  - Route comparison pilot: maternal systemic (IV/SC) vs direct fetal/neonatal (if ethically/technically allowed).
  - Quantify placental transfer and fetal exposure:
    - Serial sampling: maternal plasma, amniotic fluid (where feasible), fetal plasma/tissue at defined timepoints.
    - LC–MS/MS quantification of GCV.
  - Define dosing by target fetal exposure above TK EC50 window while below toxicity thresholds (guided by sentinel reporter dynamics and fetal safety endpoints).
  - Use **pulsed dosing** aligned to t_detect–t_commit map to reduce selection pressure for silencing.

4.3 Anti-escape/silencing monitoring:
  - Link TK to reporter (2A) for direct expression tracking.
  - Longitudinal ddPCR:
    - Cassette copy number/integrity in recovered tissues.
    - Quantify enrichment of cassette-negative human cells post-GCV (escape signal).
  - scRNA-seq in selected timepoints to detect transcriptional silencing signatures and lineage escape.

Step 5 — Endpoints, controls, and decision gates
5.1 Efficacy endpoints:
  - Early embryo: retention, apoptosis, localization, donor cell cycling fraction.
  - Mid-gestation/neonatal: organ-specific human contribution (ddPCR; species-resolved scRNA-seq; IHC).
  - Function: target-organ assays (e.g., glucose responsiveness for pancreatic tissue; kidney filtration markers), attributing function to human cells where possible.

5.2 Safety endpoints:
  - Whole-body mapping of human cells with emphasis on CNS and gonads.
  - Teratoma/lesion surveillance.
  - Confirm that sentinel TK+GCV reduces prohibited lineage frequency without depleting on-target progenitors.
  - Failsafe validation: ability to ablate all human cells via iCasp9 if triggered.

5.3 Controls:
  - No ligand/no GCV; ligand only; GCV only; ligand+GCV.
  - Governor dead mutants (no dimerization / destabilized synTF); output-module-only without feedback.
  - TK sentinel inactive mutant; iCasp9 inactive mutant.
  - Host-only and sham injection.

5.4 Statistical plan:
  - Power calculations for early retention and neonatal organ chimerism fraction.
  - Mixed-effects models (litter/surrogate as random effects).
  - Pre-registered exclusion criteria; blinded quantification of tissue sections and scRNA-seq label assignment.

Decision gates (go/no-go):
  - Gate A: Governor transfer function meets targets (tON, pulse width, CV, bounded output) and improves survival under disturbance in vitro.
  - Gate B: Ex vivo embryo culture shows improved retention with no increase in prohibited lineage markers.
  - Gate C: Sentinel ROC curves meet >95% sensitivity/<1% leak operating point.
  - Gate D: PK demonstrates controllable fetal GCV exposure and tolerability; escape monitoring indicates <5% cassette-loss enrichment post-treatment in pilot.
Feasibility: 1) Addressing the DMOG-sensor confound (reviewer point i): The revised governor does not attempt DMOG specificity. Instead, it uses a truly orthogonal inducer (rapalog or TMP) with well-defined pharmacology and receptor specificity in mammalian systems. DMOG is repositioned strictly as a disturbance to be buffered, aligning the design with the reality that DMOG broadly inhibits 2-OG dioxygenases and is heavily confounded by embryo microenvironment variables.

2) Implementable kinetics and low-noise operation (reviewer point ii): The governor is now explicitly parameterized as a two-loop controller with measurable ON/OFF half-times, pulse width, and cell-to-cell variability targets. The plan includes system identification (transfer function extraction) and a minimal predictive model validated first in vitro and then in ex vivo embryo culture. This directly de-risks claims of amplitude clamping by converting them into quantified, testable design specifications.

3) Containment logic de-risking (reviewer point iii & v): The containment strategy is simplified away from fragile multiplex CRISPR logic toward (a) a constitutive orthogonal failsafe (e.g., iCasp9) and (b) a small set of empirically validated lineage sentinels whose leakiness is quantified via ROC curves in both target and prohibited differentiation contexts. The proposal explicitly maps when prohibited lineages become detectable versus when colonization becomes hard to reverse, and schedules GCV pulses accordingly to address early migratory escape.

4) Concrete GCV pharmacology and fetal safety (reviewer point iv): The revised plan includes a PK program (route comparison, LC–MS/MS quantification, placental transfer assessment) and ties dosing schedules to reporter-verified TK activation and developmental timing. Pulsed dosing is chosen to reduce continuous selective pressure that would otherwise favor TK silencing/escape.

5) Escape/silencing surveillance: Reporter-linked TK expression, ddPCR cassette integrity, and scRNA-seq-based detection of silencing states provide multiple orthogonal readouts to detect and quantify escape. The inclusion of a constitutive failsafe provides a backstop even if TK modules partially fail.

6) Alignment to empirical foundations (assets): The buffering objective is grounded in evidence that αKG-dependent dioxygenases link metabolism to chromatin state and differentiation kinetics in primed hPSCs and that succinate/DMOG-like dioxygenase inhibition can derail differentiation/epigenetic homeostasis (Asset 1). The chimera/blastocyst complementation setting and its key bottlenecks (peri-implantation attrition; low contribution) are aligned with the interspecies chimera literature (Assets 2–3). The suicide-gene approach is grounded in validated TK/prodrug ablation in PSC contexts and emphasizes selective ablation design and pharmacologic considerations (Asset 4), now extended with a separate orthogonal failsafe to satisfy reviewer safety expectations.
final_critique:
The proposal is technically ambitious and substantially improves on common fragilities in chimera-control concepts by introducing (i) true input orthogonality and (ii) explicit dynamical specifications plus system identification. However, key scientific risks remain under-specified at the level needed for high confidence: (1) The choice of governor outputs (redox/anoikis protection, anaplerosis, αKG buffering, CRISPRi of HIF targets) is plausible but not yet tied to a minimal, causal set of embryo-validated failure modes with clearly ranked contributions; without a prioritized causal graph, the controller may stabilize survival at the cost of altered lineage bias or increased competitive fitness outside the target niche. (2) The two-loop controller is described conceptually but lacks concrete molecular implementations with expected parameter ranges (e.g., promoter strengths, degron half-lives in hPSC derivatives, feedback gain limits) and does not address developmental-stage–dependent silencing of safe-harbor transgenes in vivo, which can break both governor and containment. (3) Cross-species conservation of proposed sentinel regulatory elements (SOX1/PAX6, PRDM14/DPPA3 logic) is a major unresolved dependency; enhancer logic frequently diverges across species and developmental context, and ROC curves in vitro may not predict in vivo activation timing in pig embryos (risk: late activation after migration/settlement). (4) The GCV/TK containment plan is strengthened by PK mapping, but the feasibility of achieving a fetal exposure window that is simultaneously effective, non-toxic, and temporally precise—especially across variable gestational pharmacokinetics—remains uncertain; selection for TK silencing/escape may still be substantial, and the stated <5% cassette-loss enrichment threshold lacks justification relative to acceptable residual prohibited contribution. (5) The plan includes ddPCR/scRNA-seq monitoring, but it does not specify quantitative acceptance criteria for CNS/germline “zero tolerance” (limits of detection, sampling burden, anatomical coverage) nor how those detection limits translate into decision gates.

Overall, the engineering plan is well-resolved and testable, and the logical move to orthogonal control is strong; the main deductions stem from (a) insufficiently constrained biological target selection for the governor, (b) heavy reliance on cross-species enhancer conservation for containment timing, and (c) incomplete quantitative safety acceptance criteria tied to detection power and embryo pharmacology variability.

original_chain: Leucine-rich repeat -> Sequence space -> Leucine-rich repeat -> RNA display -> E. coli -> Chorismate mutase
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that chorismate mutase (CM) catalysis can be made *ligand-switchable* by embedding a minimally active CM core within a leucine-rich repeat (LRR) mechanical clamp whose conformational ensemble is biased by a *separable, engineered binding event* (not the CM substrate itself). Specifically, we will engineer a high-specificity chorismate-analog binding pocket at the CM–LRR junction (or within the LRR inner concave face) that binds a nonreactive trigger ligand with target Kd 0.1–5 µM and koff 0.01–0.2 s−1 (residence time 5–100 s). Ligand binding will stabilize a “closed/active” clamp state that compresses and geometrically preorganizes the CM active site (electrostatic compression + loop positioning) while keeping the basal state “open/inactive.” This architecture overcomes reviewer-identified limitations by (i) decoupling switching from substrate turnover (thus avoiding reliance on weak CM–chorismate binding), (ii) selecting directly for *ligand-dependent* conformational gating using a quantitatively controlled protease-accessibility readout with explicit counter-selections against unfolded/constitutively open states, and (iii) adding a late-round, activity-proximal chemical capture that requires CM turnover to prevent drift toward mere protease susceptibility. Mechanistically, LRR repeat curvature/rigidity and inter-repeat packing encode a tunable mechanical transfer function: sequence variants that optimize clamp stiffness and hinge positioning will exhibit the largest ligand-driven ΔΔG between inactive and active ensembles, thereby coupling the engineered binding energy to catalysis rather than to nonspecific unfolding.
Plan: Step 0 — Define the engineered trigger (separable from catalysis)
0.1 Trigger ligand choice: Use a nonreactive chorismate analog (e.g., 4-fluorochorismate or a dicarboxylate cyclohexadienyl analog lacking the rearrangeable enolpyruvyl ether geometry) or a designed small molecule mimicking chorismate’s two carboxylates but chemically inert to the Claisen rearrangement. Selection ligand is distinct from chorismate used in kinetic assays.
0.2 Binding pocket engineering site: Build a junctional pocket between (a) CM N-terminal helix/loop region that can tolerate mutation without abolishing fold and (b) the first 1–2 LRR repeats on the concave face. Design pocket to present a paired cationic motif (Arg/Lys) for the two carboxylates, plus an H-bond donor/acceptor network for the ring hydroxyl/ether positions; avoid placing catalytic CM residues in the pocket to maintain separability.
0.3 Quantitative design targets: Aim for Kd 0.1–5 µM at 25–37°C; kon ≥ 10^4 M−1s−1; koff 0.01–0.2 s−1. These kinetics match the time window of protease challenge (seconds–minutes) while allowing reversible switching.
0.4 Pilot validation: Express 10–20 rational designs (no library yet) as soluble proteins in E. coli; measure ligand binding by MST or fluorescence anisotropy using a fluorescently tagged analog (or competition vs labeled probe). Advance only variants meeting the kinetic window.

Step 1 — CM–LRR switch scaffold architecture (minimally active CM core + clamp)
1.1 CM core: Use a truncated/attenuated CM (e.g., remove stabilizing helices or introduce a small set of activity-reducing mutations) that retains fold but exhibits ≤1–5% wild-type catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) and cannot rescue a CM-knockout strain.
1.2 LRR clamp: 5–8 repeats with consensus hydrophobic core positions fixed to preserve fold; inter-repeat interface and solvent-exposed concave-face residues diversified to tune curvature/rigidity. Include defined hinge elements: a short glycine/serine-rich linker (5–10 aa) and a second, stiffer linker option (EAAAK repeats) to bracket mechanical regimes.
1.3 Mechanical coupling geometry: Position the LRR concave face to contact a CM loop/helix adjacent to the active-site cleft so that clamp closure can reposition this structural element by ~1–3 Å (enough to alter preorganization). Generate two fusion topologies (N-terminal vs C-terminal LRR) in parallel to avoid dead-end geometry.

Step 2 — Protease-gated RNA display with explicit positive/negative selections
2.1 Display format: Use an RNA display system maintaining genotype–phenotype linkage (mRNA–protein fusion). Include N- and C-terminal epitope/affinity tags (e.g., N-term FLAG, C-term His6) so intact fusions can be captured and unfolded/truncated products excluded.
2.2 Cleavage-site placement (conformation gate): Insert a single, unique protease cleavage motif into a loop engineered to be buried in the ligand-free open state and exposed only in the ligand-bound closed state. Two orthogonal gates will be tested:
  • TEV protease site (ENLYFQ\G) engineered into a CM-adjacent loop that becomes solvent-accessible upon clamp closure.
  • HRV 3C protease site (LEVLFQ\GP) as an alternative to reduce sequence-context artifacts.
Placement will be guided by (i) AlphaFold/Rosetta models of open vs closed states and (ii) accessibility prediction (SASA change) with a target ΔSASA ≥ 25–40 Å^2 between states.
2.3 Protease regime compatible with fusions: Perform cleavage at 4–10°C (to reduce nonspecific unfolding) for 5–20 min with low protease:substrate ratio titrated so that ligand-free cleavage is <5% and ligand-bound cleavage is 20–60% in pilot constructs.
2.4 Positive selection (ligand-dependent cleavage): Incubate translated fusion library with trigger ligand (at 1–10× Kd target range), then add protease under calibrated conditions. Capture cleaved products by exposing a hidden tag upon cleavage (e.g., N-terminal tag masked by an inhibitory peptide released by proteolysis) OR by designing cleavage to remove a steric block enabling affinity capture. Enrich only cleaved-and-tag-intact products.
2.5 Negative selection 1 (ligand-independent openness): Run an identical protease treatment *without ligand* and deplete any sequences that cleave (>baseline) by discarding cleaved fraction or explicitly capturing and removing cleaved products.
2.6 Negative selection 2 (unfolded/protease-hyperaccessible): Before the protease step, pass fusions through an intact-tag capture requiring both N- and C-terminal tags (dual affinity). This removes truncated, aggregated, or prematurely terminated products. After protease, require retention of a distal structural tag (e.g., a small folded domain such as GB1) to bias toward folded constructs.
2.7 Negative selection 3 (aggregation-prone constructs): Include a mild solubility partition step (e.g., centrifugation/filtration) and only propagate sequences remaining in the soluble fraction.
2.8 Iteration schedule: Rounds 1–3 emphasize stringent negative selections (no-ligand cleavage depletion + intact-tag capture). Rounds 4–6 progressively lower ligand concentration (e.g., 10 µM → 1 µM → 0.1 µM) while keeping protease constant to select for improved coupling and binding kinetics.

Step 3 — Add an activity-proximal in vitro filter in later rounds (prevents drift)
3.1 CM turnover-coupled chemical capture: Introduce a product-capture step that requires formation of prephenate. Implement a reaction condition where prephenate is rapidly derivatized by an added trapping reagent to generate a biotinylated (or affinity-handle) adduct; only variants producing product above a threshold generate captureable signal. (Operationally: perform short CM reaction, quench into derivatization mix, capture via streptavidin; recover linked RNA from captured complexes.)
3.2 Dual-objective selection: In rounds 5–8, require both (i) ligand-dependent protease gating and (ii) product-dependent capture. This enforces that the “open→closed” transition is catalytically productive, not merely exposing a loop.

Step 4 — Benchmark LRR curvature/rigidity tuning before scaling library size
4.1 Pilot panel: Construct 20–30 variants sampling the intended randomization positions (including extremes: predicted high-curvature/low-curvature, high-rigidity/low-rigidity).
4.2 Structural/mechanical assays in the fused context:
  • FRET reporter: Place donor/acceptor labels (or fluorescent proteins) at defined CM and distal LRR sites; measure ligand-dependent distance changes and baseline conformational heterogeneity.
  • Limited proteolysis mapping (no ligand vs ligand) to confirm designed burial/exposure behavior independent of selection.
  • SAXS (or SEC-MALS + SAXS subset) for global compaction changes upon ligand.
Criteria to proceed: at least 30% of pilot variants show ligand-dependent FRET shift and proteolysis pattern consistent with gating, and ≥70% express soluble in E. coli.

Step 5 — E. coli functional validation and mechanistic characterization
5.1 In vivo rescue (orthogonal validation): Transform enriched variants into CM-deficient E. coli. Measure growth rescue in minimal media with graded aromatic amino acid supplementation. Confirm that the trigger ligand modulates growth only if it is cell-permeable; otherwise use permeabilized assays or rely on in vitro switching for ligand dependence and in vivo for basal activity.
5.2 Enzyme kinetics: Purify top 10–20 variants; quantify kcat, KM, and ligand-dependent activation factor (kcat/KM with ligand ÷ without ligand). Target activation ≥5–20× while maintaining measurable basal stability.
5.3 Mechanism mapping: HDX-MS or differential scanning fluorimetry + limited proteolysis to identify regions stabilized by ligand. Map sequence motifs in LRR inter-repeat interfaces that correlate with (i) FRET-derived compaction, (ii) protease gating ratio, and (iii) catalytic activation.
5.4 Second-generation library: Focus randomization on motifs/positions statistically associated with high coupling (e.g., specific inter-repeat salt bridges or aromatic packing at predicted hinge repeats).
Feasibility: Addressing trigger realism (reviewer point i): The refined design no longer assumes substrate-driven switching. The trigger is a *nonreactive chorismate analog* bound in an engineered pocket with explicit kinetic targets (Kd 0.1–5 µM; koff 0.01–0.2 s−1), making conformational switching controllable on the timescale of selection. This separates binding energy used for allostery from catalytic turnover and avoids failure modes where a weak CM core cannot bind chorismate strongly enough to gate states.

Protease gate specificity (reviewer point ii): The proposal now specifies proteases (TEV and HRV 3C), cleavage motifs, placement criteria (ΔSASA target), temperature/time windows, and—critically—dual-tag intact-capture and multiple negative selections to prevent enrichment of unfolded, aggregation-prone, or constitutively open variants. Using two orthogonal proteases reduces sequence-context artifacts where a single motif might be cleaved due to local sequence effects unrelated to conformation.

LRR library engineering and benchmarking (reviewer point iii): Rather than relying solely on elastic network modeling, we will empirically benchmark that the chosen LRR randomization positions tune curvature/rigidity *in the fused construct* using a pilot set and direct readouts (FRET distance shifts, ligand-dependent limited proteolysis patterns, and SAXS/SEC-MALS compaction). Proceeding to large libraries is gated by predefined success criteria (solubility + measurable ligand-dependent conformational change).

Preventing selection drift away from catalysis (reviewer point iv): Early rounds use conformational gating for enrichment efficiency, but later rounds add a turnover-dependent chemical capture step requiring product formation. This introduces an activity-proximal constraint so the population cannot win solely by becoming protease-sensitive. Final confirmation is performed via in vitro kinetics and E. coli rescue, aligning selection outputs with true CM throughput.

Why this is a credible advantage (tempered claim): The approach is expected (not guaranteed) to outperform static scaffold embedding because it explicitly selects for *dynamic coupling* (ligand→mechanics→active-site preorganization) while filtering out trivial protease susceptibility and enforcing catalytic function in later rounds. This directly operationalizes the sequence-space exploration and repeat-protein modularity principles (LRR tunability) under an RNA display workflow optimized for conformational switching rather than binding alone, and ends with stringent E. coli functional validation.
final_critique: This is a technically sophisticated and largely coherent proposal that addresses prior reviewer criticisms with concrete design constraints, quantitative kinetic targets, and layered selection logic. Engineering resolution is high: protease choice, cleavage placement criteria, ligand kinetic windows, and selection stringency are well specified. The logical chain from ligand binding → LRR mechanics → CM active-site preorganization is mechanistically plausible and supported by known properties of repeat-protein elasticity and CM catalysis. Minor weaknesses remain: (i) the feasibility of a clean, high-yield prephenate derivatization compatible with RNA display recovery is nontrivial and under-specified; (ii) the assumption that protease accessibility can be cleanly inverted (buried→exposed upon closure) across a large library may reduce selection efficiency; and (iii) cell permeability and off-target effects of the trigger ligand are deferred rather than solved. These are execution risks rather than conceptual flaws.

original_chain: Cholangiopathies -> Primary sclerosing cholangitis -> Biliary epithelial cell -> Fibrosis -> Senescence-associated secretory phenotype -> Cholangiocarcinoma -> Primary sclerosing cholangitis
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: In primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), cholangiocyte senescence is not merely a bystander state but a mechanically reinforced, bile-acid–patterned program in which hydrophobic bile acids and inflammatory cues drive a persistent DNA-damage/NF-κB axis that locks biliary epithelial cells into a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). This SASP (IL-6/IL-8, TGF-β–activating factors, MMPs, and EV cargo) instructs portal fibroblasts/stellate cells to adopt a pro-fibrotic state and simultaneously creates a pro-oncogenic niche that accelerates cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) initiation. We hypothesize that selectively eliminating or silencing senescent cholangiocytes will decouple fibrosis from carcinogenic niche formation. Methodological adaptation: we will engineer a bile-duct–tropic, cholangiocyte-selective senolytic/senomorphic delivery system by structurally adapting lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) with (i) an apical bile-acid–mimetic corona to exploit cholangiocyte bile-acid transport/uptake routes (ASBT/OSTα-OSTβ–linked trafficking) and (ii) a senescence-activated RNA switch (p16INK4a- and/or p21-responsive miRNA logic gate) controlling translation of either a senolytic payload (e.g., BCL-XL degraders via PROTAC-encoding mRNA or siRNA against BCL2L1) or a senomorphic payload (IKKβ/NF-κB pathway suppression). This dual adaptation overcomes the key limitation of standard systemic senolytics—off-target toxicity (platelets, immune cells) and poor ductal specificity—by requiring BOTH cholangiocyte entry and senescence-state–specific gene-regulatory context for activity, thereby reducing fibrosis-driving SASP and lowering CCA-promoting inflammation.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Establish a PSC-relevant in vitro tri-culture platform: human iPSC-derived or primary human cholangiocyte organoids grown in a microfluidic bile-duct-on-chip with controlled bile-acid gradients (hydrophobic vs hydrophilic; UDCA as comparator), co-cultured with portal fibroblasts/hepatic stellate cells and myeloid cells (mast cells/macrophages) to reflect PSC inflammatory-fibrotic crosstalk.
1.2 Induce and phenotype cholangiocyte senescence using PSC-relevant stressors (hydrophobic bile acids, cholestatic shear stress, inflammatory cytokines/LPS). Quantify senescence (p16INK4a, p21, SA-β-gal, γH2AX foci) and SASP (multiplex cytokines, proteomics, EV profiling) alongside fibroblast activation readouts (COL1A1, ACTA2, LOXL2, TGF-β signaling reporters).
1.3 Create a matched ex vivo human dataset from PSC explants/biopsies: spatial transcriptomics + multiplex immunofluorescence to map senescent cholangiocytes, SASP factor gradients, mast cell density, and fibrotic architecture; define targetable uptake transporters and senescence miRNA signatures for switch design.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 LNP bile-duct tropism adaptation: redesign standard ionizable LNPs by decorating the surface with a bile-acid–mimetic amphiphile (e.g., cholic/chenodeoxycholic acid analog tethered to PEG-lipid at controlled mol% and linker length) to bias partitioning into bile and promote cholangiocyte uptake via bile-acid transport-associated endocytosis. Iteratively tune physicochemical parameters (pKa, size 60–120 nm, PEG shedding kinetics) to maximize cholangiocyte organoid uptake under bile flow while minimizing hepatocyte/Kupffer uptake.
2.2 Senescence-activated RNA switch adaptation: incorporate untranslated-region (UTR) logic gates and miRNA target sites to enforce state specificity. Example design: (i) 5' UTR containing an uORF arrangement that requires high p16INK4a/p21-associated RNA-binding protein context for efficient scanning, plus (ii) 3' UTR miRNA sites that are active in non-senescent cholangiocytes/other liver cells (to suppress translation there) but lost in senescent cholangiocytes per Step 1.3 profiling, yielding ON-target expression in senescent cholangiocytes only.
2.3 Payload modules:
- Senolytic module: siRNA (or mRNA) targeting BCL2L1 (BCL-XL) and/or pAI-based dual knockdown (BCL2L1 + MCL1 partial) optimized to avoid hepatocyte apoptosis; alternatively encode a short-lived degrader strategy (mRNA encoding an E3-recruiting peptide/degrader) constrained by the senescence switch.
- Senomorphic module: siRNA/mRNA targeting IKKβ or RELA to suppress NF-κB-driven SASP without killing the cell; compare to senolytic outcomes to determine which better reduces fibroblast activation and oncogenic signaling.
2.4 In-chip functional testing: deliver adapted LNPs through the bile channel (apical) versus vascular channel (basolateral) to quantify route dependence; measure (i) selective uptake in cholangiocytes, (ii) switch fidelity (reporter translation only in senescent cells), (iii) SASP suppression, (iv) fibroblast activation reversal, and (v) epithelial integrity/bile transport function.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 In vivo validation in complementary PSC/cholangiopathy models (e.g., Mdr2-/- for sclerosing cholangitis-like fibrosis; DDC diet model; and a carcinogenesis-permissive model combining chronic cholestasis with oncogenic insult). Administer LNPs via routes designed to access bile ducts (systemic vs retrograde biliary infusion in a subset) and quantify biodistribution (IVIS/LC-MS lipid tracing), cholangiocyte targeting (flow cytometry of EPCAM+/KRT19+ cells), and switch-restricted expression.
3.2 Endpoints: fibrosis (Sirius Red, hydroxyproline, collagen crosslinking/LOX activity), ductular reaction and cholangiocyte senescence burden (p16/p21, γH2AX), SASP suppression (tissue cytokines, spatial proteomics), immune remodeling (mast cell activation, macrophage polarization), and early neoplastic changes (biliary dysplasia markers, Ki-67, DNA damage, oncogenic pathway activation).
3.3 Comparative controls: (i) standard LNP without bile-acid corona, (ii) bile-acid corona without senescence switch, (iii) free small-molecule senolytic (e.g., navitoclax-like) to benchmark off-target toxicity, and (iv) UDCA/FXR agonist arms as clinically relevant comparators.
3.4 Mechanistic proof: demonstrate that therapeutic benefit is mediated by SASP reduction and fibroblast deactivation using causal perturbations (add-back of recombinant SASP factors/EVs; conditioned media transfer; fibroblast TGF-β receptor blockade). Use single-cell RNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics to confirm collapse of the senescence-SASP-fibrosis-CCA signaling axis.
3.5 Safety: platelet counts and apoptosis markers (to address BCL-XL toxicity risk), liver enzymes, bile duct injury markers, and off-target gene expression in hepatocytes/immune compartments; establish therapeutic window and dosing schedule.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: PSC features chronic cholangiocyte injury with fibrosis and elevated CCA risk; cholangiocyte senescence and SASP are implicated in sustaining inflammation and remodeling, while bile-acid signaling profoundly shapes cholangiocyte stress responses. LNPs and RNA payloads are clinically validated modalities, and senescence markers (p16/p21) provide actionable state discrimination. Asset 1 supports bile-acid receptor/transport biology and therapeutic modulation (UDCA/FXR/VDR) as central to cholangiocyte injury and fibrosis; Asset 2 supports immune-fibrotic mediators targeting biliary epithelial cells; Asset 3 supports the mechanistic link between cholangiocyte SASP, fibrosis, and PSC-associated CCA.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Standard systemic senolytics fail due to non-specific exposure and toxicity. By adapting (a) LNP surface chemistry to mimic bile-acid interactions/trafficking for ductal tropism and (b) RNA regulatory architecture to require a senescence-specific intracellular context, the approach aligns with bioengineering principles of multi-layer targeting (anatomical + cellular state). The chip-based bile-duct microphysiological system provides a controllable, mechanistically informative bridge between organoids and animal models.
3. Comparative Advantage: The dual-gated design (ductal targeting + senescence switch) is expected to outperform: (i) conventional LNPs (improved cholangiocyte delivery), (ii) ungated senescence payloads (reduced off-target cytotoxicity), and (iii) small-molecule senolytics (superior safety window and programmable senomorphic vs senolytic control). Mechanistically, it interrupts a feed-forward loop (senescence → SASP → fibroblast activation/inflammation → more cholangiocyte stress) and reduces pro-tumorigenic niche signaling, addressing both fibrosis and CCA risk rather than only cholestasis symptoms.
final_critique: This is an exceptionally ambitious and technically sophisticated proposal that demonstrates deep command of PSC biology, senescence mechanisms, and RNA/LNP bioengineering. The central hypothesis—that cholangiocyte senescence constitutes an active, bile-acid–patterned, mechanically reinforced program driving both fibrosis and a pro-oncogenic niche—is logically coherent and well aligned with current literature. The dual-gated targeting strategy (ductal tropism plus senescence-state–restricted translation) is conceptually elegant and directly addresses known failures of systemic senolytics. Strengths include the microfluidic bile-duct-on-chip platform, the comparative senolytic versus senomorphic arms, and the explicit causal tests (add-back, conditioned media, spatial multi-omics). Score deductions are driven by feasibility risk rather than conceptual weakness: (i) the senescence-activated RNA switch relies on multiple layers of post-transcriptional regulation (uORFs, RBP context, miRNA loss) that are individually plausible but unproven in combination in cholangiocytes; (ii) bile-acid–decorated LNP ductal specificity in vivo, especially via systemic delivery, remains speculative and may be confounded by hepatocyte and enterohepatic uptake; and (iii) the proposal slightly overextends by attempting to solve fibrosis, inflammation, and CCA initiation within a single funding scope without a clearly prioritized primary endpoint. These issues temper, but do not undermine, the proposal’s overall scientific merit.

original_chain: 3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine -> Pluripotent stem cell -> Mitochondria-targeted antioxidant -> Self-renewal -> Expansion -> Ectopic expression
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Transient, feedback-controlled buffering of mitochondrial oxidant burden during single-cell cloning and the first ~2 weeks of clonal expansion will increase pluripotent stem cell (PSC) self-renewal and genomic stability by suppressing ROS-triggered mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening events that initiate ATM→p53 signaling and replication-associated DNA damage, while preserving physiologic ROS transients required for stemness programs. Mechanistically, the refined approach resolves key limitations of static antioxidant exposure by (i) using pre-specified mitochondria-targeted antioxidants with characterized uptake and toxicity in PSCs, (ii) regulating a mitochondrial redox ‘permissive corridor’ using a multi-sensor state estimate (mitochondrial H2O2/thiol redox + mitochondrial superoxide + pH/ΔΨm controls + probe-expression normalization) to avoid controlling reporter artifacts, and (iii) causally linking benefit to the mPTP→ATM/p53 axis via genetic/pharmacologic mPTP and pathway perturbations that should abolish (or markedly attenuate) the advantage of closed-loop microdosing. To disentangle redox conditioning from insertion-site selection, clonal ‘ectopic expression’ will be implemented through a predictable landing-pad strategy (AAVS1/CLYBL RMCE or Bxb1/ΦC31) rather than relying on nominal single-copy lentiviral integration. Finally, stress-resilience phenotyping in differentiated hepatic progeny (including DDC challenge) will be normalized to matched differentiation state and cell composition (hepatocyte maturity metrics and endothelial support), ensuring observed resilience reflects mitochondrial programming rather than altered maturation.
Plan: Step 0 — Select concrete mitochondria-targeted antioxidants and quantify PSC pharmacodynamics/toxicity (mandatory pre-specification).
0.1 Antioxidant 1 (chain-breaking lipid/peroxyl buffering): MitoTEMPO (triphenylphosphonium-conjugated piperidine nitroxide), chosen for rapid mitochondrial accumulation via ΔΨm-driven TPP+ uptake and superoxide-scavenging/nitroxide redox cycling.
0.2 Antioxidant 2 (H2O2 detox support): Mitoquinone (MitoQ; TPP+-ubiquinone), chosen for ETC-reduced ubiquinol cycling to buffer oxidative load primarily at/near inner membrane and attenuate lipid peroxidation.
0.3 Generate dose–response and time–response curves in the chosen PSC line under single-cell cloning conditions (ROCK inhibitor only for plating):
  - Doses: 0, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500 nM and 1, 2 µM.
  - Exposure modes: constant (24–72 h), and pulsed (e.g., 2–5 min pulses every 30–60 min for 24 h) to estimate actuation-to-effect kinetics.
  - Readouts: acute toxicity (Annexin V/PI at 6, 24, 48 h), proliferation (EdU), colony-forming efficiency (CFE), ΔΨm (TMRM), and mitochondrial ROS (mitoSOX) and H2O2/thiol redox (mito-roGFP2-Orp1 ratio).
0.4 Fit a simple pharmacodynamic model for each antioxidant in PSCs: actuation delay (τdelay; pulse start to reporter response), response time constant (τresp; approach to steady ratio), washout time (τwash), and saturation/inflection points. These parameters will define controller sampling rate, maximum pulse duration, and hard safety limits.

Step 1 — Engineer a robust mitochondrial redox sensing/normalization stack (avoid controlling artifacts).
1.1 Create a dual safe-harbor reporter line using targeted integration (CRISPR-assisted) into AAVS1 (or CLYBL) with single-copy donor:
  - Cassette A: mito-roGFP2-Orp1 (H2O2/thiol redox-sensitive) driven by a moderate constitutive promoter (e.g., EF1α short) to reduce overexpression burden.
  - Cassette B: mito-SypHer or mito-pHluorin (mitochondrial matrix pH) OR a pH-insensitive control roGFP variant; plus an optional constitutive mitochondrial reference fluor (mito-mCherry) for expression/segmentation normalization.
  - Rationale: mito-roGFP2-Orp1 can be pH-sensitive and expression-dependent; adding pH control + expression normalization supports a corrected redox state estimate.
1.2 Calibrate sensors:
  - Oxidized and reduced endpoints for roGFP ratio: diamide vs DTT (or H2O2 vs DTT) while recording mito-pH and ΔΨm to quantify confounding.
  - Establish correction model: corrected_redox = f(roGFP_ratio, mito_pH, mito_reference_intensity, photobleaching factor).
1.3 Add orthogonal mitochondrial ROS readouts for validation (not for control actuation):
  - mitoSOX (superoxide; short-term endpoint imaging/flow at defined times).
  - Optional: genetically encoded mito-HyPer7 (H2O2) in a subset to cross-check roGFP-Orp1 trends.
1.4 Define the “permissive redox corridor” using corrected_redox during cloning and early expansion:
  - Screen corridor setpoints against primary outcomes: CFE, OCT4/SOX2/NANOG maintenance, γH2AX burden, and minimal apoptosis.
  - Output: numerical setpoint band (e.g., corrected_redox ratio range) with acceptable variance; setpoint may be phase-specific (first 24 h post-plating vs days 2–10).

Step 2 — Implement closed-loop microdosing with explicit controller parameters and safety bounds.
2.1 Culture hardware:
  - Low-shear microperfusion plate or microfluidic chamber compatible with PSC colonies; continuous medium renewal with minimal bubble formation.
  - Actuation: two reservoirs (base medium; antioxidant-spiked medium) with fast switching valve.
2.2 Measurement and control timing (based on Step 0 fits):
  - Sampling interval: 2–5 min for ratiometric roGFP imaging (sufficient to capture mitochondrial redox dynamics without excessive phototoxicity).
  - Actuation delay compensation: include τdelay (measured) in controller (Smith predictor or simple dead-time compensation).
  - Pulse constraints: max pulse duration 5 min; minimum inter-pulse interval 10 min; daily cumulative exposure cap derived from toxicity curves (e.g., not exceeding a ‘no-effect’ AUC).
  - Saturation limits: hard concentration ceilings (e.g., MitoTEMPO ≤250 nM; MitoQ ≤200 nM unless PSC-specific curves support otherwise).
2.3 Control law:
  - Use a PI controller on corrected_redox error with anti-windup and rate limiting.
  - Secondary constraint: maintain cytosolic redox within bounds using a cytosolic roGFP (optional) so that mitochondrial correction does not globally flatten ROS signaling.
  - Decision logic: only actuate if corrected_redox exceeds upper corridor threshold for >2 consecutive samples (to avoid chasing noise).
2.4 Conditions (head-to-head during single-cell cloning + days 1–14 expansion):
  - A: no antioxidant.
  - B: constant antioxidant at ‘best tolerated’ dose (from Step 0).
  - C: open-loop pulsed antioxidant (fixed schedule matched to closed-loop mean AUC).
  - D: closed-loop feedback pulsed antioxidant (primary adaptation).
  - Repeat for both antioxidants (MitoTEMPO and MitoQ) to test whether mechanism depends on ROS species/chemistry.

Step 3 — Causal mechanistic falsification: isolate mPTP→ATM/p53 from parallel ROS pathways.
3.1 Test necessity of mPTP signaling for closed-loop benefit:
  - Genetic: PPIF (Cyclophilin D) knockdown/knockout in PSCs (inducible CRISPRi preferred to avoid clonal artifacts), confirmed by qPCR/Western.
  - Pharmacologic: use a more specific mPTP-modulating regimen than generic cyclosporin A where possible (e.g., sanglifehrin A as alternative CypD inhibitor; careful PSC toxicity titration).
  - Predicted falsification: if closed-loop benefit is mediated primarily via mPTP suppression, then in PPIF-inhibited cells the incremental gains of closed-loop vs no antioxidant/open-loop should shrink substantially for CFE, γH2AX, p-ATM, and p53 activation.
3.2 Map downstream ATM/p53 axis:
  - Perturbations: ATM inhibitor (e.g., KU-55933) and p53 modulation (e.g., transient p53 inhibitor pifithrin-α, with strict monitoring for genomic instability risks).
  - Readouts: p-ATM, p53 stabilization, p21 induction, replication stress markers (RPA phosphorylation), cell-cycle distribution.
  - Logic: show that redox control reduces ATM/p53 activation; show epistasis—if ATM/p53 blocked, closed-loop advantage on proliferation may diminish but genomic stability endpoints may diverge, clarifying mechanism.
3.3 Exclude alternative explanations:
  - NRF2 pathway: quantify NRF2 nuclear localization and transcriptional targets; optional NRF2 knockdown to test whether benefits require NRF2 activation rather than mPTP suppression.
  - Mitophagy: assess Parkin recruitment/mitophagy flux (e.g., mt-Keima) to determine whether closed-loop primarily shifts mitochondrial turnover.

Step 4 — Predictable ectopic expression without insertion-site confounding (landing pad/RMCE).
4.1 Establish a defined landing pad in AAVS1 or CLYBL:
  - Install a Bxb1 or ΦC31 attP landing pad with a promoter/insulator architecture designed for stable expression and minimal silencing (e.g., CAG promoter + cHS4/UCOE element as appropriate).
  - Validate single-copy insertion by ddPCR and junction PCR.
4.2 Perform RMCE/serine-integrase insertion of payloads during cloning across conditions A–D:
  - Payload 1: neutral reporter (e.g., GFP) for expression variance.
  - Payload 2: inducible NRF2 or PGC-1α (as originally intended) but inserted at the same locus to isolate redox-conditioning effects from position effects.
4.3 Readouts:
  - Integration efficiency (RMCE success rate per plated single cell), expression distribution (flow), silencing over passages, and scRNA-seq variance.
  - Confirm that closed-loop primarily improves cloning/expansion and genomic stability rather than selecting for rare integration-favorable states.

Step 5 — Core outcomes: self-renewal, genomic stability, and controller validation.
5.1 Self-renewal/expansion: CFE, colony size distribution, growth curves to passage 10, EdU/Ki67, apoptosis.
5.2 Pluripotency: OCT4/SOX2/NANOG (flow/IF), tri-lineage in vitro differentiation; optional teratoma only if required.
5.3 Genomic stability: karyotype + SNP-array/low-pass WGS CNV profiling; targeted sequencing of recurrent culture adaptation loci.
5.4 Controller validation endpoints:
  - Demonstrate corrected_redox is maintained in corridor in D vs C with lower variance.
  - Show orthogonal biology tracks: reduced mitoSOX spikes, stabilized ΔΨm, reduced mPTP opening events (calcein–cobalt quenching) without chronic ROS suppression (cytosolic redox not flattened).

Step 6 — Differentiation and DDC stress module with normalization for maturity and composition (avoid confounding).
6.1 Differentiate matched clones (from A–D) into hepatic lineages using the same protocol and batch, with strict maturity matching:
  - Maturity metrics: ALB, HNF4A, CYP3A4 expression; functional outputs (albumin secretion, urea).
  - Cell composition controls: quantify hepatocyte-like cells vs non-parenchymal populations by flow/scRNA-seq; gate/normalize analyses to matched compositions.
6.2 Option A (cleaner mitochondrial stress test, less lineage-specific): include a non-DDC mitochondrial challenge in parallel (e.g., antimycin A/rotenone low-dose pulse or menadione) to generalize stress-resilience beyond hepatic porphyrin biology.
6.3 DDC module (retained but controlled):
  - Apply DDC to hepatic cultures/assembloids under matched maturity/composition; include iEC co-culture where relevant to mirror assembloid logic and enable fibronectin/integrin maturation axis assessment.
  - Readouts: mitochondrial injury (ΔΨm, OCR drop), ROS (mitoSOX), inflammatory/fibrotic signaling in co-culture (LOX, SPP1), and hepatic function (albumin, urea).
  - Normalization: report DDC responses per ALB+ cell (or per HNF4A+ nucleus) and adjust using mixed-effects models controlling for maturity metrics.

Step 7 — Statistics and rigor.
7.1 Primary endpoints (pre-registered): CFE at day 10–14, γH2AX burden per cell, CNV rate, and RMCE integration efficiency.
7.2 Mixed-effects models: random effects for clone and batch; fixed effects for condition (A–D), antioxidant identity, and mPTP/ATM/p53 perturbations.
7.3 Power: based on pilot constant vs pulsed effect sizes; ensure sufficient clones per condition to estimate variance in genomic stability and expression dispersion.
Feasibility: 1) Antioxidant/controller specificity and safety: Pre-specifying MitoTEMPO and MitoQ resolves the ‘generic TPP+ antioxidant’ ambiguity and enables PSC-specific pharmacodynamic fitting (τdelay/τresp/τwash) and dose–toxicity boundaries. This directly informs sampling rate, actuation limits, cumulative exposure caps, and anti-windup logic so the controller operates within empirically safe margins.

2) Closed-loop regulates biology, not reporter artifacts: mito-roGFP2-Orp1 is ratiometric but can still be influenced by pH and expression. Adding mitochondrial pH reporting (mito-SypHer/mito-pHluorin), ΔΨm monitoring, and expression/segmentation normalization (mito-mCherry) produces a corrected_redox state estimate used for control. Orthogonal validation with mitoSOX (superoxide) demonstrates that corridor maintenance corresponds to reduced mitochondrial ROS excursions rather than optical or probe-expression artifacts.

3) Mechanistic falsification of the mPTP→ATM/p53 claim: Necessity tests using PPIF/CypD suppression and mPTP inhibitors, combined with ATM and p53 pathway modulation, create an epistasis framework. If closed-loop benefit is truly mediated by preventing ROS-triggered mPTP events that activate ATM/p53, then disabling mPTP signaling should markedly reduce the incremental advantage of feedback dosing on DNA damage signaling and cloning efficiency. Parallel measurement of NRF2 targets and mitophagy flux prevents over-attribution by identifying (or excluding) alternative dominant pathways.

4) Predictable ectopic expression without insertion-site selection: Replacing nominal ‘single-copy lentiviral’ cloning with a defined landing pad and RMCE/serine-integrase insertion yields locus-controlled, reproducible expression. This disentangles redox-conditioning effects from positional effects and avoids oxidative-stress-driven selection for rare integration configurations, addressing a central reviewer concern.

5) DDC stress test interpreted without differentiation confounds: DDC is retained for relevance to cholestatic/mitochondrial hepatic injury models, but outcomes will be normalized to maturity (ALB/HNF4A/CYP metrics) and cell composition (flow/scRNA-seq), with matched iEC support where used. Including a parallel non-DDC mitochondrial stressor provides a lineage-agnostic cross-check, ensuring that any observed ‘stress resilience’ reflects conserved mitochondrial programming from cloning-phase redox control rather than altered hepatic maturation trajectories.
final_critique: This is an exceptionally detailed and technically mature proposal with strong systems-engineering depth and a rare level of mechanistic rigor. Engineering resolution is very high: pharmacodynamic pre-fitting, sensor correction models, explicit controller laws, safety bounds, and dead-time compensation are all well specified and realistic in PSC systems. Logical consistency is strong, with a coherent causal chain from mitochondrial ROS buffering to mPTP suppression, ATM/p53 attenuation, improved cloning, and downstream stability; the inclusion of necessity tests (PPIF inhibition) appropriately guards against post hoc storytelling. Minor logical risk remains in the assumption that mPTP opening is the dominant ROS-to-ATM conduit during early PSC cloning, as replication-stress–induced nuclear ROS or nucleotide pool oxidation could contribute independently. Evidence grounding is solid and remains within bioengineering/biomedicine; however, the DDC module, while carefully normalized, is somewhat peripheral to the core cloning-phase hypothesis and slightly dilutes conceptual focus. Rationale quality is high: the proposal directly addresses a well-known bottleneck (oxidative stress during single-cell PSC cloning and expansion) with a structurally novel solution rather than a parameter tweak of antioxidant dosing.

original_chain: Polycomb group gene -> Psc -> Temperature sensitive mutation -> Polycomb group gene -> Wnt signaling pathway -> Noncanonical Wnt signaling -> Stem cell
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that transient, spatially confined disruption of Polycomb silencing complex integrity—achieved via a bioengineered temperature-sensitive (ts) destabilization module coupled to Psc-dependent chromatin binding—selectively unleashes noncanonical Wnt/PCP signaling in stem cells, thereby triggering epithelial extrusion independently of canonical Wnt self-renewal signals. The core mechanism is that Polycomb-mediated chromatin compaction buffers stem cells against PCP-driven cytoskeletal remodeling; acute thermal destabilization of Psc-containing complexes lowers the epigenetic energy barrier at PCP effector loci, biasing Wnt pathway output toward noncanonical signaling without globally derepressing β-catenin–dependent transcription.
Plan: Step 1: System setup and genetic engineering.
Engineer a Drosophila follicle stem cell (FSC) model in which endogenous Psc is fused to a rationally designed temperature-sensitive degron (tsDG-Psc) whose folding stability is tuned in silico to partially unfold at 29–30 °C but remain stable at 18–22 °C. This degron will be calibrated to disrupt PRC1 chromatin association without complete protein loss. Introduce fluorescent reporters for canonical Wnt (TCF/LEF-GFP) and noncanonical PCP signaling (JNK/ROCK activity biosensors).

Step 2: Methodological adaptation—spatiotemporal thermogenetic control of Polycomb function.
Integrate a microfabricated infrared laser–based thermal modulation platform with live ovarian explant culture, enabling subcellular, reversible heating (±1 °C precision) of individual FSCs. This adaptation overcomes the classical limitation of temperature-sensitive mutations, which lack spatial resolution. By locally elevating temperature, induce acute, reversible dissociation of tsDG-Psc from chromatin in single stem cells while neighboring cells remain unaffected.

Step 3: Validation and mechanistic analysis.
Quantify chromatin accessibility changes at PCP and Wnt target loci using single-cell ATAC-seq immediately following thermal pulses. Correlate these epigenetic changes with real-time imaging of epithelial extrusion, cytoskeletal polarization, and clone competition dynamics. Causality will be tested by genetically blocking PCP components (e.g., Frizzled/Dishevelled) while maintaining canonical Wnt activity, determining whether extrusion requires the noncanonical branch specifically unleashed by Polycomb destabilization.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Prior evidence demonstrates that loss of Psc/Su(z)2 induces epithelial extrusion via noncanonical Wnt signaling, and that temperature-sensitive Polycomb mutations destabilize chromatin binding.
